docs.title: beamfeat.expression
docs.text:
Expression DAG with structural hashing, lazy evaluation, and unit propagation.

The central abstraction is Node, an immutable description of how to compute a feature from input columns. Nodes are descriptions, not data: they carry no arrays. Evaluation happens on demand via Evaluator, which caches intermediate results keyed by structural hash so that shared subexpressions are computed once.

Two design decisions distinguish this from eager approaches:

  1. Structural hashing. Two nodes describing the same computation compare equal and hash identically, regardless of construction order. This makes deduplication automatic and lets the evaluator cache across a whole search.

  2. Fail-fast unit checking. When dimensional metadata is supplied, unit compatibility is validated at construction time, before any array work. Invalid combinations raise UnitError immediately.

Numerical failures during evaluation are never silent. Nodes that overflow, produce non-finite values, or degenerate to near-zero variance are recorded in an EvaluationLog with a reason, and excluded from results. The log is part of the public API so users can audit what was rejected.

Many nodes can also be evaluated away from the evaluator, in another thread or process: Evaluator.plan_batch() gathers what they need into an EvaluationBatch, EvaluationBatch.run() computes them with the same checks as Evaluator.evaluate(), and Evaluator.commit_batch() records its rejections in the log.

docs.title: Evaluator
docs.text:
Lazily evaluates nodes against a data matrix, caching by structural key.

The cache is bounded and least-recently-used. Leaf columns are pinned and never evicted, since they are the base of every expression. Intermediate results are evicted under memory pressure and recomputed if needed again.

Numerical failures are recorded in log and reported by returning None from evaluate(); they never propagate as exceptions and are never silently discarded. Each failing node is recorded once: evaluating it again returns None without a second record, until the log is cleared.

Returned arrays are read-only, since they are shared with the cache.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Mapping[str, ndarray] | ndarray

Mapping of column name to 1-D array, or a 2-D array with columns supplied separately.

required columns Sequence[str] | None

Column names, required when data is a 2-D array.

None units Mapping[str, Any] | None

Optional mapping of column name to pint quantity.

None dtype dtype | type

Working dtype. Defaults to float64; float32 halves memory but makes overflow substantially more likely in deep expressions.

float64 cache_size int

Maximum number of non-leaf arrays held in the cache.

4096 variance_tol float | None

Relative constancy threshold. A column is treated as constant when its variance falls below variance_tol times the square of its mean magnitude, so the verdict does not depend on the unit the caller happened to choose. Defaults to 1e-24 for float64, a spread twelve orders below the magnitude: the cut is_constant() applies, so the columns the search drops as constant are the ones the fit-time warning names. Narrower dtypes default to 1e-10, as their rounding noise alone exceeds that cut.

None

docs.title: plan_batch(nodes)
docs.text:
Prepare distinct nodes for evaluation away from this evaluator.

Evaluating a wide round of candidates one evaluate() call at a time spends most of its time on per-column overhead, and cannot be shared between workers because the cache and the log are mutable. A batch splits the work in three: this method resolves each node's operands (and settles leaves, cached values and known failures) here; EvaluationBatch.run() then applies the search-time filters and computes the values with no access to the evaluator, so batches can run concurrently; commit_batch() records the rejections, in node order.

Operands are resolved through evaluate(), so a failing operand is recorded when the batch is planned, ahead of the batch's own rejections. Computed values are not cached: a round's candidates are each evaluated once, and the few kept are cached when next evaluated.

Expressions to evaluate. Each should appear once.

required

docs.text:
Description of a feature-construction operator.

Attributes:

Identifier used in node keys and formulas, e.g. "log".

arity int

Number of operands (1 for transforms, 2 for combinations).

fn Callable[..., ndarray]

Callable applied to numpy arrays.

Callable producing a display string from operand names.

unit_fn Callable[..., Any] | None

Callable propagating units. Receives operand units and returns the result unit. Raises to signal dimensional invalidity. If None, the operator is treated as unit-preserving for arity 1 and unit-requiring-match for arity 2.

domain Callable[..., bool] | None

Optional predicate on input arrays; returning False marks the operand as outside the operator's valid domain.

commutative bool

Whether operand order is irrelevant. Commutative operands are sorted during hashing so x+y and y+x unify.

redundant Callable[..., bool] | None

Optional predicate on input arrays; returning True marks the result as identical to its operand (abs of a column that is never negative), so it is excluded as a duplicate.

constant_grid Callable[[ndarray], list[ndarray]] | None

Set for a parametric operator, one that carries a constant fitted to the data, such as the a in exp(a*x). fn, formula, domain and redundant then receive the constant as a last argument after the operand (formula as a float). Called with the operand's values, it returns the coarse grid of constants the fit starts from, as one or more increasing segments; a fit whose best grid point is a segment's end is rejected as running into a bound. Parametric operators must be unary, and are applied through transform() with const.

Names of the registered parametric operators, in sorted order.

These are the operators BeamSearch accepts in fitted_ops.

docs.title: pole_margins(x)
docs.text:
Smallest distances a fitted pole keeps below and above the values x.

Each is the larger of POLE_MARGIN_SPREADS times the spread of the POLE_MARGIN_ROWS most extreme values at that end (all of them, for fewer rows) and POLE_MARGIN_FLOOR times the range of x.

The shifts of inv_shift and log_shift place their pole at least this far from the values. pow has its pole at 0 when its exponent is negative, so a negative exponent is fitted only when the smallest value exceeds the margin below; otherwise only exponents from 0.1 to 4 are.

docs.title: transform(op, child, const=None)
docs.text:
Apply a unary operator to a node.

Unit compatibility is checked here, before any numerical work.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default op str

Registered unary operator name.

required child Node

Operand node.

required const float | None

The constant of a parametric operator (see OperatorSpec.constant_grid), such as the a of exp_scaled, exp(a*x). Required for a parametric operator and refused for any other. A constant that reduces the operator to a plain one gives the plain node: pow with 2 is square, inv_shift with 0 is reciprocal.

None

Returns:

Type Description Node

A new Node one level deeper than child.

Raises:

Type Description NodeError

If op is unknown or has the wrong arity, if const is missing, not finite, or given to an operator without one, or if the constant makes the result constant.

UnitError

If the operation is dimensionally invalid.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Every result here comes from a script in the repository and its archived run, or from the paper (TMLR 2026), which describes release 0.4.2. Results with a random component carry Monte Carlo error, so read them at the precision given.

Most archived runs were made before 0.6.0 and 0.7.0 changed the search's defaults: constants inside expressions (fitted_ops), magnitude slots and the guard against quotients whose denominator comes near zero. Unless a result says otherwise, it was measured without them. Rerun at the current defaults, the formula-recovery suites recover the same formulas, the end-to-end calibration gives the same result, and Friedman #1 rises from 0.745 to 0.770. To reproduce an archived run exactly, install the release that made it (Installation). Where the paper's own numbers have moved, Reading the paper today says why.

docs.title: High-dimensional data
docs.text:
benchmarks/additional_experiments/ compares beamfeat with ridge, random forest and LightGBM on the raw columns of nine datasets with 81 to 4,088 columns, over five random 75/25 splits each (the paper's Table 6). Mean held-out R², the best in each row in bold:

dataset columns ridge random forest LightGBM beamfeat formulas tecator 100 0.957 0.717 0.756 0.991 3.6 geomusic 117 0.805 0.739 0.739 0.805 9.6 communities 100 0.650 0.638 0.632 0.641 11.6 riboflavin 4,088 0.579 0.436 0.493 0.544 † 17.4 eyedata 200 0.479 0.340 0.031 0.416 34.0 superconduct 81 0.725 0.884 0.884 0.731 16.2 blogfeedback 280 0.379 0.548 0.535 0.415 18.4 ct_slices 384 0.852 0.981 0.981 0.687 † 14.0 ujiindoorloc 520 0.949 0.995 0.993 0.812 † 20.0

"formulas" is the mean number of terms in beamfeat's fitted equation.

† Corrected since the paper: rerun with 0.5.0, beamfeat's mean R² is 0.340 on riboflavin, 0.664 on ct_slices and 0.816 on ujiindoorloc.

beamfeat leads where the target is a compact algebraic function of a few columns, as on tecator, where ratios of absorbance channels are features that threshold splits cannot build. It trails where the signal is spread thinly over hundreds of columns, as on ct_slices, ujiindoorloc and blogfeedback: ridge keeps every column and shrinks it, while a screen with an error-rate guarantee has little power to reject the null for features that each carry a small fraction of the signal, and leaves them out. With the corrections, it is ahead of both tree ensembles on four of the nine datasets: tecator, geomusic, communities and eyedata. fdr_controlled_ was true on all 90 beamfeat fits of the archived run (the estimator and the transformer).

On tecator, a random forest given the formulas in place of the raw channels goes from 0.739 to 0.992, on three of the five splits. On the small datasets, tree models given the formulas do worse than ridge, which is why ridge is the default.

Tecator also shows what a single fit does not. In the paper's stability study, thirty fits with different seeds on one partition (the design of stability_report(..., resample="seeds")) held R² at 0.989, with a standard deviation of 0.004, while selecting 79 distinct features, counting value-equivalent ones once, none of them in more than 8 of the 30 fits. Adjacent channels correlate at 0.99988, so many band pairs are near-substitutes and each fit picks among them. One equation or one of many shows how to run the same check on other data.

docs.title: Tecator and the methods of chemometrics
docs.text:
On spectra, chemometrics uses partial least squares (PLS) on preprocessed spectra, and kernel methods on derivative spectra are among the most accurate. benchmarks/tecator_chemometrics/, added after the paper, fits them on the same five splits, each tuned by cross-validation on its training rows:

method held-out R² RMSE (% fat) size SVR, second-derivative spectra 0.998 0.66 all 100 channels kernel ridge, second-derivative spectra 0.997 0.79 all 100 channels Gaussian process, second-derivative spectra 0.996 0.85 all 100 channels beamfeat, second-derivative spectra 0.996 0.89 1 to 3 terms beamfeat 0.990 1.44 3 to 4 terms PLS, after the standard normal variate 0.971 2.33 5 to 18 components PLS, derivative spectra 0.958 2.89 12 to 20 components ridge 0.957 2.94 all 100 channels PLS 0.951 3.14 17 to 18 components

beamfeat's error is about half that of PLS, the field's standard (46 to 62% of it). The kernel methods' error is about half of beamfeat's (46 to 59%), from all 100 channels and with no formula to read; on derivative spectra beamfeat comes close to them with one to three terms. Its formulas are mostly ratios of differences between nearby channels, and the channels it uses most lie at 920 to 946 nm, near the band around 930 nm usually attributed to fat.

The data's documentation defines a split of its own: samples 1 to 172 to train, 173 to 215 to test, and two extrapolation sets, E1 (eight samples with more fat than any training sample) and E2 (more protein). beamfeat is averaged over five seeds:

method test RMSE E1 RMSE E2 RMSE kernel ridge, SVR, Gaussian process (derivative) 0.54 to 0.55 2.69 to 3.76 0.41 to 0.44 beamfeat, second-derivative spectra 0.64 1.74 0.43 beamfeat 1.33 1.99 1.17 PLS (raw, SNV, derivative) and ridge 1.98 to 2.20 8.08 to 8.47 1.66 to 2.19

beamfeat had the lowest errors on E1, though eight samples make that a hint rather than a measurement. Releases before 0.7.0 missed E1 badly (RMSE 47.7) with a ratio whose denominator came near zero beyond the training samples; the search now rules such ratios out, and predict warns when a new row takes a feature far beyond its training range (New rows beyond the training data).

docs.title: Selection calibration
docs.text:
• Selector level (benchmarks/selector_calibration.py). On Gaussian designs over 100 trials, Benjamini–Hochberg realised 0.046 ± 0.008, 0.084 ± 0.012 and 0.161 ± 0.016 at nominal 0.05/0.10/0.20, against its ceiling of q·m₀/m = 0.040/0.080/0.160; Benjamini–Yekutieli, stricter by a harmonic factor, realised 0.013 ± 0.005, 0.018 ± 0.005 and 0.046 ± 0.008. Power was 1.00 throughout. The bounds are computed from the design, and the script stops with an error if a bound falls below a realised rate's whole 95% interval.
  • End to end (benchmarks/calibration_study.py). Search plus holdout selection at nominal FDR 0.10, on 500 rows and 6 input columns of which 2 carry signal through their product, with noise at 5% of the signal's standard deviation: no false discovery in 200 replicates, a 95% upper bound of 0.015 on the true rate, power 1.000 and no fallbacks. Over 60 global-null replicates, nothing was selected.
  • Pure noise (benchmarks/selector_calibration.py). Over 100 global-null pipelines, where every selection is false by construction, BH returned features in 7 trials and BY in 1: false discovery proportions of 0.07 and 0.01, both under the nominal 0.10. On the same 100 datasets, BY's one selecting trial is among BH's seven, and an exact paired test rejects equal rates (p = 0.03). BY, valid under any dependence, is the default. The paper, on 0.4.2, reports 6 and 1.

The guarantees page states what each procedure guarantees and under which assumptions.

docs.title: Formula recovery
docs.text:
• Known formulas (benchmarks/run_benchmarks.py, one 70/30 split per dataset). Mean R² over the ten core-suite problems, and recovery of the generating columns over the ten synthetic problems that declare them; the two sets differ by one dataset each. beamfeat: mean R² 0.9989, fits of about 0.2 s, 10/10 recovered. autofeat: 0.9970, about 12 s, 8/10. LightGBM 0.9798, ridge 0.8442. On the purely linear problem, where feature construction has nothing to add, ridge ties beamfeat.
  • Feynman equations (benchmarks/feynman_panel.py, 12 physics laws, 0.1% noise). In the archived run, 10/12 solved at the SRBench criterion, and the exact symbolic form on 8 of the 9 laws that have one. The misses are limits of the search space: a depth-3 rational, a literal constant, depth-4 nesting and the Gaussian's exponential. With constants inside expressions (fitted_ops, the default since 0.6.0), the last two are found, the Gaussian as exp(-0.5*(x0)^2) and relativistic velocity addition as (x0 + x1)/((x0*x1) + 1): the exact form on 10 of the 11 laws that have one within the depth, still 10/12 solved, at 0.4 s per equation.
  • Heavy-tailed noise (Student t(2), infinite variance). The exact formula is recovered, at R² 0.956 against LightGBM's 0.866. The permutation test is distribution-free, so heavy tails do not affect its validity.

docs.title: Distractors and false features
docs.text:
Signal hidden among ten distractor columns. A false feature is a returned formula touching only irrelevant ones; the count is over the five stress datasets that declare which columns their formula uses. Regenerate with python benchmarks/make_figures.py, which writes six other figures alongside it.

  • Stress suite (signal among ten distractor columns). beamfeat's false-feature rate, the share of returned formulas that touch only irrelevant columns, is 0.000 at noise levels from 5% to 50% of the signal scale and at n as small as 120, with recovery and the guarantee intact throughout. autofeat recovers the formula as often but returns distractor-only features on 2 of the 5 scoreable datasets. The comparison is a count rather than a mean, since a mean over five datasets carries a standard error of about 0.15, and autofeat's output varies between processes.
  • OpenFE on the same suite (its features feeding LightGBM, after shimming a removed scikit-learn parameter): a false-feature rate of 0.000 as well, but 0/5 formulas recovered and a lower R² on all five. It optimises a tree model's lift rather than equations.
  • Selection alone (knockpy on the raw columns, with the modified-FDR offset, the only satisfiable configuration at these dimensionalities): 0/15 formulas recovered, a core-suite R² at the ridge level (0.845), and distractor-only features on 2 of the 5 scoreable stress datasets. The difference from beamfeat is the construction step and the holdout.

docs.title: Real datasets
docs.text: Seven datasets, numeric columns only. beamfeat leads on mpg (0.864 against LightGBM's 0.853) and on tips, where gradient boosting overfits below ridge while the FDR screen keeps beamfeat at the top. It ties ridge on diamonds with one interpretable feature. It trails LightGBM on penguins, breast cancer and California housing (0.700 against 0.843, where the signal is spatial), and ridge on diabetes (0.376), where there is no nonlinear structure to find and beamfeat adds none.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Piecewise targets suit trees: on a threshold problem, LightGBM reaches 0.998 and beamfeat 0.808. When a tree model beats beamfeat by a wide margin, the signal is likely piecewise rather than algebraic. OpenFE also records 0.998 there, but bit-identically to raw LightGBM and from a feature touching only an irrelevant column, so the result belongs to its tree model.
  • Laws whose parts do not correlate with the target (benchmarks/search_stress/). With centred inputs, the parts of x0*x1*x2, and of x0*x1 among hundreds of columns, do not correlate with the target, so a search without magnitude slots can drop them before it combines them. Over 50 fits per cell, on inputs uniform on (-1, 1), x0*x1*x2 is recovered exactly in every fit with 5 columns but in 0.54, 0.18 and 0.10 of them with 20, 100 and 300, and x0*x1 in 0.32 with 1,000 columns; on shifted inputs the same laws are recovered in every fit. A wider beam does not close the gap. The magnitude slots, on by default for regression, recovered every lost cell but one crowded sum law (0.88), at 1.2 to 1.7 times the fit time, and left the real-data suites and the false-discovery rates essentially unchanged (guide).
  • Friedman #1 (benchmarks/friedman_decomposition.py). Over six draws, a representation oracle reaches 0.960 ± 0.003, a screening-admissible ceiling 0.874 ± 0.006, and the pipeline 0.780 ± 0.013. About 0.086 is lost to what marginal screening cannot see: the centred quadratic term is nearly uncorrelated with the target on its own, so a marginal screen has almost no power to reject its null. The other 0.094 is lost in the search. The guarantees page explains the marginal null.

docs.title: Independent comparison
docs.text:
benchmarks/independent/ holds a 360-fit study (nine datasets, eight methods, five splits, average ranks and a Friedman test) with its harness, pinned environment, data, and a notebook that reproduces the analysis. Mean held-out R²: random forest 0.810, beamfeat 0.803, LightGBM 0.798, OpenFE 0.736, ridge 0.704, autofeat −1.561 and featuretools −2.478. The worst of each method's 45 fits: beamfeat 0.355, autofeat −103.2 and featuretools −57.3; no beamfeat fit fell below zero. beamfeat ran at about 60 times autofeat's speed, and fdr_controlled_ was true on 45 of 45 fits. The featuretools figures come from a harness that filled its non-finite test cells with 0; with the training medians, as the harness now fills them, they read 0.461 and −12.882 (see Reading the paper today).

PROVENANCE.md records what reproduces and what does not. beamfeat's selections reproduce bit-identically, though the fitted model's cross-validated penalty can flip on marginal problems. autofeat sets no random_state and draws its decoy features from the global NumPy generator: six runs on one identical split ranged from +0.952 to −109.8.

docs.title: Relationship to autofeat
docs.text: beamfeat's design began from a code review of autofeat (Horn et al., 2019). It keeps autofeat's central idea, compact symbolic features feeding a linear model, and replaces exhaustive expansion with beam search, noise-threshold selection with FDR-controlled procedures, and upper-pinned dependencies with tested floors. The generate-then-filter design has a direct precedent in tsfresh (Christ et al., 2018), which filters mass-generated time-series features under Benjamini–Yekutieli control; beamfeat applies it to symbolic expressions on tabular columns. Migrating from autofeat maps one API onto the other.

docs.title: Three settings
docs.text: benchmarks/three_settings/ fits the default, parsimony_alpha=0.05, input_test=True and both together on the same data: a noise sweep on y = x0/x1 among unrelated columns, the release comparison's datasets and splits, and the paper's own studies with their own settings. Choosing a setting summarises it. In short, at noise as large as the signal the default printed a median of 9.5 terms, most of them reading an unrelated column, and parsimony_alpha printed the one true term in every fit; on the 12 real datasets the default had the best mean held-out score (0.693, against 0.675 with parsimony_alpha and 0.675 with input_test). At the paper's settings the comparison study's mean R² is 0.803 at the default, 0.784 with parsimony_alpha and 0.803 with input_test, against the paper's 0.803.

docs.title: Release comparison
docs.text:
benchmarks/release_comparison/ runs the same benchmarks, data, splits and seeds through six releases, from 0.4.2, the paper's, to 0.8.0, on one software stack: about 30,000 fits. The paper's release against the current one, at their defaults:

measure 0.4.2 (the paper's) 0.8.0 Feynman panel, fits solved of 60 47 50 search stress laws, exact recovery 0.883 1.000 riders at signal to noise 1 (conditional FDR) 0.736 0.722 7 real datasets, mean held-out score 0.725 0.727 fit time, relative to 0.4.2 1 0.6 peak fit memory, relative to 0.4.2 1 0.2

The report has the releases in between, and measures each option against its release's default.

docs.title: Test suite
docs.text: 1,079 tests at 97% statement coverage, with a 90% floor enforced in CI, including scikit-learn's full estimator-conformance checks.

docs.title: Reading the paper today
docs.text: The paper describes release 0.4.2, archived with its run records at 10.5281/zenodo.23417132. Some of its numbers differ from what current releases give, for three reasons: two bugs, figures from runs made under an earlier release, and speed. The archived records are kept as they were run. Comparisons added since the paper, such as the chemometrics baselines on tecator and the three settings, have folders of their own and change none of the paper's numbers.

docs.title: Two bugs, fixed in 0.5.0
docs.text:
• Comparison harness. The harness filled non-finite test cells of the constructed features with 0, while the training cells got the training median. This understated featuretools, whose ratio features divide by columns that contain zeros. With the training medians on both, featuretools has a mean R² of about 0.461 rather than −2.478 in the independent comparison, a worst fit of −12.882 rather than −57.320, and one fit below zero rather than six. Every other method's row, and every conclusion about beamfeat, is unaffected (PROVENANCE.md).
  • Search. When max_candidates_per_depth bound at depth 1, the first round proposed parents in column order, so from about 258 inputs, pairs among the last columns were never proposed. The first round now proposes the inputs in order of their score, as documented. Three datasets of the high-dimensional study reach the ceiling. Rerun with 0.5.0, beamfeat's mean R² is 0.340 on riboflavin, 0.664 on ct_slices and 0.816 on ujiindoorloc, against 0.544, 0.687 and 0.812 in the paper; the archived riboflavin run was made with an earlier version, and 0.4.4 gives 0.523 there. With the ceiling raised so that every input is proposed, ct_slices and ujiindoorloc give the new results exactly; the old ones depended on which columns came first in the file. beamfeat now leads both tree ensembles on four of the nine datasets rather than five.

docs.title: Figures from runs made under an earlier release
docs.text:
These are not bugs. The method is the one the paper describes, but the release that produced the figure is not the one it names, and the figures move little:

  • riboflavin, in the high-dimensional study, as noted under the search bug above.
  • The independent comparison. Its archived run predates 0.3.0, when the internal ridge penalty was fixed at alpha=1. Rerun with 0.4.2, beamfeat_ridge matches 37 of the 45 archived fits to four decimals, with a mean of 0.8034 against 0.8033 (PROVENANCE.md).
  • threshold_step, in run_benchmarks.py's robustness results, which were regenerated under 0.3.0. The paper quotes beamfeat's held-out R² there as 0.808, and 0.4.2 with the script's own settings gives 0.843. It reproduces the script's other 19 datasets and the Feynman panel exactly, and the five other robustness datasets to within 0.003 with the same number of terms (release comparison). That check cannot tell whether the release or the software environment causes the difference.

docs.title: Speed and memory
docs.text: Later releases are faster, so the paper's timings and memory figures describe 0.4.2. 0.5.0 runs the high-dimensional study 2 to 28 times faster per dataset without changing any feature, p-value or prediction, and a default fit on 1000 columns and 600 rows that peaked at 2.6 GB of memory peaks at 0.35 GB in 0.5.0. Over the eight timing items of the release comparison, 0.8.0 fits in about 0.6 of 0.4.2's time with a fifth of its memory. The changelog lists every change.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: Notable changes to beamfeat. Format follows Keep a Changelog; versions follow Semantic Versioning.

Every fit at the defaults is 0.7.0's: on all 1,430 items of benchmarks/release_comparison/ the printed formulas and held-out scores are the same. What is new: screen_equation, three options that are off by default (residual_slots, max_search_rows, and the sign_shift operator with sign), and a note in the printed equation. An option is on by default only where measurement shows it does better than the default it would replace; the residual slots did not.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• residual_slots: places added to the search's final ranking for the first terms of a greedy forward path through its candidates, so that a term much weaker than the leading one is not cut: on x0*x1/x2 + 0.5*log(x3) the default never printed log(x3), and residual_slots=10 printed the exact law in 33 of 60 fits (benchmarks/weak_terms_and_switches/). The path also compares each of its terms with the other transforms of its operand, which a depth may have dropped as near copies (log(x3) beside 1/x3). On its own it adds riders, a term built only from unrelated columns in 19 of 800 calibration-design fits against none, and it left held-out score within 0.005 on 8 of the 11 real regression datasets, raising it on one and lowering it on eyedata (by 0.89, through one split) and California housing (by 0.017). With parsimony_alpha=0.05 beside it the riders go and the weak term prints as often, which is the setting the docs give for a law with a weak term. Off by default; regression only.
  • max_search_rows: the search runs on that many of its rows, drawn at random, and its expressions are then checked on every search row; the screen still runs on every selection row, so its guarantee is unchanged. On 200,000 rows a search on 10,000 of the 100,000 search rows cut the median fit from 110 to 33 seconds. A product carrying 2% of the signal's variance, x4*x5, came out as x4 and x5 terms in every fit, as with the full search, and R² against the signal was 0.002 lower; peak memory fell by a sixth, since the screen and the final fit see every row (benchmarks/search_rows/). Off by default.
  • sign_shift, a fitted operator sign(x + a) (off by default; list it in fitted_ops), and sign, its form at zero (list it in unary_ops): a product with a switch, such as x2*sign(x0 - 0.7), becomes a candidate. On targets that switch at a threshold it printed the switch in 20 of 20 fits and predicted to R² 0.997 to 0.999, against 0.76 to 0.88 for the default and 0.983 to 0.996 for gradient-boosted trees; on the main suite's threshold_step it raised held-out score from 0.841 to 0.999. Elsewhere it changed little, though it lowered the classifier's accuracy on breast_cancer by 0.022.
  • equation() and latex() end with a note when parsimony_alpha=0.05 would print fewer terms, such as parsimony_alpha=0.05 prints 1, selection-row R^2 0.935 against 0.939, and equations() marks that line a. The count is the one a fit with that level gives: the check runs on the same path, from the same random stream, apart from the fit, which it leaves unchanged.
  • screen_equation: tests the equation another tool reports (PySR, Operon, gplearn, PySINDy and the like) term by term on rows the tool never saw, with the permutation test beamfeat's fits use under the Benjamini-Yekutieli or Benjamini-Hochberg step-up, and with input_test=True each variable inside each term of more than one. It returns an EquationScreen with the terms, their p-values and what was kept. It reads the equation with sympy, from the display extra.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • certify_test="conditional" after the forward step without parsimony_alpha, deprecated in 0.7.0, raises a ValueError. Pass parsimony_alpha=0.05, or parsimony=None to re-test the whole screened set. The studies in benchmarks/parsimony_holdout/ that ran the combination reproduce with 0.7.0.

Two changes to fits, under "Changed": magnitude_slots="auto", 10 beam slots for regression, and a guard in the search against quotients whose denominator comes near zero. With magnitude_slots=0 a fit gives 0.6.1's features, p-values and predictions on 1,243 of the release comparison's 1,430 items; the others are fits whose search met such a quotient. Predictions warn when a new row takes a feature far beyond its training range (under "Added"). The code is split into smaller modules, and the conditional re-test after the forward step without parsimony_alpha is deprecated.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • ExtrapolationWarning: predict, transform and the probability methods warn when a new row takes a feature more than one width of its training range beyond that range, and say on how many rows, which features and how far; the predictions are unchanged. feature_ranges_ holds each feature's range on the training rows. A model saved with an earlier release has no ranges and predicts as before, without the check. On tecator's own split it was raised only where a fit missed the high-fat extrapolation set by far, and on no row of the test set.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• magnitude_slots="auto" is the default, where it was 0: 10 beam slots for regression and none for classification, whose labels carry no magnitude. The slots keep candidates whose magnitude tracks the target's, so that the search recovers laws whose parts do not correlate with the target, such as x0*x1*x2 with centred inputs. In benchmarks/release_comparison/, against 0.7.0 with the slots off, they recovered every such stress law (exact recovery 0.40 and 0.55 without them, 1.00 with), moved the held-out score of 10 of 12 real datasets by less than 0.005 (riboflavin fell by 0.011 and eyedata rose by 0.009), added a junk column to two more equations (27 of 40 against 25), and cost 1.19 times the fit time and 1.07 times the memory. The end-to-end calibration gives the result it gave without them.
  • The search rules out a quotient whose denominator comes near zero. A quotient or reciprocal whose denominator comes within the pole margin of zero on the search rows, or crosses it, is excluded as a value outside an operator's domain is. The margin is the one fitted poles keep since 0.6.0: twice the spread of the ten values nearest zero, and at least 1% of the range. Such a denominator can cross zero on a new row a little beyond the training data, where the quotient takes any size and either sign. On tecator's own split, one 0.6.1 fit predicted fat contents from -299% to 507% on the eight high-fat extrapolation samples, and 0.6.1's error there averaged 47.7 over five seeds, against 2.0 with the guard (benchmarks/tecator_chemometrics/). In benchmarks/release_comparison/ the guard changed the fit on 187 of 1,430 items, raised the held-out score on 3 of 12 real datasets (eyedata 0.110 to 0.312, riboflavin 0.506 to 0.527, tips 0.461 to 0.472) and lowered none by more than 0.005, left the riders on the calibration designs and exact recovery on the stress laws and the Feynman panel within two standard errors of 0.6.1's, and cost 5% of the fit time. In the pure-noise pipeline stress Benjamini-Hochberg now selects in 7 of 100 trials, against 6, and Benjamini-Yekutieli in 1. The guard is always on, so a fit that 0.6.1 made with such a quotient is reproduced only by 0.6.1.
  • The largest modules are split into smaller private ones, so that each stage of a fit can be read on its own. estimators.py keeps the three public classes; the fitting machinery they share is in _base.py, with _run_pipeline in named stages (rows, search, screen, choice of terms, final record) instead of one method of 378 lines; the forward step and its chance check are in _forward.py, the equation and LaTeX renderings and the equation list in _rendering.py, and the evaluation of new rows in _prediction.py. The built-in operators are defined in _operators.py, the place to add one. BeamSearch.run runs one method per depth instead of a loop of 264 lines. The public API and its import paths are unchanged. The split itself changed nothing that is fitted or printed: compared field by field on 327 fits across the benchmark datasets and options, its fits, predictions, p-values, equations, LaTeX, verbose output and warnings were those of 0.6.1, and models saved with 0.6.1 load and predict identically. Private helpers imported from beamfeat.estimators by name, such as _chance_p_value, now live in those modules. ARCHITECTURE.md maps the modules and a fit's stages.
  • ruff checks function size in src/: complexity 18 and 60 statements, the largest after the split, so that new code is split rather than grown.
  • The package's keywords, in pyproject.toml, CITATION.cff and .zenodo.json, name what it does (feature construction, multiple testing, Benjamini-Hochberg and Benjamini-Yekutieli, equation discovery, among others), and its classifiers add the operating system, the topics and Typing :: Typed. It stays in beta until 1.0.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
• release_comparison/ includes 0.7.0: its default, with the magnitude slots off, with parsimony_alpha, and with the conditional re-test alone and with parsimony_alpha, timed in a pass of its own beside 0.6.1.
  • three_settings/ fits the default, parsimony_alpha=0.05, input_test=True and both together on the same data: a noise sweep on y = x0/x1 among unrelated columns, the release comparison's datasets and splits, and the paper's own studies with their own settings.
  • tecator_chemometrics/, added after the paper, sets beamfeat beside the methods of chemometrics on tecator: partial least squares on raw, SNV-corrected and derivative spectra, and kernel ridge, SVR and a Gaussian process on derivative spectra, on the paper's random splits and on the split of the data's documentation with its extrapolation sets. beamfeat's error is 46 to 62% of that of PLS and about twice that of the kernel methods; on derivative spectra it is close to them, and on the high-fat extrapolation set its errors were the lowest.
  • selector_calibration.py prints the exact paired test behind the pure-noise comparison of Benjamini-Hochberg and Benjamini-Yekutieli: both fit the same 100 problems, and it tests the trials where only one selected.
  • tecator.csv now carries Tecator's permission note (additional_experiments/data/TECATOR_PERMISSION.txt), which its redistribution requires.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• A "Choosing a setting" page sets the default, for prediction, beside parsimony_alpha=0.05, for a short equation, and input_test=True, for an equation whose every column was tested: what each prints, what it costs and what was measured. The Getting started tutorial ends on the same choice.
  • The user guide is split into four pages (Reading a fit, The printed equation, Search options, Data and prediction), with a quickstart before them and a table that finds the section for each parameter. The site's navigation groups the pages under Get started, User guide, Tutorials and Reference and API, and the changelog is on the site. Links in the text are underlined, and the mechanics behind an option fold away under it.
  • A "Citing beamfeat" page gives the paper, the software archive and, for each option, the statistical method to cite, with BibTeX checked against the publishers' records.
  • Each page of the site has its own title and description, a link preview (Open Graph and Twitter cards) and schema.org data: the software and its paper on the home page, an article on the others.
  • Every example in the quickstart and the guide was run again at 0.7.0, and the outputs that the magnitude slots and the guard changed are updated.

docs.title: Deprecated
docs.text: • certify_test="conditional" after the forward step without parsimony_alpha. On a noisy target the forward step hands the re-test riders it cannot certify, the re-test rejects no null, and the whole screened set is returned: in benchmarks/release_comparison/ 40 terms on diabetes and mpg, and 46 on the calibration designs at signal to noise 1, where the default prints 18 and the same re-test with parsimony_alpha=0.05 1.0 to 1.5. It warns with a FutureWarning and will raise from 0.8. With parsimony_alpha, or with parsimony=None, which re-tests the whole screened set, the conditional re-test is unchanged.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The parsimony_holdout re-test's warnings name the line of fit that raised them, as every other fit-time warning does, rather than a line inside the fit's internals.
  • A formula that divides by a fitted shift prints its divisor in brackets, (a / (1/(b - 2.5))), where it printed (a / 1/(b - 2.5)), which reads as (a/1)/(b - 2.5). Only the text changes; the expression, its values and to_sympy() were right.
  • to_sympy(), latex() and latex_formulas() without sympy raise an ImportError that says to install beamfeat[display], rather than a bare No module named 'sympy'.

Default fits are those of 0.6.0, feature for feature. This release fixes the memory of input_test, adds two options that are off by default (parsimony_alpha and KnockoffSelector(s_method="ci")), and adds a comparison of the releases since the paper's.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• s_method on KnockoffSelector: "equicorrelated" (the default, as before) or "ci", the conditional-independence knockoffs of Liu & Rigollet (2019), which give each column its own s_j = c/(Σ⁻¹)_jj instead of one value set by the smallest eigenvalue. The guarantee is the same. In benchmarks/knockoff_s_method.py (fixed-X, nominal FDR 0.1, 50 trials) on 76 constructed columns, power rose from 0.000 to 0.217 with knockoff+ (realised FDR 0.000 and 0.038) and from 0.073 to 0.596 with offset=0 (0.096 and 0.112); on Gaussian block and factor designs the two were within a few points.
  • parsimony_alpha on BeamFeatTransformer, BeamFeatRegressor and BeamFeatClassifier, a chance check on the forward step (default None, which leaves every fit unchanged). On a noisy target the best of many remaining terms adds more than parsimony_tol to R² by fitting noise, so the step kept riders, 18 terms on average at signal to noise 1 in benchmarks/parsimony_holdout/. With a level, the step also stops at the first term whose gain fails to reject the null that it is no larger than the best gain the remaining terms reach against noise (200 wild-bootstrap draws of the residual, net of the terms already added; Fan & Zhou, 2016). In benchmarks/parsimony_holdout/parsimony_alpha.py (its designs at q = 0.1, 50 replicates per cell), parsimony_alpha=0.05 printed 1.1 terms instead of 18.4 at signal to noise 1 and 3.8 at 3; the conditional false rate fell from 0.70 to 0.05 and from 0.42 to 0.02, power to print the generating term went from 0.89 to 0.88 at 1 (1.00 at 3), and held-out R² rose by 0.007 on average at 1, though 9% of those fits lost more than 0.01. With parsimony_holdout and certify_test="conditional" it ends the re-test's fallback to the screened set (92% of fits at signal to noise 1, under 1% with the check). On real data it costs accuracy: in benchmarks/release_comparison/ (5 splits each) held-out score fell on 8 of 12 real datasets (tips 0.461 to 0.397, diabetes 0.430 to 0.381, riboflavin 0.506 to 0.306) and rose on one, eyedata, where the default's 32 terms overfit 84 training rows. Real targets carry many modest effects, each adding little, so the step stops after one to four terms. It suits a search for a short law, not prediction.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Memory of input_test. The expression evaluation behind it was a nested function that called itself, a reference cycle that kept the intermediates of every evaluation alive until Python's garbage collector happened to run. On California housing (7,224 selection rows, 133 term-column pairs) a fit passed 7 GB without finishing; it now finishes in 80 s using 0.55 GB, with the same terms. The undefined-row pass behind predict had the same cycle, holding its input until collected.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: • release_comparison/ runs the same benchmarks, data, splits and seeds through 0.4.2 (the paper's release), 0.5.0, 0.6.0 and 0.6.1 on one software stack, at their defaults and with the options of 0.6.0 and 0.6.1: about 16,000 fits, with speed and memory. 0.5.0 gives 0.4.2's fits on 1,415 of 1,430 items, 3.2 times faster with a fifth of the memory; 0.6.0 with fitted_ops=() gives 0.5.0's on all 1,430, and 0.6.1's defaults give 0.6.0's. archive_check.py refits 0.4.2 with the paper scripts' own settings: it reproduces the archived Feynman panel and 19 of the 25 run_benchmarks.py datasets exactly.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• The Benchmarks page's "Corrections since the paper" is now "Reading the paper today", with the two bugs, the figures from runs made under an earlier release (riboflavin, the independent comparison and, newly noted, threshold_step: 0.808 in the paper, 0.843 from 0.4.2) and speed kept apart. The old link still leads there.
  • The Benchmarks page and the README link the release comparison.

0.5.1 was prepared but not released; its options are part of this release and listed under "Added". One default changes: the estimators fit constants inside expressions, fitted_ops (under "Changed"). The other new options are off by default (max_inputs=None, certify_test="marginal", magnitude_slots=0, input_test=False), and a fit that leaves them there and passes fitted_ops=() gives the features, p-values and predictions of 0.5.0, to the last bit, except with selector="knockoff", whose fixed-X statistic is fixed (under "Fixed").

The re-test's figures below are from benchmarks/parsimony_holdout/: 48,000 fits of a global null and of y = a*b/c plus noise among 5 or 20 distractors, with and without a column correlated 0.9 with a, at signal-to-noise ratios 1 and 3, 300 and 1,000 rows, 200 replicates per cell, q = 0.1 and 0.2. A printed term counts as false in the conditional sense when it uses any column outside the formula, as a rider such as (a*b/c) * x7 does.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• fitted_ops on BeamSearch, BeamFeatTransformer, BeamFeatRegressor and BeamFeatClassifier (on by default in the three estimators, under "Changed"; BeamSearch defaults to (), which leaves every result unchanged): operators with one constant fitted inside the expression, exp_scaled (exp(a*x)), pow (x^a), inv_shift (1/(x + a)) and log_shift (log(x + a)). At each depth each is fitted to each member of the previous depth's beam and to that depth's beam_width best candidates the redundancy check kept out of the beam (a linear near-duplicate need not stay one under 1/(x + a) or exp(a*x)), and as a factor of a beam member where the depth limit allows, by maximising |corr| with the target on the search rows. A fitted pole keeps a margin from the data, twice the spread of the operand's ten most extreme values and at least 1% of its range: the shifts' grids start at it, and pow fits a negative power, whose pole is at 0, only where the operand stays more than the margin above 0. The constant snaps to a simple value (0, ±1, ±2, ±3, ±1/2, ±3/2, ±1/3, ±1/4) when a likelihood-ratio test at level 0.001 fails to reject the null that it takes that value, never past the margin, and is exact in to_sympy() and latex(). At the end of the search, a kept feature with fitted constants gives way to a near copy with fewer (correlation at redundancy_threshold, and no near copy of another kept feature) when the same test, on the same rows, fails to reject the null that the copy fits the target as well; the simplest such copy is taken. Without that step, a constant fitted on the search rows bends an expression into a near copy of a simple law that outscores the law there, and the equation prints (x0)^(-0.02) for log(x0): at 10% noise, log(x0), sqrt(x0), 1/x0 and x0^2 were printed as themselves in 0, 0, 2 and 2 of 10 fits, and with it in 10, 7, 10 and 8 (10, 9, 10 and 8 with fitted_ops=()). The screen sees fixed expressions, so its guarantee is unchanged. Node.const, Node.n_constants, transform(..., const=...), OperatorSpec.constant_grid, pole_margins, SearchTrace.n_fitted and beamfeat.parametric support it.

  • max_inputs on the same four classes (default None): the most distinct input columns one feature may use, checked before evaluation. An expression of depth d uses at most 2^d columns, so at the default depth a value of 4 or more changes nothing. Measured at max_inputs=3 against 0.5.0, mean held-out R² over 5 splits:

  • gains on wide data with diffuse signal: eyedata 0.416 to 0.488, ct_slices 0.664 to 0.684, riboflavin 0.340 to 0.378;
  • losses: the twelve-law panel loses the gravitational law, which needs four inputs, and diabetes falls from 0.382 to 0.360;

  • one blogfeedback split falls from 0.533 to −2.14, where a three-input product extrapolates far past its training range on one test row.

  • SearchTrace.n_rejected_constraints, the candidates max_inputs ruled out at each depth (0 when it is off).

  • .zenodo.json, so that the Zenodo record of each release links the TMLR paper as the work the software supplements. Zenodo read the title, author and keywords from CITATION.cff but not its preferred-citation, so the records up to 0.5.0 do not mention the paper.

  • certify_test on BeamFeatTransformer, BeamFeatRegressor and BeamFeatClassifier: the test the parsimony_holdout re-test applies. "marginal" re-runs the screen, as before, and so rejects the null of a term that only rides on a true one, x0*x7 when the target depends on x0 alone. "conditional" tests each re-tested term given the others with a Freedman-Lane permutation test: the target and the term are residualised on the other terms and an intercept, the target's residuals are permuted, the statistic is the partial correlation, and the screen's step-up correction is applied at the screen's level. Its null is a zero coefficient in a linear model of the target on the re-tested terms, and its p-values are approximate: exact for a single term, otherwise resting on exchangeable errors of a linear model of the target on the other terms. Regression only; classification raises. At a signal-to-noise ratio of 3 it brought the conditional rate of the printed equation to 0.18 to 0.22, against 0.42 to 0.44 at the defaults and 0.53 to 0.62 with the marginal re-test, and in the fits where it rejected at least one null it printed 1.1 to 1.2 terms at a rate of 0.026 to 0.040 (q = 0.1), with power 0.98 to 0.99. When the re-tested subset is long and its terms nearly reproduce one another the test rejects no null, and the screened set, which carries the marginal guarantee only, is returned: in 87 to 92% of fits at a ratio of 1, where the forward step retains 18 terms on average, and in 18 to 26% at 3.

  • beamfeat.stability: stability_report(estimator, X, y), also exported from beamfeat, makes the paper's stability study (Appendix E) a package feature; by default n_splits=30, test_size=0.25, random_state=0 and n_jobs=1. It refits clones of a regressor, classifier or transformer on random splits. Each split's test part is kept out of every step of its fit and scored once after it, and the clones' seeds are spawned from random_state by SeedSequence, so the report is the same for every n_jobs. The StabilityReport holds:

  • each split's rows, formulas, equation and held-out score;
  • the distinct features and equations, with how often each recurs;
  • a summary that states the ambiguity plainly. On diabetes it reads "30 distinct equations in 30 splits; none recurs", with held-out R² from 0.389 to 0.575.

Two features are one when their values on the rows of X correlate above 0.999 in absolute value, as in the paper, and an equation is the set of its features. The regressor and classifier are scored by their own score. A transformer is scored by a ridge regression (R²) on its features, or by a logistic regression (accuracy) for classification. The paper held one test part fixed and varied only the seed, so its spread is narrower: on diabetes, an R² standard deviation of 0.015 against 0.050 here.

  • resample on stability_report, which picks what varies. "splits", the default and the behaviour above, measures split-to-split variability. "seeds" keeps the first split's partition for every split and varies only the clones' seeds, as the paper's study did, and measures seed-to-seed variability. With the paper's transformer on diabetes it gives an R² standard deviation of 0.008 to 0.019 over five partitions, with 75 to 84 classes, the commonest in 8 to 18 of 30 splits. The paper reports 0.015, 79 and 22 for its own partition. On that partition, its own code with other lists of 30 seeds gives 79 to 88 classes, the commonest in 18 to 23.

  • magnitude_slots on BeamSearch, BeamFeatTransformer, BeamFeatRegressor and BeamFeatClassifier (default 0, which leaves every result unchanged; regression only, and a classifier raises): beam slots for laws whose parts do not correlate with the target, which the score ranks among noise, such as x0 and x1 in x0*x1 or the pairwise products in x0*x1*x2 when the inputs are centred. At every depth but the last, after the beam_width candidates the score keeps, up to that many more are kept, ranked by the absolute correlation of log(1 + |c|/rms(c)) with the same transform of the centred target or of its residuals; one residual is on the best-scoring columns kept so far, at most a quarter as many as the rows, since the residual on every input is empty once they outnumber the rows. When max_candidates_per_depth can bind at the first depth, the inputs are proposed in an order that interleaves that ranking with the score's. Measured at 10 slots on benchmarks/search_stress/, the three-way product on centred inputs went from 0.54, 0.18 and 0.10 to 1.00 with 20, 100 and 300 columns, the centred pair with 1,000 columns from 0.32 to 1.00, and x0*x1 + x2 with 300 columns and 250 search rows from 0.00 to 0.88; no cell got worse. The score is computed on at most 1,000 search rows, evenly spaced. Fits took 1.2 to 1.7 times as long on the stress grid and 1.4 times on the three 10,000-row high-dimensional sets; the main suite's mean held-out score over its 24 regression sets went from 0.8851 to 0.8841 (diabetes and california housing about 0.01 lower) and the high-dimensional study's from 0.647 to 0.649. The ranking uses the search rows only, so the screen sees fixed expressions and its guarantee is unchanged; on four null and two planted designs, 200 paired replicates each, the share of fits with a false discovery moved by at most one in 200. magnitude_scores and SearchTrace.n_magnitude support it.

  • benchmarks/search_stress/: a stress test of the search on x0*x1, x0*x1*x2 and x0*x1 + x2 among distractors, on centred and on positive inputs, with 5 to 1,000 columns, 500 and 2,000 rows, 1% and 10% noise and beams of 50 and 200: 5,700 fits at the defaults, each followed through the search to the stage that lost the law. On positive inputs every law was recovered in every fit. On centred ones with 500 rows, x0*x1*x2 was recovered in 54%, 18% and 10% of fits with 20, 100 and 300 columns, every miss the first depth's beam dropping the pairwise products, and a beam of 200 lifted 54% to 96% and 18% to 26%; a centred pair was never proposed in 68% of fits with 1,000 columns, and x0*x1 + x2 was lost in every fit with 300 columns and 250 search rows, crowded out by sums with x2. A paired null study and a launcher that runs the other suites with new option defaults measure magnitude_slots as well.

  • input_test on BeamFeatTransformer, BeamFeatRegressor and BeamFeatClassifier (default False): after the screen, each column inside each candidate that reads more than one is tested by permuting that column alone and recomputing the screen's statistic, with the screen's step-up correction across every (candidate, column) pair, and a screened term is dropped before parsimony when the test fails to reject the null for one of its columns. It removes riders such as (x0*x1)/(x1 + x8), whose null the screen rejects because x0*x1 carries them. The null for a column is that it is independent of the target and of the candidate's other columns, under which the p-values are exact; a junk column correlated with a real one is not null in that sense, so its null can be rejected and the term kept. A pair stops at its tenth exceedance (Besag & Clifford, 1991). input_report_ lists every pair with its p- and q-value and null_rejected, and equation() counts the terms it dropped. If the test would drop every screened term, the screened set is used with a warning. Measured against the default, 20 seeds of y = x0*x1 plus 25% noise among 10 junk columns, 500 training and 500 test rows: printed equations with a junk column 14 → 1, printed terms with one 23/45 → 1/28, held-out R² 0.9413 → 0.9416 (true formula 0.9425), 0.25 → 2.6 s a fit. With the junk x8 correlated 0.82 with x1: 10 → 3. The physics panel is unchanged at 10/12 solved, 8 exact; with five junk columns appended, equations with one 2 → 0, solved and exact unchanged. On pure-noise targets the screen rejects no null either way. Real data, mean over 5 splits: diabetes R² 0.429 → 0.415 (6.2 → 5.0 terms), breast cancer accuracy 0.969 → 0.969 (24.2 → 13.4 terms). The cost grows with the rows: california housing (15,480 training rows) took 135 s against 2.6 s, R² 0.655 → 0.664 on one split. n_jobs threads share the tests, with the same p-values for every value: on california housing, 77 s with 8 threads against 202 s with one, in a later run on the same machine.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• fitted_ops is on by default in BeamFeatTransformer, BeamFeatRegressor and BeamFeatClassifier: all four operators, DEFAULT_FITTED in beamfeat.search (BeamSearch itself still defaults to none). fitted_ops=() restores the previous default. It is a list of its own: restricting unary_ops leaves it on, so log(x + a) can appear unless fitted_ops=() too. Measured at the new default against fitted_ops=(): the physics panel solves the same 10/12 and gives the exact form of the Gaussian, exp(-0.5*(x0)^2), and of relativistic velocity addition, (x0 + x1)/((x0*x1) + 1), which it previously approximated; the core suite recovers the same 10/10, Friedman #1 rises from 0.745 to 0.765 and the other problems move by at most 0.0004; the robustness suite recovers the same 5/5 with R² lower by at most 0.004; the end-to-end calibration gives no false discovery in 200 replicates (power 1.000) and no selection in 60 global-null replicates, as before; the pure-noise pipeline stress is unchanged (BH 6/100, BY 1/100). On five high-dimensional sets (communities, superconductivity, tecator, eyedata, riboflavin; 3 splits) the mean R² is 0.669 against 0.670, within noise. Fits take about 1.9 times as long on small data and 1.3 times on california housing. The benchmark scripts build their estimators at the defaults; benchmarks/search_stress/with_options.py with BEAMFEAT_OPTIONS='{"fitted_ops": []}' reproduces the archived results, and the Benchmarks page says which results predate the change. The tutorials are re-executed at the new default.
  • fitted_ops fits run in batches: each operator is fitted to all of a depth's parents at once, with the golden-section refinements, the snapping and the rounding run side by side as array operations (fit_constants_many, which fit_constants calls), and the coarse grid is applied to every constant at once. Against the first implementation, prepared for 0.5.1, this halves their cost, from 3.4 to 1.9 times a plain fit's time on 18 fits (five distractor sets, the physics panel and diabetes), whose formulas, screened candidates and predictions are the same to the last bit. The search also counts each subexpression's operators and constants once per ranking instead of once per candidate, which speeds up fits without fitted_ops slightly too.
  • parsimony_holdout is calibrated, and the guarantees page reports the figures in place of the sentence saying it had not been. In the marginal sense, the guarantee's, the printed equation's realised FDR stays far below q under every setting: 0.009 to 0.018 at q = 0.1 and 0.021 to 0.029 at q = 0.2 on the null, and no term built only from distractors printed in the 3,200 planted and proxy fits per setting and level. The re-test adds nothing measurable there: on null data it failed to reject the null for the screen's false discoveries in 20 of 22 fits at q = 0.1, and the fallback to the screened set printed them anyway. In the conditional sense no setting controls the rate: 0.67 to 0.77 under every setting at a signal-to-noise ratio of 1, and at 3, 0.42 to 0.44 at the defaults and 0.53 to 0.62 with the marginal re-test. Power and held-out R² hardly move (R² within 0.0033 of the default, paired).
  • The guide has a section on laws whose parts the score cannot see, with magnitude_slots, and the guarantees page says why the option leaves the guarantee unchanged.
  • The front page, which is also the README and the PyPI description, is shorter and leads with one result, tecator, in a figure that benchmarks/figures/tecator.py draws from the archived run. The measured results, the comparison with autofeat and the corrections to the paper's results move to a new Benchmarks page in the documentation, where the autofeat core-suite mean reads 0.9970, as in the paper, rather than 0.9968 from a superseded run. The tutorials open with an install cell, %pip install -q "beamfeat[all]", so that Run all works in Colab with units, LaTeX and export included, and the first notes which scikit-learn versions show the parameters and fitted attributes in the estimator's summary box.
  • Hypothesis-testing wording throughout the documentation, docstrings and messages. Each candidate has its own null hypothesis, and a test rejects it or fails to reject it, where the text used to say that a feature passes, fails, survives or is kept. The guarantees page opens with these definitions, and the guide has a section on input_test. Messages change with the wording: an empty model's equation() and latex() end in (no feature selected) rather than (no feature passed selection), equations() on it says that the screen rejected no null, and NoDiscoveriesWarning, NoDiscoveriesError and DegenerateFitWarning say what the screen rejected. The migration guide no longer says that beamfeat fits no constants inside expressions.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The fixed-X knockoff statistic. The fixed-X guarantee (Barber & Candès, 2015) needs a statistic that sees the data only through the Gram matrix of originals and knockoffs and their products with the target; the difference of cross-validated lasso coefficients used until now does not, since its folds look at individual rows. Regression on the fixed-X path now uses the lasso-path signed maximum, max(Z_j, Z~_j) * sign(Z_j - Z~_j) with Z_j the penalty at which column j enters the path, computed from those inner products (lars_path_gram). Model-X and classification keep the cross-validated statistic, which model-X allows. On Gaussian linear models at q = 0.2, 200 trials each, knockoff+ realised FDR 0.180, 0.172 and 0.135 (previously 0.151, 0.165 and 0.155) with power 0.96, 0.98 and 0.48 (previously 0.97, 0.99 and 0.82) at n = 300, p = 25; n = 500, p = 50; and the same with correlation 0.7 between neighbouring columns: the guarantee now covers the statistic, at a cost in power on correlated designs, and a fit is 2–4 times faster. The permutation selector, the default, is unaffected.
  • The verbose summary of a fit with parsimony_holdout said that the returned terms were "re-certified on held-back rows" even when the re-test rejected no null and the screened set was returned. It now says which happened, and for how many of the re-tested terms the re-test rejected the null. It also no longer calls the fitted terms a subset of the certified set when they are the whole of it.
  • The permutation selector's warning for a permutation budget too small to reject any null suggested correction='bh' to a selector already using it; the suggestion is now made under Benjamini-Yekutieli only.

0.4.5 was prepared but not released; its fixes are part of this release and listed under "Fixed". The default path (correlation scoring, permutation screening with Benjamini-Yekutieli) gives the same results as 0.4.4 except where a fix applies; "Changed" lists the cases that differ. The new options leave a default fit unchanged, and the search is faster and needs far less memory on wide data: the high-dimensional study runs 2 to 28 times faster per dataset, and the speed-up changes no feature, p-value or prediction.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• equations() and equations_ on all three estimators: the forward parsimony step continued through the whole screened set, one equation per number of terms, with its complexity (expression-tree nodes plus one per coefficient), in-sample R² and the R² each term adds, and the fitted one marked. The model fitted is unchanged, and the path is recorded at parsimony=None too. The output states that the FDR guarantee covers the screened set, not an equation chosen from the list.
  • latex() on BeamFeatRegressor and BeamFeatClassifier, the equation of equation() typeset through sympy with the same options and note (note=False drops it), and latex_formulas() for the features on all three estimators.
  • The guide shows how to export the features to NumPy, JAX or PyTorch with sympy.lambdify on to_sympy() (PyTorch needs sympy 1.14 or newer).
  • n_jobs on BeamSearch, BeamFeatTransformer, BeamFeatRegressor and BeamFeatClassifier (default 1). A depth's candidates are evaluated and scored in chunks on joblib threads; GradientBoostingScorer, whose fits hold the GIL, scores on worker processes, and MutualInformationScorer receives n_jobs through the joblib backend. Depths under 4096 candidates stay in the calling thread unless the scorer fits models. The result is identical for every value, for the scorers that draw random numbers too: no seed depends on a worker or a chunk.
  • BeamSearch(chunk_size=...), the candidates evaluated and scored together; by default as many as fit in 8 MiB.
  • Scorer.prepare, Scorer.score_prepared, Scorer.scores_by_column and the separable flag, set on the correlation, Spearman and gradient-boosting scorers, so that a round can be scored in pieces; scoring.ColumnStats and column_stats; Evaluator.plan_batch, EvaluationBatch.run and Evaluator.commit_batch.
  • UnitRegistryError, ExclusionReason.UNDERFLOW, an optional OperatorSpec.redundant predicate, a symbols argument to Node.to_sympy, and SearchResult.n_rejected_redundant_final.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The search evaluates and scores each depth in chunks and keeps only the scores; the candidates the redundancy pass reaches are evaluated again. Peak memory no longer grows with max_candidates_per_depth: a default fit on 1000 columns and 600 rows peaked at 2.6 GB and now at 0.35 GB. MutualInformationScorer, whose noise is drawn for the whole batch, and custom scorers that do not declare separable still receive a whole depth.
  • A candidate's mean, variance and magnitude are computed once, for the constancy filter and the scorer, and columns are standardised in blocks rather than one at a time. The same fit takes 7 s rather than 29 s, and one on 300 columns 3.3 s rather than 19 s. Features, p-values and predictions are unchanged, as are search scores and the evaluation log, to the last bit.
  • Results that differ from 0.4.4: knockoff selections on candidate pools with dependent columns, which are common among constructed features; searches whose first round reaches max_candidates_per_depth (about 258 inputs or more at the defaults); SpearmanScorer scores with ties; predictions for batches containing out-of-domain rows; the constant printed by equation(max_terms=...); fits with a single candidate, which may now return nothing; fits on columns whose spread is between 1e-12 and 1e-5 of their magnitude, which the constancy cut no longer drops; and the spelling, not the value, of some formulas, since (1/a)/b is folded into 1/(a*b) only when that keeps the depth (1/((x1 * (x0 * x2))) now reads (1/(x1) / (x0 * x2)), with the same p-values and predictions).
  • SearchResult.n_evaluated_total no longer counts the input columns, matching n_proposed_total.
  • joblib is a declared dependency (>=1.2, scikit-learn 1.6's own minimum), since the search imports it directly; scikit-learn already installs it, and the oldest-stack CI job tests 1.2.0.
  • The API reference documents every public module and the methods the three estimators share. ColumnStats, column_stats, EvaluationBatch and BatchOutcome are listed in their modules' __all__.
  • The tutorials cover the equation list, LaTeX, export, n_jobs and the chunked search, describe knockoff routing and the scorers as they now are, and are executed on 0.5.0. The guide has a section on speed and memory.
  • The release workflow runs the full CI suite and publishes only after it passes; a tag push previously published before the tests finished. CONTRIBUTING.md describes the release flow.
  • The logistic models fitted internally are built with the arguments the installed scikit-learn expects: alpha = 1/C from 1.10 rather than the deprecated C, l1_ratios rather than penalty from 1.8, accuracy as the cross-validation score explicitly (1.11 changes the default), and newton-cd rather than the deprecated liblinear from 1.10. From 1.8, where liblinear fits two classes only, each class of a multiclass target is fitted on its own; the warning 1.7 gives ahead of that change is silenced. Fits on scikit-learn 1.6 to 1.9 are unchanged. Their other warnings are silenced by category, user and runtime warnings only, so a deprecation of an argument beamfeat passes is no longer hidden with the convergence notices.
  • CI also runs weekly, a weekly workflow tests the pre-releases and nightly builds of numpy, SciPy, scikit-learn and pandas, and the test suite fails on any FutureWarning and on a DeprecationWarning raised from beamfeat or its tests, so that an upstream deprecation is dealt with before the removal.
  • Docstrings describe what the code does: ranking on the larger of the absolute and marginal scores, redundancy pruning within a depth with cross-depth duplicates removed in the final ranking, and correlation scoring as one dot product per candidate. SpearmanScorer, is_constant and the estimator warnings are listed in their modules' __all__, and SpearmanScorer is exported from the package, as the other scorers are. The estimators document all their fitted attributes.
  • 230 tests added (686 in all).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• KnockoffSelector on a classification target with three or more classes, and BeamFeatClassifier(selector="knockoff") on one, raised on scikit-learn 1.8 and later, where the liblinear solver fits two classes only. The statistic is computed one class against the rest, as it was.
  • A refit no longer keeps fitted attributes of an earlier fit: the classifier's class_prior_ after a fit that kept no feature, the regressor's alpha_ when the new fit keeps none (it is now None), and the classifier's coefficients when the new training set has one class. Predictions were not affected.
  • The model-X warning of KnockoffSelector no longer reports a fallback from fixed-X when model-X was requested with construction="gaussian". It is recorded whenever model-X runs, as the docstrings now say.
  • A row on which a fitted formula is undefined, such as the logarithm of a negative value, no longer changes the predictions for the other rows of the batch. The formula's whole column was replaced with zeros for every row whenever any row failed, so a valid row predicted 2.88 alone and -6.63 next to an out-of-domain row, with only a log message. The failing rows are now NaN in transform, predict, predict_proba and decision_function, and a UserWarning names the formula and counts the rows. The classifier's predict assigns those rows the most frequent training class, since a label cannot be NaN; the regressor's score raises.
  • KnockoffSelector leaves constant and linearly dependent columns out of the knockoff construction when the design covariance has an eigenvalue below 1e-6. Valid knockoffs of such columns equal the originals, so the lasso's tie-breaking decided the statistics in favour of the originals: with one duplicated null column, knockoff+ reached a mean FDP of 0.31 at q = 0.1, under fixed-X and model-X alike. Dropped columns get W = 0 and are named in the warning; routing and the fixed-X row requirement count the retained columns.
  • BeamSearch reaches late input columns when max_candidates_per_depth binds at depth 1. The first round proposed parents in column order, so from about 258 inputs (default ceiling) pairs among the last columns were never proposed. When the ceiling can bind, the first round now proposes the inputs in order of their score, as documented; rounds the ceiling cannot reach are proposed as before and give identical results. Three datasets of the high-dimensional study reach the ceiling. Rerunning 0.4.4 and 0.5.0 on one machine, mean R² moves from 0.523 to 0.340 on riboflavin (the archived study, made with an earlier version, reads 0.544), from 0.687 to 0.664 on ct_slices and from 0.812 to 0.816 on ujiindoorloc. With the ceiling raised so that every input of ct_slices and ujiindoorloc is proposed, the search returns the result above exactly; the 0.4.4 figures depended on which columns came first in the file.
  • SpearmanScorer gives tied values their average rank. Ordinal ranks broke ties by row order, so a score depended on how the rows were arranged and a constant candidate scored above zero. An incumbent set that explains the target exactly now zeroes every score, a 1-D incumbent is accepted, and a candidate with a non-finite value scores zero, as under CorrelationScorer. For classification only the candidates are ranked: ranking the logistic residual let a copy of an incumbent score about 0.5.
  • String and object class labels work in every scorer and in the parsimony step; both cast the target to float, so BeamFeatTransformer(problem_type= "classification") failed on string labels.
  • BeamFeatClassifier runs the post-fit check on the selection rows, so DegenerateFitWarning fires for classification as documented.
  • A lone candidate is screened like any other set; screening was skipped and the term returned unvetted. When no candidate can be evaluated on the selection rows, on_no_discoveries applies. The DegenerateFitWarning message no longer says features passed FDR screening when they did not.
  • on_no_discoveries, selection_holdout, parsimony_holdout, selection_correction and parsimony are validated at fit. A holdout fraction outside (0, 1), such as 1.5, switched the split off silently, and an unrecognised on_no_discoveries behaved like "empty".
  • A Selector instance keeps its own correction and target_fdr, and the estimator warns when its own settings disagree: selector= PermutationSelector() ran Benjamini-Hochberg where the estimators default to Benjamini-Yekutieli, without saying so. Verbose output and warnings report the correction and level that ran.
  • fdp_inflation_ describes the set the model returns, after the parsimony_holdout re-test or its fallback.
  • equation(max_terms=...) holds the omitted terms at their training mean, so the printed constant absorbs their average contribution; it kept the full model's constant, as if the omitted terms were zero.
  • Class labels print as plain values (logit P(y = 1), not np.int64(1)).
  • make_scorer warns when given a scorer instance whose problem_type differs from the one requested.
  • Node keys escape backslashes, parentheses and commas in column names, so a column named like a,leaf:b can no longer give two expressions one key and one cache entry. Keys and formulas of ordinary names are unchanged.
  • Units from different pint registries no longer drop candidates silently: Evaluator re-expresses every unit in the first one's registry, and nodes built directly from mixed registries raise UnitRegistryError.
  • Exclusion reasons name the cause: an overflowing variance is overflow (was zero_variance), an underflow is underflow (was non_finite), and abs of a never-negative operand is duplicate (was domain_error). Which candidates are excluded is unchanged; the overflow's RuntimeWarning no longer escapes.
  • The evaluation cache re-checks a value first computed without the search filters, and returns read-only arrays. A failing node is logged once per evaluator.
  • (1/a)/b is folded into 1/(a*b) only when the fold does not deepen the node; it could exceed max_depth.
  • Node.to_sympy and to_sympy() on the estimators give distinct symbols to columns whose sanitised names coincide (a b and a-b).
  • The evaluator's default constancy cut matches is_constant (spread below 1e-12 of the magnitude; was 1e-5), so a column varying by a millionth of its value is no longer dropped from the search without a warning.
  • redundancy_threshold=1.0 drops exact affine and sign-flipped copies consistently; their correlation landed a rounding error either side of 1. The redundancy check judges constancy relative to a column's magnitude.
  • BeamSearch rejects max_candidates_per_depth below 1 (0 returned the inputs), and its final verbose line reports the depth reached.
  • The guide's "honest failure" example used a seed on which pure noise certifies 12 formulas, which happens on about 1 fit in 100; it now uses one where nothing passes and says that some pure-noise fits certify features.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
• The comparison harnesses (independent/bench.py and its copy in additional_experiments/) filled non-finite test cells of constructed features with 0 while training cells got the training median; both now use the training medians. The archived results are unchanged; independent/PROVENANCE.md lists the affected featuretools and OpenFE fits and relates them to the paper's comparison table.
  • run_benchmarks.py scores knockpy recovery with the shared criterion instead of recording False.
  • calibration_study.py bounds the global-null rate by trials selecting anything rather than features selected, and says its scores are in-sample.
  • depth_ladder.py seeds with zlib.crc32 instead of the per-process hash(); the archived ladder used the old seeding.
  • additional_experiments/aggregate.py reads the highdim_*.json records, the README run order matches the archived run, and selector_comparison.py reports selector errors instead of counting them as skips.
  • Stale docstrings corrected in selector_calibration.py, feynman_panel.py, bench.py and selector_comparison.py.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Selector.select now rejects a target containing NaN or infinity, and a missing class label. A NaN made every permutation statistic NaN, so no null draw counted as an exceedance and PermutationSelector selected every candidate at the p-value floor; as a class label it formed a class of its own. The estimators were not affected: scikit-learn's validation rejects such a target before selection.
  • Fixed-X knockoffs are built orthogonal to the intercept as well as to the design, so they are centred like the standardised features. The lasso statistic fits an intercept, which centres every column; uncentred knockoffs lost part of their norm to it, and the exchangeability identities X~'X~ = X'X and X'X~ = X'X - S held for the constructed columns but not for what the lasso saw (deviation up to about 0.03 at n close to 2p). Simulations at q = 0.1 showed no measurable change in realised FDR, which stayed far below nominal either way. The complement now needs one more row: fixed-X is used when n > 2p (was n >= 2p), and at n = 2p the selector falls back to model-X.
  • Model-X knockoff noise is drawn from a seed spawned from random_state, as the fixed-X basis already was. Drawn from random_state itself, it equalled a data matrix generated from the same seed and shape, which made the knockoffs a fixed linear image of the features.
  • PermutationSelector with auto_permutations=False warns when n_permutations is below what the correction needs to select anything; an empty selection was previously returned in silence.
  • The "fixed_x" and "model_x" selector names select that knockoff construction; both previously meant construction="auto". An explicit construction argument still takes precedence.
  • The knockoff+ warning states the floor as "at least ceil(1/q)" features; it said "more than 1/q". The condition itself was correct.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Knockoff selections can differ from 0.4.3 for the same random_state, since both constructions draw differently. The permutation selector's results are unchanged.
  • Docstrings, docs/guarantees.md and the README describe permutation p-values as valid in finite samples rather than exact, as the paper does.
