  • A Benjamini-Hochberg test now uses p-values on which Bonferroni selects fewer, so it distinguishes the two procedures. 20 tests added (456 in all).

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • The TMLR paper, "Symbolic feature construction with false discovery rate control", is the preferred citation in CITATION.cff and the README.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Package metadata links point to the lowercase LD-Shell/beamfeat repository and documentation site; the 0.4.2 Documentation link returned 404.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • BeamFeatClassifier.decision_function raised AttributeError when no feature passed selection. It now returns the log prior odds (binary) or log priors (multiclass), consistent with predict and predict_proba, which already fell back to the class priors. scikit-learn's check_estimator is now also run with FDR selection on, which is what exposed it.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The tutorial notebooks no longer suggest installing from GitHub; pip install beamfeat is the install route.
  • CI now also tests Python 3.14 and 3.15, and the package metadata lists them.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • CITATION.cff shipped in 0.4.0 with unresolved merge-conflict markers, so it was not valid YAML and Zenodo could not archive the release. The 0.4.0 source distribution carries the invalid file; the wheel never contained it. No code changed.

equation() now says when the equation it prints is a subset of the certified set. The default is unchanged -- parsimony="forward" still keeps the compact predictive subset -- but a caller reading the equation next to fdr_controlled_ = True previously had no signal that the two do not describe the same terms. They now do:

y = 0.9999*(x0 * x1) - 0.003943   [1 of 25 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 25]

What the default costs is also measured rather than asserted. Across 308 paired fits the compact equation is worse by 0.001 of held-out R^2 on average and 0.019 at worst, roughly twenty-five times shorter, and fdr_controlled_ never disagreed between the two settings. The end-to-end calibration figures are identical at both. benchmarks/PARSIMONY_COST.md records the numbers, the per-study dependency map behind them, and what pruning does to the realised false discovery proportion, which in every regime tested was nothing or an improvement. Seventeen tests take the suite to 431.

The printed string is the only behavioural change, and it affects anything that parses equation() output. equation() splits cleanly on " [", and the suffix is absent whenever the printed terms are the certified ones.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• equation() appends [k of m certified terms; parsimony=None prints all m] when the parsimony step dropped terms. It is absent with no selector, with nothing screened, at parsimony=None, when the greedy pass happened to keep everything, and after a parsimony_holdout re-test, which certifies the subset on rows of its own and so leaves nothing to warn about. On a multiclass classifier the terms are shared across the lines, so the suffix appears once at the end of the block.
  • fdr_scope_ names which set fdr_controlled_ is a statement about: "printed equation" when the guarantee covers the returned features, "screened set" when it covers a larger set they were drawn from, None when the flag is not True. The flag has always meant "the returned features came from the screened set", which is not the same claim, and a caller branching on it in a script cannot see the note equation() prints. At verbose=1 the result line names the scope too.
  • benchmarks/PARSIMONY_COST.md and benchmarks/parsimony_cost.py: the measurement above, and the runner that produces it. The runner drives each study through its own module rather than a copy of its protocol, and writes only to benchmarks/parsimony_cost/; no archived result is read or written.
  • parsimony is selectable from the benchmark harnesses -- a keyword argument on feynman_panel.run_panel, calibration_study.main, friedman_decomposition.main and run_benchmarks.evaluate, a --parsimony flag on the three additional_experiments studies, and the BEAMFEAT_PARSIMONY environment variable for the two bench.py harnesses. Unset or omitted reproduces the library default exactly, and the value in force is recorded on every row.
  • feynman_panel.make_data exposes the panel's data generation, so a comparison harness scores its method on the same rows rather than on a copy of that code. It is the original code moved, not rewritten: the arrays it returns are identical to those the previous version produced.
  • benchmarks/pysr_panel/: PySR on the same twelve-law panel, in its own pinned environment with its own Julia runtime, scored by the panel's own data generators and proportionality test imported unmodified. The budget, the operator sets and the Pareto-front selection rule are fixed in advance and stated in its README. pysr is not a dependency of this package.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• The guarantees page states the three-way trade-off with the measurement attached, rather than asserting the exchange rate.
  • The user guide's opening example explains the suffix where a reader first meets it, and shows what parsimony=None returns instead.

Correctness release for the automatic permutation budget, plus two warning fixes. Selections are unchanged everywhere the previous budget was already adequate: the two widest problems in the high-dimensional study (riboflavin and superconductivity) return identical formulas, feature counts, flags and held-out scores, with fit times differing by less than the run-to-run spread. The budget binds in the selector calibration studies, where a small pool at a strict level is where the harmonic factor matters: rerun with the fix, the Benjamini-Yekutieli figures move in the third decimal (realised FDR at q = 0.05 from 0.008 to 0.013; power at that level from 0.988 to 0.989), and the figures in the README, the docs and benchmarks/additional_experiments/REPORT.md come from runs with the fix. Thirty-seven tests take the suite to 411 at 95% statement coverage.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • verbose is now a level rather than a flag, and reports to stdout instead of through the module logger -- progress a caller explicitly asked for should not require them to attach a handler first, which is the scikit-learn convention. 0 (default) is silent and unchanged; 1 prints one line per stage, covering the split, the search, the screening, the parsimony step and the fitted equation, with the FDR flag on the result line; 2 adds per-depth search detail -- proposed, evaluated, kept, what was rejected and why -- and the strongest certified candidates with their p- and q-values. Warnings and diagnostics continue to use the logger, because those are events the caller did not ask for. Reporting now covers selection as well as search; previously any positive verbose logged search progress only, and the screening step, which is where the guarantee is actually applied, was invisible.

docs.title: Added (continued)
docs.text:
• parsimony_holdout divides the selection rows a second time, so that the printed equation carries a guarantee of its own rather than being a subset of a certified set. Screening and parsimony run on the first part; the resulting subset is fixed at that point, so re-testing it on the part held back is an ordinary fixed-candidate screen and its guarantee covers the subset itself. Terms that fail are dropped; if none survives, an intercept-only model is returned with a visible warning rather than an uncertified equation. Off by default, because what it costs is rows: on 240- and 5000-row problems it returns the same terms at the same accuracy, and on a 71-row problem it loses twelve of nineteen terms. The estimator warns rather than proceeding when the selection rows cannot be split so that both parts hold at least ten. When a compact certified equation cannot be produced -- because the rows will not split, or because nothing survives the re-test -- the whole screened set is returned rather than a pruned subset of it. The caller asked for a guarantee over what is printed; the screened set supplies one and a pruned subset does not, so that is the honest way to degrade. Note that parsimony=None reaches the same corner for free, and on short samples is the better choice: a long certified equation beats a compact one whose terms were dropped for want of rows. The two-stage procedure has not been FDR-calibrated and is offered as an option rather than a measured result.
  • fdp_inflation_ reports |S|/|S'|, the factor by which pruning the screened set down to the printed equation can inflate the realised false discovery proportion. It was derivable from selection_report_ before and is now surfaced directly, since it is the number to quote alongside target_fdr.

docs.title: Added (continued)
docs.text:
• Constant input columns are reported at fit time. Such a column standardises to zeros, so its association with the target is zero at every depth it can appear in and it can never be selected; that is the correct outcome and costs neither accuracy nor multiplicity, since the beam filters it before screening. What it does cost is legibility: in the output a stuck sensor or a column emptied by a bad join looks exactly like a variable that does not matter. The test consults no response values, so reporting it cannot bias what follows. It fires on real data -- 55 of 521 columns in ujiindoorloc, five of 385 in ct_slices, four of 281 in blogfeedback.
  • is_constant is exported. Constancy is judged relative to the column's magnitude rather than against an absolute floor on the spread, because an absolute floor makes the verdict depend on the column's units: a column varying over the whole range 0 to 1e-9 has a smaller variance than a stuck sensor reading 9.81, and any floor that keeps the first also keeps the second. The estimator and the diagnostic now share the one predicate, so the warning cannot come to describe behaviour the fit no longer has.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• New tutorial, notebooks/04_reading_a_fit.ipynb. The first three notebooks plant an answer and confirm it is recovered; this one is about the fit you did not plant. On a pump-power problem hidden among noise columns it walks through the cases an applied user actually hits: why a deeper search returns a worse equation, why fdr_controlled_ stays True when noise columns appear inside a formula (the null is marginal, so a formula combining the true core with noise has a false null and selecting it is not an error), why depth counts composition levels rather than variables, how units remove the hitchhikers where statistics cannot, why unit coverage is all or nothing, where a constant factor goes, how to read selection_report_ against equation(), and how to tell an exhausted permutation budget from an absent signal. Runs in about 14 s.
  • Notebook 03 notes that knockoffs cannot prune a term out of an expression: selection operates on whole candidate columns, so switching the selector does not reach inside a composite. The conditional null invites that inference and it does not hold.
  • Notebook 01 builds its design as a DataFrame, so formulas read (a * b) / c rather than (x0 * x1) / x2, and demonstrates the verbosity levels.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The permutation count chosen when auto_permutations is on was sized to the Benjamini-Hochberg resolution bound 2m/q, while "by" is the estimator's default correction. Benjamini-Yekutieli requires the leading p-value to clear q/(m c(m)), so its bound is larger by the harmonic factor -- above five once m reaches the low hundreds. Below it the correction cannot reject at all, and the failure was silent: an empty selection reads as "no signal" rather than "budget too small". It bites hardest when few candidates reach the p-value floor together, since several tied signals relax the threshold by their count while a lone one carries it alone, which is why a sparse true set in a large pool was the exposed case. _required_permutations now takes its bound from the configured correction, and max_permutations rises from 100,000 to 1,000,000 so the larger requirement is reachable. The warning raised when it is not names the correction and offers correction="bh" as the cheaper alternative.
  • Fitting on a DataFrame no longer emits scikit-learn's "X does not have valid feature names" warning. The post-fit degeneracy diagnostic scores the estimator's own validated array, which carries no column names by construction; the warning fired on every named fit and pointed the caller at a mismatch of our own making.
  • units covering some columns but not all now warns. An unlabelled column is dimensionally unconstrained and combines freely with the labelled ones, so partial coverage leaves the check not binding on exactly the columns the caller did not vouch for -- while a mapping matching no column already raised. Labelling the known columns and leaving the rest blank looks like the careful thing to do, which is what made the silence worth removing. Pass "dimensionless" for genuinely unitless columns. The warning is raised once at fit, not on every transform or predict.

Behavioural release: the downstream ridge penalty is now selected by leave-one-out cross-validation. Fitted coefficients and held-out scores move against 0.2.0 -- in trailing digits when rows comfortably exceed the selected features, and materially at p >> n, where the fixed default could produce an effectively unregularised fit. Selections are unchanged: the search, permutation tests and FDR control sit upstream of this step. Every benchmark artifact ships regenerated under the new default; the Friedman #1 decomposition reads 0.780 ± 0.013 achieved with 0.094 to the search (from 0.776 and 0.098), and four estimator-check tests take the suite to 374 at 94% statement coverage.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• alpha on BeamFeatRegressor defaults to "auto": the downstream ridge penalty is chosen by efficient leave-one-out cross-validation over a logarithmic grid, deterministically. Pass a float for the previous fixed behaviour. The chosen strength is exposed as alpha_.
  • The fdr_controlled_ documentation states the guarantee's object precisely: the set-level q guarantee applies to the full screened set in selection_report_; the parsimony subset is not re-certified at level q.
  • The post-fit check is documented as what it is -- a degeneracy diagnostic on the selection rows, which also enter the final fit -- rather than an independent generalisation estimate, and its warning text says so.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • With many correlated certified features selected from few rows, the fixed default alpha=1.0 amounted to almost no regularisation and could produce catastrophically negative held-out scores on features the screening had correctly certified. The cross-validated default keeps such fits on the scale of the target.

Behavioural release: scale-free numerics throughout, strict unit validation, and a faithful equation(). Results are not bit-reproducible against 0.1.1, and selections on small- or mixed-unit data change deliberately.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• style parameter on equation() for both supervised estimators: "significant" (default), "fixed", and "scientific". "fixed" falls back to significant figures for any value that would otherwise display as zero.
  • units accepts a positional sequence with one entry per column, alongside the existing mapping form.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• variance_tol is judged relative to a column's squared mean magnitude, so the constant/not-constant verdict no longer depends on the caller's units. Anyone who tuned it against an absolute variance should re-check the value.
  • Candidate ranking treats scores within 1e-6 as tied and admits the smaller expression; the redundancy pass then removes the complex near-duplicate.
  • Invalid units fail loudly: a mapping matching no columns, a wrong-length sequence, or an unsupported type raises instead of silently skipping dimensional analysis.
  • equation() orders terms by standardised coefficient magnitude and prints significant figures; precision counts decimal places only under style="fixed".

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• equation() dropped any term whose raw coefficient fell below the printed precision, deleting dominant terms on large-unit features from their own equation. Only exactly-zero terms are omitted now.
  • Scoring zeroed any column whose absolute spread fell below 1e-12, which made products of small-unit columns undiscoverable; the guard is now relative to the column's magnitude.
  • A saturated incumbent yields zero candidate scores at every target scale; previously the check held only for targets near unit magnitude.
Documentation, benchmarks and packaging. No library code changed; the public API, defaults and behaviour are identical to 0.1.0.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• benchmarks/selector_calibration.py: realised FDR and power for both multiplicity corrections, the two fixed-X knockoff offsets, and the global-null stress behind the Benjamini-Yekutieli default.
  • benchmarks/make_figures.py: seven vector PDFs in paper/figures/, sized to the ACS column widths, including mean held-out R² against fit time from the comparison study.
  • benchmarks/independent/setup_env.sh: builds the comparison environment, registers a Jupyter kernel, and smoke-tests autofeat, knockpy and matplotlib.
  • beamfeat_ridge in the comparison study: beamfeat as a transformer into the shared RidgeCV, giving one row strictly like-for-like with the other feature builders.
  • docs/installation.md: three setups, from pip install beamfeat to the pinned benchmark environment.
  • benchmarks/independent/autofeat_repeatability.json: six runs of one split.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Friedman #1 decomposition is reported over six draws rather than one: oracle 0.960 ± 0.003, screening ceiling 0.874 ± 0.006, achieved 0.776 ± 0.013, with about 0.086 lost to screening and 0.098 to the search. The previous single-draw figures came from a different split for the achieved value and overstated the gap. friedman_decomposition.py now checks the ordering the argument rests on rather than comparing against recorded numbers, and computes the ceiling on the set actually admitted: the marginal null never admits c, but admits c² on some draws, so the earlier "admits only four of the six" was true of one draw rather than in general.
  • knockpy's stress false-feature rate was averaged over six datasets where only five declare their generating columns. Reported as a count of affected datasets instead, since a mean over five carries a standard error of order 0.1; knockpy is also unseeded, so the count moves between runs.
  • Selector calibration runs 100 trials rather than 25 and reports a standard error. The published 25-trial figures were noisy point estimates: BH at nominal 0.10 read 0.120, above nominal, where 100 trials give 0.084 ± 0.012 against a ceiling of 0.080. selector_calibration.py now derives each procedure's bound from the design and fails if a realised rate exceeds it, so no calibration constant is written by hand anywhere.
  • Fixed-X knockoff+ 0.201 to 0.159 and offset=0 0.289 to 0.249 at 100 trials.
  • The stress-suite false-feature rate is reported as a count of affected datasets rather than a mean over five, which carried a standard error of about 0.15 for autofeat and 0.08 for knockpy.
  • The end-to-end result is stated as no false discovery in 200 replicates with a 95% upper bound of 0.015, rather than as an empirical rate of 0.0000.
  • Pure-noise stress at 100 trials: BH returned features in 6 trials against BY's 1, both under the nominal 0.10 and not significantly different (the one BY trial is among BH's six; exact paired test p = 0.06, which replaces an unpaired Fisher p = 0.12 reported earlier). BY is the default because it is valid under arbitrary dependence, not because a BH failure was observed.
  • autofeat reproducibility: it exposes no random_state and draws decoy features from the global NumPy generator, so six runs of one identical split returned R² from +0.952 to -109.8 with 17 to 26 selected features. Thread pinning does not help; the previous "seeds no internal subsampling" was wrong.
  • Real-data panel is seven datasets; California housing uses all 20,640 rows rather than a 2,000-row subsample.
  • Every measured figure now comes from one machine (Dell Inspiron 16 Plus 7640, 22 logical cores, Linux 7.0, Python 3.11.15, scikit-learn 1.7.2, numpy 1.26.4), the pinned environment the compared tools require.
  • Reproducibility is stated from two measured machines: deterministic given a seed within a stack, with marginal fits moving in the third decimal across scikit-learn 1.6 to 1.9.
  • pytest-cov moved into the test extra, so floor-versions in CI and a local pip install -e ".[test]" both get it without naming it separately.
  • The comparison notebook calls bench.py rather than duplicating it, dropping from 523 lines to 136.
  • Removed benchmarks/independent/run_all.sh: it re-implemented the notebook's full-run path, so a method added in one place was missing from the other.
  • The sdist ships the benchmark scripts and archived results, which benchmarks/README.md already documented.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• feynman_panel.py seeded each equation's data with hash(name). Python randomises string hashing per process, so the panel drew different data on every run and reported 9/12 or 10/12 at random; the earlier claim that this varied "across numeric stacks" mistook the cause. Seeded with zlib.crc32, it now reproduces exactly at 10/12 solved and 8/12 exact form.

  • Both OpenFE patchers imported the package before rewriting it, so the kernel kept running unpatched code while reporting success.

  • benchmarks/independent/requirements.txt installs beamfeat[all], so the test suite runs there; pins setuptools<82, without which every featuretools fit fails on the removed pkg_resources; and adds knockpy under the existing numpy pin rather than letting it pull numpy 2.
  • aggregate.py takes the results directory as an argument and writes its CSV beside the files it read.
  • Independent study regenerated in a single pass on one machine: 360 fits, nine datasets, eight methods. It replaces an archive stitched from several partial runs that contained one hand-transcribed fit.
  • Removed an unsupported OpenFE figure on the diabetes dataset from the README.

Initial release.

  • Beam search over an expression DAG with commutative canonicalisation, local algebraic normalisation, and record-and-exclude handling of numerical failures. Unary operators log, sqrt, reciprocal, square, abs by default, with cube and exp available; binary mul, div, add, sub.
  • FDR-controlled selection: exact permutation test of marginal association with Benjamini--Hochberg or Benjamini--Yekutieli correction (BY default), and the knockoff filter in fixed-X and model-X forms. Default holdout split separates search from selection; fdr_controlled_ states whether the guarantee applies; selection_report_ exposes per-candidate p- and q-values.
  • Estimators BeamFeatTransformer, BeamFeatRegressor, BeamFeatClassifier, passing scikit-learn's estimator-conformance checks. Parsimony (forward selection within the screened set) on by default; on_no_discoveries in "empty" (default), "fallback", and "raise" modes; a post-fit holdout check (DegenerateFitWarning) separating association from generalisation; readable equation() on both supervised estimators (log-odds form for classification).
  • Optional dimensional analysis via pint quantities or unit strings, enforced at expression construction.
  • Committed benchmark harness, physics-equation panel, calibration studies, and a vendored independent comparison study.
  • Supported: Python >= 3.10, numpy >= 1.26, scikit-learn 1.6 through 1.9 verified, no upper version pins.

docs.title: Citing beamfeat
docs.text:
If you use beamfeat in published work, please cite:

  1. The paper, which describes the method. Always cite it.
  2. The software release, when your results depend on a particular version.
  3. The statistical methods behind the options you used, which beamfeat implements but did not invent.

docs.title: The paper
docs.text:
Daramola, O. M. (2026). Symbolic feature construction with false discovery rate control. Transactions on Machine Learning Research. https://openreview.net/forum?id=UibXoy4h3u

@article{daramola2026symbolic,
  title   = {Symbolic feature construction with false discovery rate control},
  author  = {Daramola, Olanrewaju M.},

  issn    = {2835-8856},
  year    = {2026},

}

The paper describes version 0.4.2. Later releases correct two of its results: a harness bug understated featuretools, and fixing a search bug lowers the number of datasets where beamfeat leads both tree ensembles from five to four. Reading the paper today has the details.

docs.title: The software release
docs.text:
Each release is archived on Zenodo with its own DOI:

what to cite DOI beamfeat in general (resolves to the latest release) 10.5281/zenodo.21619567 0.4.2, the version the paper describes, with the run records behind its results 10.5281/zenodo.23417132

To cite the release you used, open the first DOI, choose that version from the list of versions on the Zenodo page, and use its DOI. The page also gives the citation in several formats.

@software{daramola_beamfeat,
  author    = {Daramola, Olanrewaju M.},
  title     = {beamfeat: beam-search feature construction with FDR-controlled selection},
  publisher = {Zenodo},
  doi       = {10.5281/zenodo.21619567},
  url       = {https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21619567}
}

For one release, add version = {...} and replace the DOI with that release's. CITATION.cff in the repository has the same details in machine-readable form, and GitHub's "Cite this repository" button reads it.

docs.title: The statistical methods
docs.text:
beamfeat's guarantee rests on established procedures. If your work relies on one of them, please cite its source as well:

if you use beamfeat relies on please also cite any fit with the default selector permutation p-values with the add-one estimator, and the Benjamini–Yekutieli correction Phipson & Smyth (2010); Benjamini & Yekutieli (2001) selection_correction="bh" the Benjamini–Hochberg correction, in place of Benjamini–Yekutieli Benjamini & Hochberg (1995) selector="knockoff" or KnockoffSelector fixed-X knockoffs with knockoff+ when there are more than twice as many rows as columns, model-X Gaussian knockoffs otherwise Barber & Candès (2015); Candès et al. (2018) KnockoffSelector(s_method="ci") the conditional-independence knockoff Liu & Rigollet (2019) parsimony_alpha the multiplier bootstrap for the best fit noise can reach Fan & Zhou (2016) input_test=True sequential Monte Carlo p-values Besag & Clifford (1991) parsimony_holdout with certify_test="conditional" the Freedman–Lane permutation test Freedman & Lane (1983); Anderson & Robinson (2001); Winkler et al. (2014) screen_equation permutation p-values with the add-one estimator and the Benjamini–Yekutieli correction, or Benjamini–Hochberg; with input_test=True, sequential Monte Carlo p-values Phipson & Smyth (2010); Benjamini & Yekutieli (2001) or Benjamini & Hochberg (1995); Besag & Clifford (1991)

Statistical guarantees explains what each procedure guarantees in beamfeat, and under which assumptions.

docs.title: Statistical guarantees
docs.text: This page states, for each selection procedure, exactly what is guaranteed, under which assumptions, and what was measured. Every number here is reproduced by the committed test suite (tests/test_selection.py, tests/test_estimators.py) or benchmark scripts. Calibration figures come from 100 trials and are quoted with their standard error; read them at that precision rather than at the last digit.

docs.title: What "FDR control at level q" means
docs.text:
Each candidate j carries its own null hypothesis H₀ⱼ. For the default screen, H₀ⱼ is that candidate j is independent of the target. A selection procedure rejects some of these nulls, and the candidates whose nulls it rejects are its discoveries: the selected features, which beamfeat also calls the screened or certified set. Rejecting a true null is a false discovery, a Type I error. With R rejections of which V are false, the false discovery proportion is FDP = V / max(R, 1), and the false discovery rate is its expectation over repetitions of the experiment, FDR = E[FDP]. A single run with FDP above q is consistent with control; a mean over trials above q is not. All documentation and tests in beamfeat use this definition.

Under the global null, where every H₀ⱼ is true, V = R, so the FDR is the probability of rejecting any null at all. Controlling it at q then means that at most a fraction q of pure-noise fits select anything.

docs.title: Permutation selector (default)
docs.text:
Statistic. |Pearson correlation| (regression) or eta-squared (classification) between each candidate and the target — a fixed function of the data, which is the condition for a permutation test to be valid. Statistics that re-tune themselves on the observed target (e.g. a cross-validated lasso penalty) violate exchangeability unless the tuning is repeated inside every permutation; beamfeat deliberately avoids them.

P-values. Add-one estimator (1 + #exceedances)/(B + 1) (Phipson & Smyth, 2010): valid in finite samples, and never zero. The floor 1/(B+1) interacts with the multiplicity correction — Benjamini–Hochberg needs the leading feature to reach q/m, Benjamini–Yekutieli the smaller q/(m c(m)) — so B is auto-raised to twice the bound belonging to the configured correction (satisfiability plus headroom for one null exceedance), capped at max_permutations. The requirement binds hardest when few candidates reach the floor together: several tied signals relax the threshold by their count, a lone one carries it alone. If the pool is large enough that even the cap cannot meet it, the selector says so in warnings_raised and an empty selection should be read as an exhausted budget rather than an absent signal.

Null semantics. Marginal independence: H₀ⱼ is that candidate j is independent of the target. A near-duplicate of a genuine signal is not independent of the target, so rejecting its null is a true discovery; de-duplication is performed by the search's redundancy threshold, not the error-control procedure.

Multiplicity. The estimators (BeamFeatRegressor, BeamFeatClassifier, BeamFeatTransformer) default to Benjamini–Yekutieli, valid under arbitrary dependence; PermutationSelector used directly defaults to Benjamini–Hochberg, valid under positive regression dependence (PRDS). Engineered candidates share parents and are mutually correlated by construction, so PRDS cannot be taken for granted and the estimators take the conservative option. Over 100 pure-noise pipelines BH returned features in 7 trials against BY's 1 (FDP 0.07 and 0.01, benchmarks/selector_calibration.py), both under the nominal 0.10. Both corrections saw the same 100 datasets, and the one trial on which BY selected is among BH's seven, so the exact paired test rejects equal rates (p = 0.03): under the global null BY selects less often, as a stricter correction should. Neither rate exceeds the nominal level, so this is no evidence that BH loses control here. A selector instance passed to an estimator keeps its own settings, so selector=PermutationSelector() runs BH at the instance's target_fdr; the estimator warns when its selection_correction or target_fdr disagrees with the instance's.

Measured calibration (Gaussian designs, 300 rows, 25 candidates, 5 signals, 100 trials). BH controls the FDR at q·m0/m, here q·20/25, and realised 0.046 ± 0.008, 0.084 ± 0.012 and 0.161 ± 0.016 at nominal 0.05/0.10/0.20 against ceilings of 0.040/0.080/0.160. BY is stricter by a harmonic factor and realised 0.013 ± 0.005, 0.018 ± 0.005 and 0.046 ± 0.008. Power 1.00 throughout. benchmarks/selector_calibration.py derives each bound from the design and stops with an error if a bound falls below a realised rate's whole 95% interval, so these figures cannot drift from the behaviour.

What the marginal null cannot see. A feature can be jointly essential yet nearly marginally independent of the target — a centred quadratic (c − 0.5)² contributes almost no marginal correlation until its linear complement is fitted. The marginal screen has almost no power to reject the null for such a feature, and where the feature is exactly marginally independent of the target, failing to reject is correct under that null. The cost is measurable on targets built from them (Friedman #1, over six draws: the screen never rejects the null for c, giving a screening-admissible ceiling of 0.874 ± 0.006 against a representation oracle of 0.960 ± 0.003, with the pipeline reaching 0.780 ± 0.013. Around 0.086 is lost to screening and 0.094 to the search. The null for c² is rejected on some draws and not others, since (c − 0.5)² expands to carry a little marginal signal through it.) Joint selection recovers such features but certifies nothing; that trade is the design.

docs.title: Knockoff selector
docs.text:
Fixed-X (Barber & Candès, 2015), used when n > 2p: no distributional assumption on the features — deterministic engineered columns are fine. The guarantee requires the linear model with Gaussian, homoskedastic noise. The construction's exchangeability identities X̃'X̃ = X'X and X'X̃ = X'X − S are verified to numerical precision by the tests, also after the centring the lasso statistic applies (the knockoffs are built orthogonal to the intercept as well, which takes one row more than 2p). On a near-singular design (smallest covariance eigenvalue below 1e-6) valid knockoffs of the dependent columns would equal the originals, and the lasso's tie-breaking would then favour the originals; constant and linearly dependent columns are therefore left out of the construction, get W = 0, and are named in a runtime warning. Routing and the n > 2p requirement count the retained columns.

How far knockoffs are from the originals. S = diag(s), and the correlation of column j with its knockoff is 1 − s_j. The default, s_method="equicorrelated", uses one value for every column, min(1, 2λ_min), so one tight group of near copies, common among constructed candidates, makes every knockoff nearly equal its original. s_method="ci" (Liu & Rigollet, 2019) sets s_j = c/(Σ⁻¹)_jj, the share of column j the other columns leave unexplained, times the largest c ≤ 1 that keeps S ≤ 2Σ; the guarantee is the same. In benchmarks/knockoff_s_method.py (nominal 0.1, 50 trials) on 76 constructed columns, six transforms per input and the pairwise products, knockoff+ power rose from 0.000 to 0.217 (realised FDR 0.000 and 0.038), and offset=0 power from 0.073 to 0.596 (0.096 and 0.112). On Gaussian designs with correlated pairs or shared factors the two were within a few points of each other.

Statistic. The fixed-X guarantee holds for a statistic that sees the data only through [X X̃]'[X X̃] and [X X̃]'y. On the fixed-X path for regression beamfeat uses the lasso-path signed maximum, W_j = max(Z_j, Z̃_j)·sign(Z_j − Z̃_j), where Z_j is the penalty at which column j enters the path, computed from those inner products alone; a test checks that rotating the rows, which preserves them, leaves W unchanged. On Gaussian linear models at q = 0.2 (200 trials each), knockoff+ with this statistic realised 0.180, 0.172 and 0.135, under the level, with power 0.96, 0.98 and 0.48. A difference of cross-validated lasso coefficients, whose folds look at individual rows and which the guarantee therefore does not strictly cover, had power 0.97, 0.99 and 0.82: the valid statistic costs power when columns are correlated (0.7 between neighbours in the third design). Model-X, which admits any statistic that swaps sign with the pair, keeps the cross-validated one.

Model-X Gaussian (Candès et al., 2018), used only when n ≤ 2p: assumes jointly Gaussian features, which engineered features violate; a warning is recorded, and the permutation selector is recommended in this regime.

The estimators surface every selector diagnostic — assumption strain, unsatisfiable configurations — through the warnings module, so an empty knockoff result reads as "could not have selected at this configuration" rather than "no evidence"; when knockoff+ selects nothing but offset=0 would have, the warning says so and names the trade-off.

Offsets. offset=1 (knockoff+) carries the finite-sample FDR guarantee and realised 0.170 at nominal 0.20 over 100 trials; it is unsatisfiable with fewer than 1/q features, and a warning fires on narrow designs. offset=0 controls only a modified FDR and realised 0.260, above offset=1 as expected. Both move across numeric stacks, since knockoff construction depends on matrix decompositions; treat the ordering and the nominal bound as the claim, not the second decimal. benchmarks/selector_calibration.py regenerates both, and the committed tests pin the ordering rather than the decimals.

docs.title: Selective inference: why the estimators split their data
docs.text:
The search retains candidates because they correlate with the target in its sample. P-values computed on that same sample are therefore optimistically biased, and the nominal FDR is not guaranteed for them. By default the estimators search on one half of the training rows and run selection on the other (selection_holdout=0.5), restoring the fixed-candidate-set premise. Measured end-to-end over 200 replicates at nominal 0.10 (500 rows, 6 input columns of which 2 carry signal through their product, noise at 5% of the signal's standard deviation, max_depth=2, beam_width=25): not one false discovery, a 95% upper bound of 0.015 on the true rate, power 1.000, no fallbacks; 60 global-null replicates selected nothing. That is a far stronger signal than the selector-level design above — the generating feature correlates with the target at 0.999 — so read it as an end-to-end check that the split does its job, not as a power measurement at the margin. benchmarks/calibration_study.py regenerates it. If the holdout is disabled, the estimator refuses to claim the guarantee (fdr_controlled_ = False).

Constants fitted inside expressions (fitted_ops) are part of the search. Each is chosen inside the search, on the search rows, before selection sees the candidates, and the selection rows receive every expression with its constant fixed, as they receive its structure. The fixed-candidate-set premise therefore holds as before and the guarantee is unchanged. A fitted constant is one more way the search adapts to its sample, so with selection_holdout=None, where search and screen share rows, it adds to the optimism for which the estimator already declines the claim. On pure-noise targets (50 seeds, 200 rows, 5 columns, defaults otherwise) the fraction of fits with any discovery was the same with all four fitted operators as without: 0/50 for regression, 2/50 for classification. The four are on by default, and with them the end-to-end study above gives the same result as without them (no false discovery in 200 replicates, power 1.000, nothing selected in 60 global-null replicates).

magnitude_slots changes which expressions the search keeps, not how they are tested. Its magnitude score is computed inside the search, on the search rows, as the score is; the expressions it keeps are built on and ranked like any other; and the selection rows receive the search's output as a fixed set of expressions, chosen without them. The premise of the screen holds as before and its guarantee is unchanged. Measured on 200 paired replicates per design at q = 0.1 (benchmarks/search_stress/null.py, the screened set), the share of fits with at least one false discovery was the same with the option as without on four null designs, 0.015 to 0.025, among them centred and Gaussian inputs and 200 columns on 150 search rows; on a planted x0*x1*x2 among centred distractors it was 0.025 against 0.020, one fit in 200, with a false discovery rate of 0.005 either way. With the slots on, as they are by default for regression, the end-to-end study gives the result it gave without them: no false discovery in 200 replicates, power 1.000, nothing selected in 60 global-null replicates. At the defaults, with the slots and the denominator guard, the pure-noise pipeline stress gives BH 7/100 and BY 1/100.

residual_slots changes only which expressions the search returns, in the same way: its forward path runs inside the search, on the search rows, and the terms it adds reach the screen as fixed expressions like the rest. The guarantee is unchanged. On the six designs of null.py (four null, two planted), 200 paired replicates each, the share of null fits with any false discovery was 0.015 to 0.020 with the option and without it; in one replicate of the wide design the default screened three false features and the option none. On the planted designs the option added one false feature in 4 fits of 200, each a fit that also screened the law: the share of fits with any went from 0 to 0.020 on x0*x1/x2 and from 0.020 to 0.040 on x0*x1*x2, and the false discovery rate from 0.0000 to 0.0004 and from 0.0047 to 0.0055 (benchmarks/search_stress/results/residual_slots/).

docs.title: Columns inside a term (input_test)
docs.text:
The screen's null is that a term is independent of the target, so (x0*x1)/(x1 + x8) is a true discovery when y = x0*x1: x0*x1 carries it, however unrelated x8 is. A reader of the equation still takes x8 to matter. input_test=True tests each column inside each candidate that reads more than one: the column's rows are permuted, wherever it occurs in the expression, and the screen's statistic is recomputed. The null for a column is that it is independent of the target and of the candidate's other columns together; under it, with independent rows from one distribution, permuting the column leaves the distribution of the data unchanged, so the p-values are exact. The screen's step-up correction runs across every (candidate, column) pair of every candidate, so which pairs are tested does not depend on the screen's outcome. A screened term is dropped before parsimony when the test fails to reject the null for any of its columns; input_report_ lists every pair, with null_rejected marking the pairs whose null the test rejected.

What it does not cover: a junk column correlated with a real one is not null in this sense, so its null can be rejected and the term kept. Testing it given the other columns needs a model of the column given the others (knockoffs or the conditional randomisation test), which this test does not assume. The screen's guarantee is unchanged and still covers the screened set.

Measured on 20 seeds of y = x0*x1 plus 25% noise among 10 junk columns (500 training and 500 test rows), against the default: printed equations with a junk column 14 → 1, printed terms with one 23/45 → 1/28, held-out R² 0.9413 → 0.9416. With the junk x8 correlated 0.82 with x1, 10 → 3. On pure-noise targets the screen rejects no null with the option or without it, and the physics panel is unchanged. On the release comparison's 12 real datasets (benchmarks/three_settings/) held-out score fell on 7, by 0.06 at most, and fits took 3.6 times as long.

docs.title: Parsimony within the screened set
docs.text:
Three things can be wanted of the fitted equation: that it be short, that the guarantee cover the terms actually printed, and that it cost no selection rows. Any two are available together, and the choice is one parameter. Choosing a setting sets the default beside parsimony_alpha and input_test on the same data.

parsimony="forward" (the default) applies greedy forward selection within the screened set and fits the compact subset. It is short and costs no rows. What it gives up is the second property: the subset is chosen on the rows selection already used, so the q-level guarantee certifies the set it was drawn from and not the terms the forward step retained. equation() says so on its own output whenever terms were dropped —

y = 0.9999*(x0 * x1) - 0.003943   [1 of 25 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 25]

— and fdr_scope_ records the same thing for code, which never sees that string: "screened set" here, "printed equation" when the guarantee covers the returned features themselves. fdr_controlled_ says whether there is a guarantee; fdr_scope_ says what it is over. The full screened set with exact p- and q-values per candidate stays auditable in selection_report_. fdp_inflation_ reports |S|/|S'|, the factor by which pruning can inflate the realised false discovery proportion: the denominator shrinks faster than the numerator, so the count of false discoveries cannot rise but the proportion can.

parsimony=None prints the screened set entire. The guarantee covers what is printed — the equation is the certified object, not a selection from it — and it still costs no rows. The price is length: on wide data the equation runs to dozens of terms. fdp_inflation_ is 1.0, because the printed set and the screened set are the same set.

parsimony_holdout buys both, and pays in rows. It splits the selection rows again: screening and parsimony use the first part, and the resulting subset — fixed at that point, and so an ordinary fixed-candidate set — is re-tested on the part held back. Terms whose null the re-test fails to reject are dropped, and because the guarantee then does cover the printed terms, equation() prints no subset note. The cost is real: comfortable above a few hundred rows, unaffordable below roughly a hundred, where parsimony=None is the better choice. If a compact certified equation cannot be produced, the whole screened set is returned rather than a pruned subset — the pruned subset is the one thing a caller asking for certification did not want.

Measured. benchmarks/parsimony_holdout/ calibrates the procedure over 48,000 fits: a global null, and y = a*b/c plus noise among 5 or 20 distractors, with and without a column correlated 0.9 with a, at signal-to-noise ratios 1 and 3 and with 300 and 1,000 rows, 200 replicates per cell, at q = 0.1 and 0.2, beside the default and parsimony=None on the same data. The figures below are means over replicates. Their Monte Carlo standard errors are in the study's report, and are at most 0.012 for a design pooled over its four cells.

  • In the marginal sense, the guarantee's, the printed equation's realised FDR stayed far below q under every setting. On the global null it was 0.009 to 0.018 at q = 0.1 and 0.021 to 0.029 at q = 0.2 (a term printed in 7 to 14 and 17 to 23 fits of 800), and on the planted and proxy designs no setting printed a term built only from distractors in 3,200 fits per level. The re-test added nothing measurable here. On null data it failed to reject the null for the screen's rare false discoveries, in 20 of 22 fits at q = 0.1, and the fallback to the screened set then printed them anyway, so the printed equation's error is the screen's own.
  • In the conditional sense, counting a printed term that uses any column outside the generating formula, such as a rider (a*b/c) * x7, no setting controls the rate and the marginal re-test does not lower it. It was 0.67 to 0.77 under every setting at a signal-to-noise ratio of 1, where the forward step retains 18 terms on average. At a ratio of 3 it was 0.42 to 0.44 at the default and 0.53 to 0.62 with the re-test: on its smaller share of rows the forward step retains more riders, and each rider is associated with the target, so the re-test rejects its null.
  • Power to print the generating term (0.85 to 0.93 at a ratio of 1, 0.99 to 1.00 at 3) and held-out R² (within 0.0033 of the default, paired) hardly moved under any setting.

certify_test="conditional" re-tests each frozen term given the others rather than on its own, with a Freedman–Lane permutation test (Freedman & Lane, 1983): the target and the term are residualised on the other terms and an intercept, the target's residuals are permuted, the statistic is the partial correlation, and the screen's step-up correction is applied at the screen's level. The null for a term is that its coefficient is zero in the linear model of the target on all the frozen terms: given the others, it adds nothing linear. That null is relative to the frozen set, so a term standing in for a true one the set leaves out is not null under it, and rejecting its null is not a false rejection. The p-values are approximate. For a single term the test is the marginal permutation test and exact. With others present its validity rests on the errors of a linear model of the target on the other terms being exchangeable (independent and identically distributed, so of constant variance), and even then the residuals it permutes are estimated and only nearly exchangeable, so the p-values are close to exact rather than exact (Anderson & Robinson, 2001; Winkler et al., 2014). The test is for regression only, and the step-up correction inherits its own condition: Benjamini–Yekutieli holds under any dependence among the p-values, Benjamini–Hochberg needs positive dependence.

Measured in the same study, at a signal-to-noise ratio of 3 it brought the conditional rate to 0.18 to 0.22, paired −0.21 to −0.26 against the default. In the fits where it rejected at least one null it printed 1.1 to 1.2 terms, with a conditional rate of 0.026 to 0.040 at q = 0.1 and 0.052 to 0.073 at q = 0.2, and power 0.98 to 0.99. Its weakness is the fallback. When the frozen subset is long and its terms nearly reproduce one another, no term adds anything given the rest, the test rejects no null, and the screened set is returned, which carries the screen's marginal guarantee only. That happened in 87 to 92% of fits at a ratio of 1 and in 18 to 26% at 3 (37 to 52% with 300 rows, under 1% with 1,000). certification_result_.n_selected is 0 on such a fit. With the chance check below, the fallback all but disappears: under 1% of fits at a ratio of 1. The conditional re-test after the forward step without parsimony_alpha raises a ValueError. With parsimony=None, which re-tests the whole screened set, it needs no parsimony_alpha.

The forward step's chance check, parsimony_alpha. The riders above are a property of the forward step's stopping rule. The best of the many remaining terms adds more than parsimony_tol to R² by fitting noise alone: on n rows its chance gain is about the largest of m χ²₁ draws over n, times the share of variance left, so around 0.01 to 0.03 at signal to noise 1 on 500 to 150 selection rows, against a tolerance of 0.001. parsimony_alpha (off by default) also stops the step at the first term whose gain fails to reject the null that it is no larger than the best gain the remaining terms reach against noise. The null distribution is that best gain for 200 wild-bootstrap draws of the current residual, each row's residual times an independent standard normal, net of the terms already added: the multiplier bootstrap of Fan & Zhou (2016) for the best spurious fit. On columns that add nothing beyond the chosen one, five of them correlated with it, it rejected in 4% of 400 trials at level 0.05 and 10% at 0.10. It shapes the returned subset, as parsimony_tol does, and leaves the screen and its guarantee alone; it is a stopping rule, not a guarantee on the subset. benchmarks/parsimony_holdout/parsimony_alpha.py reran the designs above at q = 0.1, 50 replicates per cell, with parsimony_alpha=0.05:

design setting terms FDR, conditional power held-out R² planted, snr 1 default 18.4 0.703 0.890 0.482 planted, snr 1 parsimony_alpha=0.05 1.1 0.048 0.875 0.489 planted, snr 3 default 3.8 0.420 1.000 0.897 planted, snr 3 parsimony_alpha=0.05 1.1 0.022 1.000 0.899 proxy, snr 1 default 18.1 0.738 0.895 0.481 proxy, snr 1 parsimony_alpha=0.05 1.1 0.080 0.865 0.489 proxy, snr 3 default 4.0 0.429 1.000 0.897 proxy, snr 3 parsimony_alpha=0.05 1.1 0.020 1.000 0.899

Held-out R² rose by 0.007 to 0.008 on average at signal to noise 1, paired, and by 0.002 at 3, but 9% of the fits at 1 lost more than 0.01 and the worst lost 0.10. Those were fits on 300 rows whose first term only approximates a*b/c with a distractor inside, such as (x1 + x10) * (x0 / x2): the check stops after it, where the default's further terms made up part of the difference. Under the global null nothing changed. Combined with parsimony_holdout=0.3, certify_test="conditional", the re-test receives a short subset, so its fallback to the screened set went from 92% of fits at signal to noise 1 and 20 to 24% at 3 to under 1%, and the conditional rate was 0.07 to 0.09 at 1 and 0.000 at 3; power at 1 fell to 0.82, from 0.88 to 0.90.

On real data the check costs accuracy. These designs have one strong term and noise; real targets tend to carry many modest effects, each of which adds little on its own, often less than the best of the remaining terms reaches against noise, so the step stops after a few terms: one to five on 10 of these 12 datasets. In benchmarks/three_settings/, on the datasets and splits of benchmarks/release_comparison/ (5 splits each, 70/30), held-out score fell by more than 0.005 on 9 of 12 real datasets, was within 0.005 on 2, and rose on one:

dataset rows (train) default parsimony_alpha=0.05 diabetes 309 0.433 (6.6 terms) 0.381 (1.4) tips 170 0.472 (8.6) 0.433 (1.0) penguins 239 0.803 (7.8) 0.768 (1.4) riboflavin 49 0.516 (18.6) 0.489 (1.0) breast_cancer (accuracy) 398 0.971 (25.8) 0.952 (2.8) communities 1,395 0.647 (11.6) 0.629 (2.4) mpg 274 0.868 (9.4) 0.858 (1.6) superconduct 3,500 0.747 (18.8) 0.737 (12.6) california_housing 14,448 0.690 (21.2) 0.681 (13.4) diamonds 980 0.852 (3.4) 0.851 (1.0) tecator 168 0.992 (3.0) 0.991 (2.2) eyedata 84 0.321 (30.6) 0.330 (1.0)

The one gain is on eyedata, where the default fits 31 terms to 84 training rows. Two synthetic targets built from many terms behaved like the real ones (friedman1 0.796 to 0.759, threshold_step 0.841 to 0.808). The check suits a search for a short law, where the target is a few strong terms; for prediction, leave it off.

The equation list. equations() and equations_ record the forward path through the whole screened set, one equation per number of terms, at every setting above. Each line is a subset of the screened set chosen on the rows screening used, the same kind of selection as the default fitted equation, so the guarantee covers none of them but the last, which is the screened set itself, and, under parsimony_holdout, the re-tested fitted equation. An equation picked from the list after reading it is not covered; the list says so in its last line.

docs.title: What the default costs
docs.text:
The exchange above is stated rather than assumed elsewhere in this page, so it is measured here. benchmarks/parsimony_cost.py re-runs the affected studies at both settings and pairs them fit by fit; benchmarks/PARSIMONY_COST.md records which studies depend on the setting and why. Over 308 paired fits across four studies:

study fits mean ΔR² (forward − None) worst ΔR² terms, None ÷ forward fdr_controlled_ disagreements end-to-end calibration 260 −0.0001 −0.0003 25.0× 0 known-formula + stress suites 18 −0.0008 −0.0148 26.0× 0 Feynman physics panel 24 −0.0009 −0.0111 30.6× 0 Friedman #1 decomposition 6 −0.0095 −0.0192 3.6× 0

Compactness costs about a thousandth of R² on average and at most 0.019 on a single fit, and buys an equation roughly twenty-five times shorter. R² is held out in every study but the end-to-end calibration, which fits and scores on the same rows. fdr_controlled_ never disagreed between the two settings on any of the 308 fits, and the end-to-end calibration figures above — empirical FDR, its upper bound, power, fallbacks, null selections — are identical at both settings to every digit reported.

Pruning was also never observed to inflate the realised false discovery proportion. That is not a theorem and should not be read as one: |S|/|S'| is the only bound available, and it is weak. It is an empirical observation with a mechanism behind it — greedy forward selection ranks by predictive contribution, and a marginally null feature contributes nothing, so it tends to be dropped first rather than kept. On a selector-level stress where screening was made to reject many true nulls (Gaussian design, nominal q = 0.5, 300 trials), the screened set realised FDP 0.397 and the greedily pruned subset realised 0.000, with the proportion rising in none of the 300 trials.

docs.title: Association is not generalisation
docs.text:
FDR screening bounds the expected share of selected features that are not associated with the target. It does not certify that the linear model assembled from them generalises: a true discovery can carry extreme leverage — a reciprocal or logarithm evaluated near its pole — that destabilises the least-squares fit at points close to the singularity. The estimators keep these claims separate with a post-fit check on the selection holdout: a negative held-out R² (regression) or held-out accuracy below the majority-class rate (classification) raises a visible DegenerateFitWarning naming the gap. Rank-based scoring deserves particular attention here, since rank transformation hides exactly the magnitudes that cause the problem.

New rows can reach a pole the training rows stayed clear of. The search rules out a quotient whose denominator comes within the pole margin of zero on the search rows, and predict and transform raise ExtrapolationWarning when a new row takes a feature more than one width of its training range beyond it. Neither touches the screen or its guarantee; New rows beyond the training data describes both.

docs.title: When no null is rejected
docs.text: When the screen rejects no null, the default (on_no_discoveries="empty") uses no constructed features: the model degrades to an intercept-only fit (training mean, or class prior for classification), fdr_controlled_ is False, and a visible NoDiscoveriesWarning is raised. "fallback" uses the unfiltered search output, also with fdr_controlled_ = False; "raise" raises. In every mode, check fdr_controlled_ before treating fitted features as statistically vetted.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Three levels, depending on what you need. Most people only need the first.

docs.title: Use the library
docs.text:
pip install beamfeat              # numpy, scikit-learn, joblib
pip install "beamfeat[units]"     # + pint, for dimensional analysis
pip install "beamfeat[display]"   # + sympy, for to_sympy() and latex()
pip install "beamfeat[all]"       # + both, pandas and the test dependencies

Python 3.10 or newer. There are no upper version pins. The test suite is run against the newest releases on Python 3.10 to 3.15, where all 1,079 tests pass (scikit-learn 1.9.1 from Python 3.11, and 1.7.2, the newest that supports it, on 3.10; numpy 2.2 to 2.5), and against the oldest supported stack (scikit-learn 1.6.1, numpy 1.26, joblib 1.2), which leaves pint and pandas out so that the tests that need them show they skip cleanly without them. CI repeats this every week, and runs the suite against the upcoming releases of numpy, SciPy, scikit-learn and pandas too, so that a breaking change upstream is seen before it ships.

Nothing below is needed to use beamfeat.

docs.title: Run the test suite
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/LD-Shell/beamfeat
cd beamfeat
pip install -e ".[all]"
pytest

1,079 tests, a few minutes, including scikit-learn's check_estimator conformance suite. pytest --cov=beamfeat reports 97% statement coverage.

The units extra matters here: without pint, every unit-aware test skips (listed with its reason by pytest -rs) and coverage reads about 95%. [all] includes it.

docs.title: Reproduce the benchmarks
docs.text:
Only needed to regenerate the published comparison figures. The competing tools constrain the environment sharply, so this gets its own:

  • autofeat 2.1.3 requires scikit-learn below 1.8 and, through numba, numpy 2.2 or lower
  • current knockpy releases require numpy 2 or newer, and must therefore be installed under the same pins rather than added afterwards
conda create -n af315 python=3.11 -y
conda activate af315
bash benchmarks/independent/setup_env.sh

That installs the pinned dependencies, beamfeat from the working tree, JupyterLab and a Jupyter kernel, then prints the resolved versions and runs smoke tests for autofeat and knockpy. It refuses to install into a base or system interpreter, since the pins would downgrade a general-purpose environment. A plain python -m venv works equally well.

Then, in that kernel:

notebook what it does runtime benchmarks/reproduce_all.ipynb regenerates every figure in the paper and on the Benchmarks page except those of the two studies below, and asserts the load-bearing ones 20-30 min benchmarks/independent/beamfeat_benchmark.ipynb the comparison against autofeat, OpenFE, featuretools and raw baselines 2 min from archived results, 45-70 min with FULL_RUN = True

The higher-dimensional studies have their own driver, benchmarks/additional_experiments/run_all.ipynb, and python benchmarks/figures/tecator.py redraws the figure on the home page from their archived run in a few seconds.

Three studies need none of the competing tools and run wherever beamfeat is installed: the release comparison (benchmarks/release_comparison/), the three settings (benchmarks/three_settings/) and the chemometrics baselines on tecator (benchmarks/tecator_chemometrics/). Each folder's PROVENANCE.md gives its commands and the versions it pinned.

The scripts build their estimators at the current defaults. To run one at the defaults of the archived runs, set them through the options launcher:

BEAMFEAT_OPTIONS='{"fitted_ops": [], "magnitude_slots": 0}' \
    python benchmarks/search_stress/with_options.py benchmarks/run_benchmarks.py

The guard against quotients near zero has no switch, so an exact reproduction of a run made before 0.7.0 needs the release that made it.

reproduce_all.ipynb also builds a throwaway virtual environment with the newest numpy and scikit-learn and runs the suite there, so the pinned kernel does not become the only evidence that the package works on current releases.

docs.title: Migrating from autofeat
docs.text:
Examined against autofeat 2.1.3, the current release as of July 2026, in the pinned comparison environment (scikit-learn 1.7.2); the version-compatibility failures below were reproduced on scikit-learn 1.8 and 1.9.

beamfeat's design began from a review of autofeat (Horn et al., 2019) and keeps its central idea — compact symbolic features feeding a linear model. The APIs are close enough that most code ports in a few lines. This page is a reference for doing so; it is not a claim that one tool supersedes the other, and autofeat's exhaustive expansion still finds structure a beam search prunes (see the Where autofeat does better section below).

docs.title: Version compatibility
docs.text:
If you arrived here from an error, this is likely the one:

TypeError: check_array() got an unexpected keyword argument 'force_all_finite'

autofeat 2.1.3 raises this when transforming or predicting on unseen data after engineering at least one feature, on scikit-learn ≥ 1.8 — the argument was renamed ensure_all_finite in 1.6 and removed in 1.8. fit still succeeds, so the failure appears only when you apply the fitted model to a test set. Its declared pins (numpy<2.0, pandas<3.0) will also downgrade a current environment on installation.

beamfeat declares no upper version bounds and its test suite runs unpatched from scikit-learn 1.6 through 1.9.

docs.title: Class mapping
docs.text: autofeat beamfeat AutoFeatRegressor BeamFeatRegressor AutoFeatClassifier BeamFeatClassifier AutoFeatModel, FeatureSelector BeamFeatTransformer

docs.title: Parameter mapping
docs.text: autofeat beamfeat notes feateng_steps=2 max_depth=2 same meaning: composition depth featsel_runs=5 (no equivalent) selection is a single FDR-controlled test; tune target_fdr (default 0.1) instead of a repetition count transformations=('1/','exp','log','abs','sqrt','^2','^3') unary_ops=("reciprocal","exp","log","abs","sqrt","square","cube") all seven exist; beamfeat's default omits exp and cube (no equivalent) binary_ops=("mul","div","add","sub") binary operators are configurable units={...}, apply_pi_theorem=True units={...} accepts pint quantities or strings ("kg", "m / s**2"); enforced at expression construction rather than as a separate theorem pass categorical_cols=[...] (not supported) compose explicitly: make_pipeline(ColumnTransformer(...), BeamFeatRegressor(...)) feateng_cols=[...] (not supported) subset X before fitting n_jobs=1 n_jobs=1 parallelises the search over cores; the fitted result is the same for every value verbose=0 verbose=0 same

docs.title: Fitted attributes
docs.text: autofeat beamfeat new_feat_cols_ feature_formulas_, or formulas() good_cols_ formulas() (post-selection) prediction_model_ model_ (no equivalent) fdr_controlled_ — whether the returned features carry the FDR guarantee (no equivalent) selection_report_ — per-candidate p-values, q-values, and screening decisions (no equivalent) equation() — the fitted model as a readable equation (no equivalent) equations() — the equation at every size along the forward path (no equivalent) latex() — the fitted equation typeset for a document

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
# autofeat
from autofeat import AutoFeatRegressor
model = AutoFeatRegressor(feateng_steps=2, featsel_runs=5, verbose=0)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(model.new_feat_cols_)
predictions = model.predict(X_test)

# beamfeat
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor
model = BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, target_fdr=0.1, random_state=0)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(model.formulas())
print(model.equation())          # the fitted model, readable
print(model.fdr_controlled_)     # check before treating features as vetted
predictions = model.predict(X_test)

docs.title: Where autofeat does better
docs.text: Exhaustive expansion does not need to see a signal marginally in order to generate the right basis. On targets with a strong non-monotone interaction — Friedman #1 is the standard example — autofeat's brute-force expansion finds structure that correlation-guided beam search prunes. On four of five splits of Friedman #1 it reaches R² 0.94 to 0.96 where beamfeat reaches 0.72 to 0.79; on the fifth it returns −103. Take the win on the typical split as real and the mean as unusable, which is the shape of the trade: beamfeat accepts a lower ceiling as the price of a guarantee and a floor. Quantified in Statistical guarantees.

docs.title: Behavioural differences to expect
docs.text:
• Fewer features. Selection is a multiple hypothesis test rather than a noise-threshold heuristic: a feature is selected when the test rejects its null, and a parsimony step then retains a compact subset of the selected features. Expect single-digit feature counts where autofeat returns tens. equation() records how many of the certified terms it printed, and parsimony=None returns the whole certified set if you want it.
  • A guarantee, and an honest empty result. If the screen rejects no null, beamfeat returns no constructed features, warns, and sets fdr_controlled_ = False rather than returning unvetted candidates. Check that flag.
  • Determinism. random_state makes the whole pipeline reproducible, whatever n_jobs is set to. autofeat exposes none, and cannot be made reproducible from outside: its noise-injection screen draws decoy features from the global NumPy generator before its own internal seeding applies, so each process starts from different entropy. Six runs of one identical split returned R² from +0.952 to −109.8.
  • Constants inside expressions. autofeat fits none. beamfeat fits one constant inside an expression by default, such as exp(-3.2 x) or 1/(x + a) (fitted_ops; fitted_ops=() turns it off). If a law needs several constants fitted jointly, a symbolic regressor such as PySR is the right instrument.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Install beamfeat, fit a model and read what it prints. Every example runs as shown, and the outputs are from real runs. The Getting started tutorial covers the same ground in a notebook.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install beamfeat              # core: numpy, scikit-learn, joblib
pip install "beamfeat[units]"     # + pint, for dimensional analysis
pip install "beamfeat[display]"   # + sympy, for to_sympy() and latex()
pip install "beamfeat[all]"       # + both, pandas and the test dependencies

See Installation for running the test suite or reproducing the benchmarks.

docs.title: Sixty seconds to a vetted equation
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(1, 6, (400, 4))
y = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 0.05, 400)

model = BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, beam_width=25, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
print(model.equation())
print(model.fdr_controlled_)

y = 0.9999*(x0 * x1) - 0.003943   [1 of 25 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 25]
True

Three things matter. equation() is the fitted model itself — evaluate it on raw feature values and you reproduce predict(). fdr_controlled_ states whether the features carry the false-discovery-rate guarantee; check it before treating them as statistically vetted. And the suffix says that those two do not describe the same set of terms; Reading a fit explains it.

That last point has an attribute as well as a suffix, because a script never reads the printed string:

print(model.fdr_controlled_, "|", model.fdr_scope_)

True | screened set

fdr_controlled_ says whether there is a guarantee. fdr_scope_ says what it is over: "screened set" when the printed terms were pruned from a larger certified set, "printed equation" when the guarantee covers the terms you are looking at, None when there is no guarantee to scope. Branch on fdr_scope_, not on the equation text.

docs.title: Column names flow into formulas
docs.text:
Fit on a DataFrame and formulas use your names:

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"mass": rng.uniform(1, 5, 300),
                   "vol":  rng.uniform(1, 5, 300)})
target = df["mass"] / df["vol"] + rng.normal(0, 0.02, 300)
print(BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0).fit(df, target).formulas())

['(mass / vol)']

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
BeamFeatClassifier prints the log-odds of the positive class, whose zero level set is the decision boundary:

from beamfeat import BeamFeatClassifier

labels = (X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] > X[:, 2] * X[:, 3]).astype(int)
clf = BeamFeatClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(X, labels)
print(clf.equation(max_terms=3))

logit P(y = 1) = 1.678*((x0 / x2) - log(x3)) - 0.1561*((x2 * x3) - (x0 * x1)) - 1.014*((x2 / x1) + (x3 / x0)) + 1.101   [20 of 50 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 50; parsimony_alpha=0.05 prints 2]

The fitted equation has 20 terms; max_terms=3 displays the three with the largest standardised coefficients and holds the rest at their training mean. With parsimony_alpha=0.05 the model itself has two terms, and its accuracy on 2,000 new rows is about the same, 0.981 against 0.979:

short = BeamFeatClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0, parsimony_alpha=0.05).fit(X, labels)
print(short.equation())

logit P(y = 1) = - 0.526*((x2 * x3) - (x0 * x1)) - 1.005*((x2 / x0) + (x3 / x1)) + 2.455   [2 of 50 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 50]
