docs.title: Choosing a setting
docs.text:
Every fit runs the same search and the same screen, and the screen's FDR guarantee covers the same certified set whatever the setting. What changes is which certified formulas the printed equation uses. The default and two options cover what most fits need:

you want write the printed equation the cost the best prediction BeamFeatRegressor() the formulas that predict best; on a noisy target, some extra terms none a short equation BeamFeatRegressor(parsimony_alpha=0.05) usually one to three terms some accuracy where the target is not one compact formula every column tested BeamFeatRegressor(input_test=True) no formula with a column whose null the test fails to reject 2 to 7 times the fit time, and some accuracy on real data

The same parameters work on BeamFeatClassifier and BeamFeatTransformer, and the two options combine.

docs.title: The three on one dataset
docs.text:
The target is x0 * x1 with 25% noise, among ten columns that play no part in it:

import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
X = rng.uniform(1, 6, (500, 12))
signal = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1]
y = signal + rng.normal(0, 0.25 * np.std(signal), 500)

for options in ({}, {"parsimony_alpha": 0.05}, {"input_test": True}):
    print(BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0, **options).fit(X, y).equation())

y = 1.052*(x0 * x1) - 0.4088*((x0 * x1) / (x0 + x6)) - 0.1452*((x3 / x0) - x1) + 0.1295*((x5 / x0) - x1) + 0.04642   [4 of 50 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 50; parsimony_alpha=0.05 prints 1, selection-row R^2 0.935 against 0.939]
y = 1.013*(x0 * x1) - 0.1608   [1 of 50 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 50]
y = 1.013*(x0 * x1) - 0.1608   [1 of 50 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 8; input_test dropped 42]

The default adds three terms to the product, and each brings in a column the target does not use: x6, x3 or x5. Each adds a little to R² on the rows the equation was chosen on, by fitting noise. The note at the end of the line says how much: parsimony_alpha=0.05 would print one term, for an R² of 0.935 against 0.939 on the selection rows, and it does stop before them. input_test drops 42 of the 50 certified formulas, those with a column whose null the test fails to reject, and the forward step then stops at the product.

docs.title: The default: the best prediction
docs.text:
BeamFeatRegressor() adds certified formulas to the equation while each adds at least 0.001 to R² (parsimony_tol). That is the right rule for prediction, and on a target with little noise the equation is short anyway. On a noisy target, though, the best of the many remaining formulas clears 0.001 by fitting noise alone, so the equation grows terms that each add a little. On y = x0/x1 among ten unrelated columns, with noise as large as the signal, the default printed a median of 9.5 terms, and 78 of its 92 terms over ten fits read an unrelated column.

Keep the default when prediction comes first, and read its equation with equations(), which shows how much each term adds. When parsimony_alpha=0.05 would print fewer terms, equation() ends with a note saying how many, and the R² of both equations on the selection rows; equations() marks that line a.

docs.title: A short equation: parsimony_alpha=0.05
docs.text:
The forward step also stops at the first term whose gain fails to reject the null that chance reaches it: the null distribution is the best gain the remaining formulas reach against noise. On the noisy x0/x1 above it printed the one true term in every fit, and its predictions were closer to the true function than the default's (R² 0.998 against 0.981).

Use it for an equation to read or report, or to look for a law. Real targets tend to carry many modest effects, each adding little, so the step stops after a few terms (one to five on 10 of 12 real datasets) and costs some accuracy: held-out score fell on 9 of the 12, by 0.01 to 0.05, and rose a little on eyedata, where the default fits 31 terms to 84 training rows. It is a stopping rule, not a guarantee on the terms it keeps. A short equation has the details.

docs.title: Every column tested: input_test=True
docs.text:
The screen tests each formula as a whole, so a formula that attaches an unrelated column to a true one, such as (x0 * x1) / (x0 + x6) when y = x0 * x1, is a true discovery. input_test=True tests each column inside each formula that reads more than one, by permuting that column's rows, and drops a certified formula when the test fails to reject the null that the column is independent of the target and of the formula's other columns.

Use it when every column in the equation must be shown to matter. It takes 2.4 to 7 times as long as the default (3.6 times on the real datasets), more on more rows, and n_jobs threads share the tests. Held-out score stayed within 0.005 of the default's on 5 of 12 real datasets and fell on 7, by 0.06 at most. It does not remove riders built only from the target's own columns, as parsimony_alpha does, and a junk column correlated with a real one is not null in its sense. Every column tested has the details.

docs.title: Both
docs.text: BeamFeatRegressor(parsimony_alpha=0.05, input_test=True) gives a short equation whose every column was tested. It is no more accurate than parsimony_alpha alone and takes as long as input_test.

docs.title: Tall data: max_search_rows
docs.text: The search's time and memory grow with its rows. On a tall table, BeamFeatRegressor(max_search_rows=10_000) runs the search on 10,000 of its rows, drawn at random, and the screen on every selection row as before, so the guarantee is unchanged. On 200,000 rows, a search on 10,000 of its 100,000 rows cut the median fit from 110 to 33 seconds. A product carrying 2% of the signal's variance, x4*x5, came out as x4 and x5 terms in every fit, as with the full search, and R² against the signal was 0.002 lower (benchmarks/search_rows/). Memory fell by a sixth only, since the screen and the final fit still see every row. A term weak enough to need every row to stand out can be lost.

docs.title: A target that switches: sign and sign_shift
docs.text:
A target that follows one formula on one side of a threshold and another on the other side is outside what products, quotients and smooth transforms build. The sign_shift operator, off by default, fits sign(x + a) with its threshold a, so that a term such as x2*sign(x0 - 0.7) can be built:

# The default fitted operators and sign_shift.
BeamFeatRegressor(fitted_ops=("exp_scaled", "pow", "inv_shift", "log_shift", "sign_shift"))

On y = s(x0)*x2 + x1, where s is 2 above a threshold on x0 and -1 below it, it printed the switch term in all 20 fits and predicted the target to R² 0.997 to 0.999, against 0.76 to 0.88 for the default and 0.983 to 0.996 for gradient-boosted trees; on the main suite's threshold_step it raised held-out score from 0.841 to 0.999. Where the target does not switch it changes little, though it lowered the classifier's accuracy on breast_cancer by 0.022. sign, listed in unary_ops, builds a switch at zero only, which sign_shift also finds. Switches at a threshold has the details.

docs.title: A law with a weak term: residual_slots=10
docs.text: The search ranks its candidates against the target, so a term much weaker than the leading one can be left out of the ranking, as log(x3) is from x0*x1/x2 + 0.5*log(x3). BeamFeatRegressor(residual_slots=10, parsimony_alpha=0.05) adds to the ranking the terms that explain what the leading ones leave, and stops the riders they would otherwise bring. On that law it printed the exact equation in 33 of 60 fits, the default in none. On the comparison's 11 real regression datasets its held-out score was within 0.005 of parsimony_alpha alone on 10, and 0.012 lower on California housing. A weak term beside a dominant one has the details.

docs.title: What was measured
docs.text:
benchmarks/three_settings/ fits the default, parsimony_alpha=0.05, input_test=True and both together on the same data with the same seeds:

default parsimony_alpha=0.05 input_test=True both Noise sweep, noise as large as the signal median terms 9.5 1 2 1 terms reading an unrelated column 78 of 92 0 of 10 3 of 21 0 of 10 R² against the true function 0.981 0.998 0.995 0.998 12 real datasets mean held-out score 0.693 0.675 0.675 0.667 mean terms 13.8 3.5 10.5 3.1 better / same / worse than the default — 1 / 2 / 9 0 / 5 / 7 1 / 1 / 10 18 synthetic datasets: within 0.005 of the default — 15 17 16 Fit time, × the default's 1 1.0 3.6 3.6 The paper's comparison study: mean R² (paper 0.803) 0.803 0.784 0.803 0.786

The noise sweep is ten fits of y = x0/x1 among ten unrelated columns; the real and synthetic datasets are those of the release comparison, five splits each. At the paper's own settings all four recover the same formulas, solve the same Feynman laws and print no formula built only from distractors, as the paper reports; the benchmark's report has every table.

Whatever the setting, a single fit shows one equation from one random split of the rows. stability_report refits on many splits and shows whether that equation is the only good one or one of many; run it before reading much into which formula was picked.

docs.title: Other options that change the equation
docs.text:
Two more options trade length against the guarantee:

  • parsimony=None prints every certified formula, so the guarantee covers the printed equation itself; on wide data that is dozens of terms.
  • parsimony_holdout re-tests the printed terms on rows held back for it, so the equation is short and the guarantee covers it; it costs those rows.

The printed equation describes both.

docs.title: When beamfeat is the wrong tool
docs.text: If a tree model beats beamfeat by a wide margin, your signal is likely piecewise, not algebraic. A single switch is within reach of sign_shift (above); for anything more piecewise, use the tree. fitted_ops covers one constant per operator, fitted one operator at a time; if your law needs several constants fitted jointly (exp(-a·x)·cos(b·x + c)), constants inside sums or products (a·x0 + b·x1 under a logarithm), or deeper nesting than the beam reaches, use a symbolic regressor such as PySR. The guarantees page states every boundary with the measurement behind it.

docs.title: User guide
docs.text:
The guide explains each part of a fit with examples you can run; the outputs shown are from real runs. Each page runs on its own: its first code block sets up the data the rest of the page uses. New to beamfeat? Start with the quickstart and choosing a setting.

docs.text:

max_depth, beam_width and the scorers are covered in the Search and scoring tutorial, and target_fdr, the selectors and their corrections in Selection and units and on the guarantees page. The API reference lists every parameter.

docs.title: Data and prediction
docs.text:
What beamfeat expects of a table, and how a fitted model behaves on new rows. The examples start from:

import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(1, 6, (400, 4))
y = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 0.05, 400)
model = BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, beam_width=25, random_state=0).fit(X, y)

docs.title: Columns that carry no data
docs.text:
A column with no variation cannot be selected: it standardises to zeros, so its association with the target is zero wherever it appears. That costs nothing, but it looks the same as a column that does not matter, so it is reported. Real tables have such columns more often than one would think: in the UJIIndoorLoc Wi-Fi fingerprints, dozens of access points never register.

stuck = np.full((400, 1), 9.81)               # a sensor stuck at one reading
BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0).fit(np.hstack([X, stuck]), y)

UserWarning: beamfeat: 1 of 5 columns are constant (x4) and cannot be selected.
They are ignored and cost nothing, but check whether they are meant to carry
data.

Constancy is relative to the column's magnitude, not an absolute floor on the spread — a column varying over 0 to 1e-9 has a smaller variance than a stuck sensor reading 9.81, and only the second is constant. Use is_constant to apply the same test when screening a table before fitting.

A constant with a genuine unit is a different matter: gravity is m/s² whether or not it varies, and expressions built from it are unit-checked, so label it. Its absence from a recovered formula is not a miss — a multiplicative constant is absorbed into the fitted coefficient rather than returned as a symbol.

docs.title: Real data with missing values or categoricals
docs.text:
beamfeat never imputes or encodes silently — compose explicitly:

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

pipe = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
                     BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0))

docs.title: Rows outside a formula's domain
docs.text:
A fitted formula can be undefined on new data that the training data never reached: log(x0) at a negative x0, or 1/(x0) at zero. Such a row is NaN in that formula's column of transform, and predict returns NaN for it; every other row gets exactly the value it would get on its own, whatever else is in the batch. A UserWarning names the formula and counts the rows. The classifier's predict cannot return NaN as a label, so it assigns those rows the most frequent training class, while predict_proba and decision_function return NaN for them, which is how to find them. The regressor's score raises rather than scoring the remaining rows.

Fitted constants do not change this. (x0)^1.5 is NaN for a negative x0, as sqrt(x0) is. A fitted pole keeps a margin from the training rows, but a row far enough outside them can still reach it: (x1)^(-0.5), fitted where x1 lies between 1 and 3, is infinite at x1 = 0, as 1/(x1) would be.

docs.title: Predicting with the original columns as well
docs.text:
The regressor predicts from the certified features alone, so the fitted model is the equation it prints. When accuracy matters more than a readable model, fit the final model on the original columns plus the certified features:

from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline, make_union
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

from beamfeat import BeamFeatTransformer

model = make_pipeline(
    make_union("passthrough", BeamFeatTransformer(random_state=0)),
    SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),  # rows outside a formula's domain
    StandardScaler(),
    RidgeCV(),
).fit(X, y)

This helps when the signal is spread thinly over many columns, which a few certified features cannot capture but a penalised fit on every column can, and when the certified features add structure a linear model on the raw columns misses. Two things change:

  • The model is no longer interpretable. It has a coefficient for every input column, so it reads like ridge regression, not like an equation.
  • The guarantee is unchanged but narrower in scope. The FDR guarantee covers which constructed features are reported, and those are the same as without the original columns. It says nothing about the coefficients the final model puts on the raw columns.

If the combined model scores no better than ridge on the original columns alone, the certified features are adding nothing to prediction on that data.

docs.title: New rows beyond the training data
docs.text:
A formula is fitted where the training rows lie, and beyond them it can behave unlike anything the fit saw. A ratio is the usual case: its denominator can stay clear of zero on the training rows and reach it a little beyond them, where the quotient takes any size and either sign. Two things guard against it.

The search rules out a quotient whose denominator crosses zero on the search rows, or comes closer to it than a margin: twice the spread of its ten values nearest zero, and at least 1% of its range. On the 172 training samples of tecator's own split, the denominator of (x41 - x43) / (x41 - x54) runs from -0.75 to -0.10, its ten values nearest zero spread over more than half their distance from it; on 986 of 1,000 random halves of those samples, the search rules the formula out.

predict, transform and the probability methods compare each feature on the new rows with its range on the training rows, kept in feature_ranges_, and raise ExtrapolationWarning when a row takes a feature more than one width of that range beyond it:

import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(1.0, 3.0, (400, 3))
y = X[:, 0] / X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 0.01, 400)
model = BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=1, beam_width=8, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
print(model.formulas(), model.feature_ranges_)

['(x0 / x1)'] [[0.35937791 2.7401815 ]]

new_rows = np.array([[2.0, 2.0, 2.0], [2.0, 0.1, 2.0]])
print(model.predict(new_rows))

ExtrapolationWarning: beamfeat: on 1 of 2 rows, a feature lies beyond its
training range by more than 1 width of that range: '(x0 / x1)' by up to 7.25
widths. The predictions on those rows extrapolate the equation, where a
formula can behave unlike anything the fit saw, such as a ratio whose
denominator nears zero; check them.
[ 1.00053387 19.99928935]

The predictions are returned unchanged. Here the formula is the law itself, so 20.0 is right: the warning cannot tell a law from a formula that only fits the training range. It says how many rows to check, and feature_ranges_ holds the ranges to find them. A row a little beyond the training range does not raise it, and a model saved with an earlier release has no feature_ranges_ and predicts without the check.

docs.title: Screening another tool's equation
docs.text: A symbolic regression tool such as PySR, Operon, gplearn or PySINDy reports an equation with no statement about whether its terms are real. screen_equation tests each term on rows the tool never saw, with the permutation test beamfeat's own fits use, and keeps the terms whose null is rejected under false discovery rate control. It needs sympy (pip install 'beamfeat[display]').

docs.title: Hold rows out, then screen
docs.text:
The guarantee needs rows the tool did not search. Split first, fit the tool on one part, and screen on the other:

import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from beamfeat import screen_equation

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(1, 3, size=(600, 4))
y = 1.5 * X[:, 0] + 0.8 * X[:, 1] ** 2 + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=600)
X_search, X_held, y_search, y_held = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.5, random_state=0)

# the tool searches X_search only; say it reports this equation
reported = "1.5*x0 + 0.8*x1**2 + 0.05*x0*x3 + 0.02*x2 + 0.1"

found = screen_equation(reported, X_held, y_held)
print(found.summary())

screen_equation: 3 of 4 terms kept (marginal BY at q = 0.1, 300 rows)
  [kept] 1.5*x0: p = 0.0004998, null rejected
  [kept] 0.8*x1**2: p = 0.0004998, null rejected
  [removed] 0.02*x2: p = 0.1654, null not rejected
  [kept] 0.05*x0*x3: p = 0.0004998, null rejected

Each top-level term of the sum is one candidate, and the constant is not a term. A term's null is that it is independent of y on these rows. The Benjamini-Yekutieli step-up, the default, controls the false discovery rate among the kept terms under any dependence between them; correction="bh" uses Benjamini-Hochberg, which needs positive dependence. The level is q (default 0.1).

With PySR, pass the model's equation directly: screen_equation(model.sympy(), X_held, y_held). A model fitted on an array names its columns x0, x1, ...; for a DataFrame, the equation uses its column names and screen_equation reads them from the DataFrame you pass, or from feature_names.

docs.title: Every column tested: the input test
docs.text:
Above, 0.05*x0*x3 is kept although x3 has nothing to do with y: the term rides on x0. input_test=True also tests each variable inside each term of more than one, by permuting that variable's rows inside the term alone:

found = screen_equation(reported, X_held, y_held, input_test=True)
print(found.summary())

screen_equation: 2 of 4 terms kept (marginal BY at q = 0.1, input test, 300 rows)
  [kept] 1.5*x0: p = 0.0004998, null rejected
  [kept] 0.8*x1**2: p = 0.0004998, null rejected
  [removed] 0.02*x2: p = 0.1654, null not rejected
  [removed] 0.05*x0*x3: p = 0.0004998, null rejected; inputs: x0 rejected, x3 not rejected

A variable's null is that it is independent of y and of the term's other variables together, and the step-up runs over the (term, variable) pairs. The test costs power where a tool's terms mix true and false variables, since it removes such a term whole. A variable correlated with a true input is not null in this sense, so the null of a stand-in for a true input can be rejected: no test of association can tell the two apart.

docs.title: What to do with the result
docs.text:
found.kept_terms holds the kept terms as the tool wrote them. To use them, refit their coefficients on the rows the tool searched, X_search, never on the rows that screened them. found.p_values, found.marginal, found.untestable and the input test's pairs and p-values are on the result as well (see the API reference).

A term undefined on any held-out row, or constant across them, cannot be tested: it is reported as untestable and never kept. A term the screen does not keep has no support on these rows, which is not a finding that it is false; with a few dozen rows a real term of modest effect is often not kept.

docs.title: A term the sum would split
docs.text:
sympy distributes a number over a sum, so reading 2*(x0 + x1) gives two terms. To test the terms exactly as a tool reported them, pass a list, each item tested whole:

screen_equation(["1.5*x0", "0.4*(x1**2 + x2)"], X_held, y_held)

docs.title: The printed equation
docs.text: The screen certifies a set of formulas, and the equation is chosen from that set. By default a forward step adds the certified formula that improves the fit most, one at a time, and stops when the next would add less than parsimony_tol (0.001) to R². The options on this page change that choice. None of them changes the search or the screen, so the FDR guarantee on the certified set is the same under each. Choosing a setting compares the default with the two options most fits need, parsimony_alpha and input_test.

docs.title: A short equation (parsimony_alpha)
docs.text:
On a noisy target the default keeps riders: the best of the many remaining formulas adds more than parsimony_tol to R² by fitting noise alone. parsimony_alpha=0.05 also stops the forward step at the first term whose gain fails to reject the null that chance reaches it. Here the target is x0 * x1 with 25% noise, among ten unrelated columns:

import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
X = rng.uniform(1, 6, (500, 12))
signal = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1]
y = signal + rng.normal(0, 0.25 * np.std(signal), 500)
print(BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0).fit(X, y).equation())
print(BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0, parsimony_alpha=0.05).fit(X, y).equation())

y = 1.052*(x0 * x1) - 0.4088*((x0 * x1) / (x0 + x6)) - 0.1452*((x3 / x0) - x1) + 0.1295*((x5 / x0) - x1) + 0.04642   [4 of 50 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 50; parsimony_alpha=0.05 prints 1, selection-row R^2 0.935 against 0.939]
y = 1.013*(x0 * x1) - 0.1608   [1 of 50 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 50]

The default's other three terms attach unrelated columns, x6, x3 and x5, to the product. At a signal-to-noise ratio of 1 the default printed 18 terms on average where one was true, and the check printed 1.1, with held-out R² slightly higher on average and a little lower in a few fits.

On real data the check costs accuracy. Real targets tend to carry many modest effects, each adding little, so the step stops after a few terms (one to five on 10 of 12 real datasets), and held-out score fell on 9 of the 12 (diabetes 0.433 to 0.381, tips 0.472 to 0.433). Use it to look for a short law, not for prediction. It is a stopping rule, not a guarantee on the terms it keeps; the path in equations() is the same either way, and only the marked line moves. Choosing a setting and the guarantees page have the figures.

docs.title: Every column tested (input_test)
docs.text:
The screen tests each term as a whole, so a term that attaches a junk column to the true one is still a true discovery: ((x0 * x1) / (x0 + x6)) is associated with the target through x0 * x1, however unrelated x6 is. input_test=True tests each column inside each term that reads more than one. The column's rows are permuted wherever it occurs in the expression, and its null is that it is independent of the target and of the term's other columns. A screened term is dropped before the forward step when the test fails to reject the null for any of its columns. On the same data:

print(BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0, input_test=True).fit(X, y).equation())

y = 1.013*(x0 * x1) - 0.1608   [1 of 50 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 8; input_test dropped 42]

input_report_ lists every (term, column) pair with its p- and q-value, and null_rejected marks the pairs whose null the test rejected. A junk column correlated with a real one is not null in this sense, so its null can be rejected and the term kept; the guarantees page states what the test covers. It is opt-in because its time grows with the rows: here the fit took about four times as long, and n_jobs threads share the tests.

docs.title: The whole certified set (parsimony=None)
docs.text: parsimony=None skips the forward step and fits every certified formula. The guarantee then covers the printed equation itself (fdr_scope_ is "printed equation"), and the equation is long: 25 terms in the first example of Reading a fit, dozens on wide data. equation(max_terms=...) shortens what is displayed without changing the model.

docs.title: Re-testing the printed terms (parsimony_holdout)
docs.text:
parsimony_holdout holds back that fraction of the selection rows. Screening and the forward step run on the rest, and the terms they return, fixed at that point, are tested again on the rows held back; terms whose null the re-test fails to reject are dropped. By default the re-test is the screen again (certify_test="marginal"), which tests each term's association with the target on its own. It rejects the null for a term that only rides on a true one, since such a term is associated with the target through the true one. certify_test="conditional" tests each term given the other printed terms instead:

import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(0.5, 3.0, (600, 8))
y = 2 * X[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, 0.5, 600)  # x0 alone

# Products only, and the whole screened set: every product of x0 with
# another column rides on x0, and the re-test sees them all.
options = dict(max_depth=1, binary_ops=("mul",), unary_ops=(), parsimony=None,
               parsimony_holdout=0.5, random_state=0)
marginal = BeamFeatRegressor(**options).fit(X, y)
conditional = BeamFeatRegressor(**options, certify_test="conditional").fit(X, y)
print(marginal.formulas())
print(conditional.equation())

['x0', '(x0 * x7)', '(x0 * x6)', '(x0 * x3)', '(x0 * x2)', '(x0 * x1)', '(x0 * x5)', '(x0 * x4)']
y = 2.009*x0 - 0.003251

The conditional re-test is a permutation test for regression only, and its p-values are approximate; the guarantees page states its null and what its validity rests on. It works when the subset it receives is short. On a long subset whose terms nearly reproduce one another, no term adds anything given the rest, the re-test rejects no null, and the estimator returns the whole screened set with only the screen's marginal guarantee (certification_result_.n_selected is 0, and a NoDiscoveriesWarning says so). After the forward step that happened in about nine fits in ten at a signal-to-noise ratio of 1 (benchmarks/parsimony_holdout/). So after the forward step the conditional re-test needs parsimony_alpha (above), which brings the fallback under one fit in a hundred; without it the combination raises a ValueError. The example above re-tests the whole screened set (parsimony=None) and needs no parsimony_alpha. Both re-tests cost rows: hold back a fraction only when the selection rows number a few hundred or more.

docs.title: Reading a fit
docs.text:
What a fitted model prints, what each part means, and what to check before relying on it. The examples continue from the quickstart's fit:

import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(1, 6, (400, 4))
y = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 0.05, 400)
model = BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, beam_width=25, random_state=0).fit(X, y)

docs.title: Why the equation says "1 of 25"
docs.text:
The screen rejected the null for twenty-five formulas, the certified set. Each formula's null is that it is independent of the target. On a strong signal every near-duplicate of the true feature really is associated with the target, so rejecting its null is correct. A forward step then picks the compact subset that predicts best, since an equation of dozens of near-duplicates would be unreadable.

The subset is chosen on the rows the screen already used, so the guarantee covers the twenty-five, not the one term printed. The suffix records that, and fdp_inflation_ prices it:

print(model.fdp_inflation_)

25.0

That is |S|/|S'|, the factor by which pruning can inflate the realised false discovery proportion. With parsimony=None the model fits the whole screened set, the printed equation is the certified set, and the suffix disappears:

full = BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, beam_width=25, random_state=0,
                         parsimony=None).fit(X, y)
print(full.n_features_out_)
print(full.equation(max_terms=3))

25
y = 0.077*(x1 * (x0 * x1)) + 0.4333*(x0 * x1) - 0.0842*((x0 * x1) / (1/(x1 - 8.17))) - 1.127

max_terms shortens the display, not the model: the terms it leaves out are held at their training mean, and their average contribution moves into the constant, which is why it differs from the full equation's.

The short equation costs little: about a thousandth of R² over 308 paired fits, for an equation about twenty-five times shorter, and pruning never inflated the realised false discovery proportion (benchmarks/PARSIMONY_COST.md). For an equation both short and certified, spend rows instead: Re-testing the printed terms.

docs.title: The equation at every size
docs.text:
The forward step adds terms one at a time and stops when the next adds less than parsimony_tol to R². equations() shows the step continued through the whole screened set, one equation per number of terms, so you can see what the stopping point traded away:

print(model.equations(max_n_terms=3))

Forward path through the 25 screened terms. R^2 is in-sample, on the rows screening used; gain is the R^2 the line's last term adds.
  k complexity    R^2      gain equation
* 1          4 0.9999    0.9999 y ~ (x0 * x1)
  2         12 0.9999  1.45e-06 y ~ (x0 * x1) + (1/(x0 - 8.1) * 1/(x1 - 8.17))
  3         18 0.9999 8.674e-07 y ~ (x0 * x1) + (1/(x0 - 8.1) * 1/(x1 - 8.17)) + ((x0 + x3) * x1)
  ...
* the fitted model (the forward step stops before the first gain below parsimony_tol=0.001).
The FDR guarantee covers the screened set of 25 terms (line 25), not an equation chosen from this list.

On a noisy target the marked line can sit further down the list, each term after the first adding a little by fitting noise. parsimony_alpha stops the step earlier; the list is the same, and only the marked line moves. At the default settings, a line marked a is where parsimony_alpha=0.05 would stop, and a footer line says so; equation() then ends with a note such as parsimony_alpha=0.05 prints 1, selection-row R^2 0.935 against 0.939. Neither appears when that level would print as many terms.

Complexity counts the nodes in each term's expression tree — operators and input columns, (x0 * x1) being 3 — plus one per term for its coefficient and one per fitted constant. The lines are written y ~ a + b, without coefficients, because only the marked one has been fitted; equation() prints its coefficients. For a classifier the R² is that of the integer-coded labels, the heuristic the forward step ranks by, not a classification metric.

Keep the output's last line in mind: every line is chosen on the rows the screen used, so picking line 3 because it looks better is the same kind of choice the forward step makes, and the guarantee covers it no more than the marked line. The records behind the text are in equations_, one dict per line (n_terms, complexity, r2, formulas, features, and model, which marks the fitted line).

docs.title: Audit what selection did
docs.text:
Every candidate's permutation p-value and its adjusted q-value is recorded:

for row in model.selection_report_[:3]:
    print(row["formula"], round(row["q_value"], 4), row["kept"])

A feature is kept only if the screen rejects its null at target_fdr (default 0.1, Benjamini–Yekutieli) on the held-out split and the parsimony step then retains it. screened marks the certified set, the candidates whose nulls the screen rejected, which is what the guarantee covers; kept marks the compact subset the equation prints. Set parsimony=None and the two agree.

docs.title: One equation or one of many
docs.text:
A fit prints one equation, found on one random split of the training rows into the part the search sees and the part selection tests on. Where many expressions predict about equally well, another split prints another equation, and nothing in a single fit says which case you are in. stability_report finds out. It refits clones of the estimator on random splits of the data, scores each once on a test part its fit never saw, and counts the distinct equations:

from beamfeat import stability_report

report = stability_report(BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, beam_width=25), X, y, n_splits=30)
print(report)

BeamFeatRegressor refitted on 30 random splits (random_state=0), each fitted on 300 rows and scored on the other 100.

Held-out R^2: mean 1.000, sd 0.000, min 1.000, max 1.000.
1 distinct equation in 30 splits: every split printed it.
1 distinct feature, selected in 30 of the 30 splits.

Equations printed in more than one split, most frequent first:
  30/30  y ~ (x0 * x1)

Features, most frequent first:
  30/30  (x0 * x1)

Features whose values on the rows of X correlate above 0.999 in absolute value are counted as one; an equation is the set of its features, whatever its coefficients.

Every split found the planted product. The diabetes data are another matter:

from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes

diabetes = load_diabetes(as_frame=True)
report = stability_report(BeamFeatRegressor(), diabetes.data, diabetes.target, n_splits=30)
print(report.summary(max_rows=3))

BeamFeatRegressor refitted on 30 random splits (random_state=0), each fitted on 331 rows and scored on the other 111.

Held-out R^2: mean 0.491, sd 0.052, min 0.395, max 0.575.
30 distinct equations in 30 splits; none recurs.
98 distinct features; the most frequent in 12 of the 30 splits.

Features, most frequent first:
  12/30  ((bmi + s5) + (bp - s3))
  10/30  ((bmi + s5) - (s3 + sex))
   7/30  ((bmi + s5) + (age * sex))
  ... and 95 more features

Features whose values on the rows of X correlate above 0.999 in absolute value are counted as one; an equation is the set of its features, whatever its coefficients.

No two of the thirty splits printed the same equation, and held-out R² ranges from 0.395 to 0.575, a spread one fit's score would hide. What recurs is a family of sums and differences of bmi, s5, bp and s3. Report that family, with its frequencies, rather than one equation.

What the report holds, and how it scores

Two formulas count as one feature when their values on the rows of X correlate above 0.999 in absolute value. A rewriting such as (x1 - x0) for (x0 - x1) is then not counted twice, and neither is a rescaling or a near-duplicate. An equation is the set of its features, whatever its coefficients. The report keeps everything behind the summary:

  • report.splits[i] has the rows split i was fitted and scored on, its formulas, its equation(), its score and the fitted clone;
  • report.features and report.equations hold the classes, most frequent first, each with the splits it appeared in;
  • report.scores holds the held-out scores.

The splits and the clones' seeds come from random_state (default 0), so a report is reproducible, and n_jobs fits splits in parallel processes without changing it. The regressor is scored by R² and the classifier by accuracy, as their score methods are. A transformer has no score of its own, so it is scored by a ridge regression on its features, or by a logistic regression for classification. When a test row is outside a selected formula's domain, the classifier predicts its most frequent training class there, as its predict does. A regressor or transformer has no score on such a test part, so that split goes unscored, and the summary counts it.

resample chooses what varies. The default, "splits", draws new training and test rows and a new seed for every split: how far the equation and its score move with another sample of the data. resample="seeds" keeps the first split's rows and varies only the seed, as in the paper's stability study (Appendix E): how much the equation owes to one random draw. On diabetes it still prints 30 distinct equations in 30 fits, but the standard deviation of R² falls from 0.052 to 0.009, so most of the score's spread comes from the test rows, while the turnover of equations remains.

docs.title: When no null is rejected
docs.text:
On a target with no structure the screen rejects no null, and the model says so instead of returning junk:

noise = np.random.default_rng(1).standard_normal(400)
empty = BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0).fit(X, noise)
# NoDiscoveriesWarning: ... Returning no constructed features ...
print(empty.equation())

y = -0.08207  (no feature selected)

Not on every draw. Under the global null every rejection is a false rejection, so the FDR is the probability that a fit rejects any null at all: up to target_fdr of pure-noise fits still certify features, and when one does, the nulls of correlated candidates tend to be rejected together. The same noise under another search seed can certify a dozen formulas with fdr_controlled_ = True: that is the error the guarantee bounds in expectation, not a breach of it.

Prefer the old behaviour? on_no_discoveries="fallback" keeps the unfiltered search output (flagged fdr_controlled_=False); "raise" raises.

docs.title: LaTeX
docs.text:
latex() typesets equation(): the same terms, coefficients and options (precision, max_terms, style), and the same note when the guarantee covers more terms than are printed. It needs sympy (pip install "beamfeat[display]"), as to_sympy() does.

print(model.latex())
print(model.latex_formulas())

y = 0.9999 x_{0} x_{1} - 0.003943 \quad \text{[1 of 25 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 25]}
['x_{0} x_{1}']

latex(note=False) leaves the note off, for pasting into a document; the guarantee still covers the screened set, so say so where the equation appears. The string has no math delimiters; wrap it in $...$, or in a notebook use IPython.display.Math(model.latex()). The classifier's latex() gives the log-odds of the positive class, or one softmax score per class in an aligned block, as its equation() does.

docs.title: Export to NumPy, JAX or PyTorch
docs.text:
to_sympy() returns each feature as a sympy expression in real symbols named after the input columns, so sympy.lambdify turns the features into a function for any array library sympy can print to. No extra dependency is involved beyond sympy and the target library:

import sympy

columns = sympy.symbols("x0:4", real=True)  # one symbol per input column, in order
features = sympy.lambdify(columns, model.to_sympy(), modules="numpy")

raw = model.coef_ / model.scaler_.scale_
offset = model.intercept_ - raw @ model.scaler_.mean_
prediction = np.column_stack(features(*X.T)) @ raw + offset  # model.predict(X), to rounding

modules="jax" or modules="torch" (sympy 1.14 or newer) gives the same function on JAX or PyTorch arrays, with jnp.stack(..., axis=1) or torch.stack(..., dim=1) in place of np.column_stack; the coefficients and offset are plain arrays to convert once. Columns of a DataFrame keep their names as symbols when the names are valid identifiers, and are sanitised otherwise; read the symbols from free_symbols of the expressions in that case.

Two differences from transform remain. sympy may rewrite an expression into an equivalent form, so a value can overflow in one and not the other. And a row outside a formula's domain gives whatever the array library gives there, with no warning from beamfeat.

docs.title: Search options
docs.text:
How the search builds its candidates, and the options that change what it can find and what it costs. The examples that use X and y start from:

import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(1, 6, (400, 4))
y = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 0.05, 400)
model = BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, beam_width=25, random_state=0).fit(X, y)

docs.title: Dimensional analysis
docs.text:
Give units as pint quantities or plain strings; dimensionally invalid expressions (metres plus kilograms) are ruled out before any numerical work — so x0 + x1 (kg plus m) is never even scored:

y_phys = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] / X[:, 2]          # kg·m/s
model = BeamFeatRegressor(
    units={"x0": "kg", "x1": "m", "x2": "s"}, random_state=0
).fit(X[:, :3], y_phys)
print(model.formulas())

['((x1 / x2) * x0)']

The recovered form, kg·m/s, is exactly the target's dimension — and the dimensionally invalid spellings never consumed a beam slot.

Give every column a unit. A column without one combines freely with the others, so the check stops binding on exactly the columns you left out. Give unitless columns "dimensionless"; the estimator warns when coverage is partial, and raises when no key matches a column. Keys are column names, so with a DataFrame you can write {"rho": "kg/m**3"}.

docs.title: Constants inside expressions
docs.text:
The linear model supplies the coefficients outside the expressions. That alone cannot write exp(-x²/2), x^1.5 or (x0 + x1)/(1 + x0·x1), where the constant sits inside a nonlinearity, so the estimators also use operators that carry one fitted constant each, listed in fitted_ops. All but sign_shift are on by default; fitted_ops=() keeps every expression free of constants and fits about twice as fast on small data. They are a list of their own: restricting unary_ops leaves them on, so unary_ops=() still allows log(x + a) unless fitted_ops=() too.

name expression operand "exp_scaled" exp(a·x) dimensionless "pow" x^a positive, dimensionless "inv_shift" 1/(x + a) any; a takes the operand's unit "log_shift" log(x + a) x + a positive, dimensionless "sign_shift", off by default sign(x + a) any; a takes the operand's unit (Switches at a threshold) 
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(0.1, 1.0, (500, 2))
y = np.exp(-X[:, 0] ** 2 / 2) + rng.normal(0, 1e-3, 500)
model = BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
print(model.formulas(), model.to_sympy())

['exp(-0.5*(x0)^2)'] [exp(-x0**2/2)]

With fitted_ops=() the same data give (x0 + (x0)^2) and log(x0), a surrogate that scores well on this range and says nothing about the law.

How the constants are chosen
  • Where. At each depth, every listed operator is fitted to every expression in the previous depth's beam (at the first depth, the beam_width best input columns), and to the previous depth's beam_width best candidates that the beam dropped as near-duplicates: two expressions that correlate at 0.95 need not stay alike under 1/(x + a) or exp(a·x). The results join that depth's candidates, to be scored, pruned and kept like any other. The ceiling max_candidates_per_depth counts the operator proposals only.
  • How. Each constant maximises the absolute correlation with the target: a coarse grid scaled to the operand (for exp_scaled, |a| up to 10/max|x|; for pow, a from -4 to 4; for the shifts, poles kept off the observed range; for sign_shift, the operand's 5% to 95% quantiles), then a golden-section refinement. A fit that runs to the edge of its grid is discarded, and so is one for which the likelihood-ratio test of the snapping step below does not reject the null that the operand on its own fits as well (each operator but sign_shift becomes linear in x at one end of its range, and sign_shift is held to the same test). Correlation is used whatever the scorer; the scorer then ranks the result.
  • Poles. inv_shift and log_shift keep their pole away from the data they were fitted on: at least twice the spread of the operand's ten most extreme values at that end, and at least 1% of its range. A pole just past the edge of the data is shaped by the few rows next to it, and the first new row a little further out falls beyond it: NaN for the logarithm, a value of the wrong sign and any size for the reciprocal. A fit that wants its pole closer runs into the bound and is discarded, and snapping never moves a constant past it. The margin widens where the data thin out towards the edge and narrows where they are dense. On 18 real datasets, poles inside it were crossed by a row the fit had not seen in 14% of fits, and poles outside it in 0.3%. A negative power has its pole at 0, so pow fits one only when the operand stays more than the same margin above 0. Otherwise a runs from 0.1 to 4, and a fit that wants less is discarded, since x^a then takes the shape of log(x), which has the same pole. The denominator of every quotient and reciprocal in the search keeps the same margin from zero, fitted constant or not; see New rows beyond the training data.
  • In context. 1/(x0·x1 + a) on its own correlates best with the target as a runs to the pole; only as the denominator of (x0 + x1) is a = 1 identifiable. While the depth limit leaves room, each constant is also fitted as a factor of a beam member, and that product joins the next depth's candidates.
  • Snapping. The constant is replaced by the simplest of 0, ±1, ±2, ±3, ±1/2, ±3/2, ±1/3, ±1/4 for which a likelihood-ratio test at level 0.001 fails to reject the null that the constant takes that value, so exp(-0.49991·x²) is reported as exp(-x²/2). If the test rejects every one of them, the constant is rounded to the fewest significant digits that cost nothing measurable. A snapped constant is exact in to_sympy(), latex() and the printed formulas.
  • Near copies. A fitted constant can also bend an expression into a near copy of a simple law. With 10% noise on log(x0), (x0)^(-0.02) correlates with log(x0) at 0.99999, and since its constant was fitted on the search rows it fits them a little better. So at the end of the search, each kept expression with fitted constants is compared with its near copies among everything the search found (correlation at redundancy_threshold) that carry fewer constants and are not near copies of another kept expression. The snapping test decides, on the same rows: if it fails to reject the null that a copy fits the target as well, the simplest such copy takes the expression's place. Without this step, log(x0), sqrt(x0), 1/x0 and x0² at that noise were printed as themselves in 0, 0, 2 and 2 of 10 fits; with it, in 10, 7, 10 and 8, against 10, 9, 10 and 8 with fitted_ops=(). A law that needs its constant keeps it while the data reject the simpler forms, as the Gaussian and relativistic velocity addition of the physics panel do at 0.1% noise.
  • Stored. The constant is part of the expression: transform, predict and a pickled model reuse it on new data without refitting.

The constants are fitted inside the search, on the search rows only, so the screen on the selection rows sees fixed expressions and its guarantee is unchanged; see the guarantees page.

What it costs. A fit on the Feynman panel takes about five times as long (0.2 s to 1.1 s per equation). Fitted expressions also take beam places, so they can change what else a depth keeps: a constant-free candidate can be out-ranked by a fitted one, though never dropped as its near-duplicate. And constants are fitted one at a time, greedily, so a law needs its constant-free parts among a depth's best candidates first.

docs.title: Laws whose parts the score cannot see
docs.text:
The search keeps, at each depth, the candidates that correlate best with the target and builds the next depth from them. A law can need a part that does not correlate with the target at all. With inputs centred on zero, x0 and x1 are each uncorrelated with x0*x1, and every pairwise product is uncorrelated with x0*x1*x2: the score ranks those parts among the noise, and the beam drops them before they can be combined. On positive inputs, as in most physical tables, each factor of a product correlates with it, and the problem does not arise.

benchmarks/search_stress/ measures the cost. Without magnitude slots, on 500 rows with 10% noise, x0*x1*x2 on centred inputs was recovered in 54% of fits with 20 columns, 18% with 100 and 10% with 300 (in every fit on positive inputs), and x0*x1 in 32% with 1,000 columns. A wider beam barely helps: 200 places lifted the 20-column figure to 96% at about nine times the fit time, and the 100-column one only to 26%. A miss mostly ends in no equation and a NoDiscoveriesWarning.

magnitude_slots adds beam slots for candidates whose magnitude tracks the target's. Its default, "auto", adds 10 for regression; 0 turns them off, as the first fit here does:

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
X = rng.uniform(-1, 1, (400, 10))
y = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] * X[:, 2] + rng.normal(0, 0.01, 400)
for slots in (0, 3):
    model = BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, beam_width=10, magnitude_slots=slots).fit(X, y)
    print(slots, model.formulas())

0 []
3 ['(x0 * (x1 * x2))']

The first fit finds nothing and warns NoDiscoveriesWarning.

How the magnitude slots work
  • The score. A candidate c is scored by the absolute correlation of log(1 + |c|/rms(c)) with the same transform of the centred target, where rms is the root mean square. The logarithm turns a product into a sum, so a factor's magnitude tracks the product's even where the factor itself does not correlate with it. The 1 keeps the rows where a product nears zero, and the noise there, from dominating, and it compresses a heavy tail, so that a ratio with a denominator near zero does not score by accident. On more than 1,000 search rows the score is computed on 1,000 of them, evenly spaced, which is plenty to rank a few slots and keeps its cost from growing with the table.
  • The slots. After the beam_width candidates the score keeps, up to magnitude_slots more are kept from the rest, best magnitude score first, under the same redundancy check. They are kept at every depth but the last, since they are there to be built on.
  • The proposals. When the first depth cannot propose every pair of inputs, the inputs are proposed in an order that interleaves their magnitude ranking with their score ranking. The magnitude ranking takes the first place and magnitude_slots / (beam_width + magnitude_slots) of those after it.
  • A part behind a visible term. In x0*x1 + x2 the product does correlate with the target, but hundreds of sums of x2 with another column can outrank it. The search then relies on scoring candidates against the residual left by the inputs, and with more inputs than search rows that residual is empty. The magnitude score is also taken against the residual on the best-scoring columns, at most a quarter as many as the rows, which keeps x0*x1 in view.

With 10 slots the search recovered x0*x1*x2 on centred inputs in every fit with 20, 100 and 300 columns, the centred pair in every fit with 1,000 columns, and x0*x1 + x2 with 300 columns on 250 search rows in 88% of fits, against none without them; it lost no law the search without them found. Fits took 1.2 to 1.7 times as long. Where no such law is hidden it changes little: the main suite's mean held-out score over 24 regression datasets went from 0.885 to 0.884, and the high-dimensional study's from 0.647 to 0.649.

It is for regression only, since a class label has no magnitude to track: "auto" adds no slot for classification, and a positive number raises. The ranking runs inside the search, on the search rows only, so the screen's guarantee is unchanged (see the guarantees page). A law whose parts the magnitude score cannot see either is still out of reach.

docs.title: A weak term beside a dominant one
docs.text:
The search ends by ranking every candidate it kept against the target and keeping the best max_features (beam_width by default). A dominant term fills that ranking with restatements of itself, and a weaker term beside it is cut although the search built it. The residual slots (residual_slots, off by default) add to the ranking the first terms of a greedy forward path through the candidates: each the one that adds most to a least-squares fit of those before it. A restatement adds nothing to the term it restates, so the weaker term comes second.

import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = rng.uniform(1, 5, (2000, 4))
signal = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] / X[:, 2] + 0.5 * np.log(X[:, 3])
y = signal + rng.normal(0, 0.1 * np.std(signal), 2000)
for slots in (0, 10):
    print(BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0, residual_slots=slots).fit(X, y).equation())

y = 0.9929*((x0 / x2) * x1) + 0.1761*((x0 + x3) + (x1 - x2)) - 0.1693*(x0 + (x1 - x2)) - 0.02271   [3 of 50 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 50]
y = 0.9968*((x0 / x2) * x1) + 0.475*log(x3) + 0.03165   [2 of 55 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 55]

The logarithm carries 0.6% of the target's variance. Without the slots, two sums stand in for it.

How the residual slots work
  • The path. It runs over every candidate the search kept, on the search rows (on more than 20,000 of them, that many evenly spaced, and fewer on a wide table, so that the values stay within 64 MiB, though never fewer than 1,000). Gains within a relative 2e-6 of the best are tied, and the simpler expression wins, as in the beam.
  • Near copies. On [1, 5], log(x3), sqrt(x3) and 1/x3 correlate above the redundancy threshold, so a depth keeps one of them and drops the others. Before the final ranking, each path term that is an input column, or has a single operand, adds that column or operand and its transforms by unary_ops to the candidates, so the path chooses among them; one of them can also take a place by score.
  • The count. At most residual_slots terms, and never more than max_features or a quarter of the search rows. A path term replaces a ranked candidate that is a near copy of it, and is dropped if it is a near copy of an earlier path term; every other candidate the score ranked stays, so the screen tests at most residual_slots more candidates than before.

Over 60 fits of that law, with 4 or 10 columns, 500 to 5,000 rows and two noise levels, the slots printed the exact law in 33, the default in none (benchmarks/weak_terms_and_switches/). They are off by default because the path terms explain whatever the leading terms leave, noise included, and the forward step prints some of them as riders. In benchmarks/release_comparison/ they printed a term built only from unrelated columns in 19 of 800 calibration-design fits, where the default printed none, raised the share of riders at a signal-to-noise ratio of 1 from 0.722 to 0.729, and left the held-out score of 8 of the 11 real regression datasets within 0.005, raising one and lowering two. With parsimony_alpha=0.05 beside them the riders go (one design fit of 800, riders 0.064 against 0.061 for the check alone, the generating term in as many fits), and the weak term prints as often. On pure noise the two together printed a term in 4 of 200 fits, against 2 at the default or with the check alone, within the guarantee's q = 0.1. For a law with a weak term, use both:

model = BeamFeatRegressor(residual_slots=10, parsimony_alpha=0.05).fit(X, y)

The slots are for regression only; a positive number raises for classification. The path runs inside the search, on the search rows only, so the screen's guarantee is unchanged.

docs.title: Switches at a threshold
docs.text:
sign (a unary operator; list it in unary_ops) and sign_shift (a fitted one, sign(x + a); list it in fitted_ops) are off by default. With sign, a product with a switch at zero, such as x2*sign(x0), is a candidate like any other, and with sign_shift one with a switch at a fitted threshold, such as x2*sign(x0 - 0.7). sign_shift tries thresholds at the operand's 5% to 95% quantiles, then refines and snaps the threshold as the other fitted operators do their constants (Constants inside expressions).

import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = np.column_stack([rng.uniform(-2, 2, (1000, 2)), rng.uniform(1, 5, (1000, 3))])
y = np.where(X[:, 0] > 0.7, 2.0, -1.0) * X[:, 2] + X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 0.3, 1000)
fitted = ("exp_scaled", "pow", "inv_shift", "log_shift", "sign_shift")
for slots in (0, 10):
    print(BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0, fitted_ops=fitted, residual_slots=slots).fit(X, y).equation())

y = 1.539*(x2 * sign(x0 - 0.7)) + 1.01*(x1 + sign(x0 - 0.7)) - 1.161*(sign(x0 - 0.7) - log(x2)) + 0.3139   [3 of 50 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 50]
y = 1.501*(x2 * sign(x0 - 0.7)) + 0.4993*(x1 + x2) + 0.4915*x1 + 0.002704   [3 of 52 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 52]

The slope in x2 is 2 above the threshold and -1 below it: 0.5 plus 1.5 times the sign. Both fits find the switch term; the rest of the law, x1 and 0.5*x2, is weaker, and a surrogate stands in for it until the residual slots add it. Over 20 fits like these, at thresholds 0 and 0.7 and two noise levels, sign_shift printed the switch in every fit, with R² against the noiseless target of 0.997 to 0.999 (1.000 with the slots), against 0.76 to 0.88 for the default and 0.983 to 0.996 for gradient-boosted trees (benchmarks/weak_terms_and_switches/). sign finds a switch at zero only; sign_shift finds that one too. On the main suite's threshold_step, 3*b*1[a > 1.5], sign_shift raised the held-out score from 0.841 to 0.999; on the other datasets of benchmarks/release_comparison/ it moved held-out score little, raising it on penguins by 0.025 and lowering the classifier's accuracy on breast_cancer by 0.022.

docs.title: Search constraints
docs.text:
max_inputs caps the distinct input columns in one feature: max_inputs=2 admits x0 * log(x0 / x1) but not x0 * x1 / x2. Use it when a feature that mixes many columns would be uninterpretable to you anyway. It is checked as each candidate is constructed, before any numerical work, so a candidate it rules out costs no evaluation and takes no beam slot. search_result_.trace counts them per depth (n_rejected_constraints).

It does not make selection more powerful. The screen's multiple-testing correction runs over the features that reach selection, which the beam already caps at beam_width and max_features however many expressions were proposed; the limit changes which features those are and how long the search takes.

It is off by default (None), and it only ever narrows the search. An expression of depth d combines at most 2^d input columns, so at the default max_depth=2 no feature uses more than four, and max_inputs=4 or more changes nothing; at max_depth=3 the limit matters up to 8. Set it at or above the number of inputs any law you look for needs. A law that needs more cannot be built, and the search returns the best expression within the limit instead:

import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamSearch

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(0.5, 3, (400, 8))
y = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] + X[:, 2] * X[:, 3] + rng.normal(0, 0.1, 400)
for limit in (None, 3):
    search = BeamSearch(max_depth=2, beam_width=30, random_state=0, max_inputs=limit).run(X, y)
    print(limit, search.names[0])

None ((x0 * x1) + (x2 * x3))
3 ((x0 + x2) * sqrt(x1))

On wide data whose signal is spread over many columns, a low limit can still help, because it keeps the beam from filling with combinations of many columns. Compare the held-out score with and without it rather than assuming either way.

docs.title: Speed and memory
docs.text:
On a tall table, max_search_rows runs the search on that many of its rows, drawn at random, while the screen keeps every selection row; see Tall data. The rest of this section is about wide tables.

n_jobs spreads the search over cores, and -1 uses all of them. The workers are threads, since numpy releases the GIL while it scores, or processes for the gradient-boosting scorer, whose model fits do not. Apart from that scorer, a depth with fewer than 4096 candidates is scored in the calling thread, so the setting pays off on wide tables rather than on a handful of columns. It never changes the fit: features, p-values and predictions are identical for every value.

model = BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X, y)

Memory does not grow with the number of candidates either. Each depth is evaluated and scored in chunks of about 8 MiB and only the scores are kept, so a default fit on 1000 columns and 600 rows peaks at about 0.35 GB. BeamSearch(chunk_size=...) sets the chunk size directly, again without changing the result. The exceptions are mutual information, which draws its noise for a whole depth, and a custom scorer that does not declare itself separable: both still receive a depth at once.

The default keeps four terms. The first is the law; each of the others adds a little by fitting noise, and one of them reads d, a column the law does not use. input_test=True tests each column inside each formula and drops that term, but keeps the two built from a, b and c, since those columns do belong. parsimony_alpha=0.05 stops at the law itself, and here, where the target is one compact formula, it is also the most accurate of the three. The screen and its guarantee are the same under all three settings; what differs is how much of the printed equation can be taken at face value.

As a rule, keep the default for prediction, use parsimony_alpha=0.05 for an equation to read or report, and add input_test=True when every column must be shown to matter, at several times the fit time. On real data, whose targets are rarely one compact formula, parsimony_alpha costs some accuracy; the documentation's Choosing a setting page has the measurements.

docs.title: Getting started with beamfeat¶
docs.text:
beamfeat constructs interpretable features from tabular data. Given columns a, b, and c, it searches expressions like log(a), a * b, and (a * b) / c, tests each against the null hypothesis that it is independent of the target, and reports the ones whose null is rejected as readable formulas.

Two things distinguish it from exhaustive feature engineering:

  1. The search is guided. Candidates are scored against the target and only the best are extended, so cost does not compound with expression depth.
  2. Selection is calibrated. A feature is retained only when a test rejects its null under false-discovery-rate control, not when it clears a heuristic threshold.

This notebook covers the basic workflow. Later notebooks cover the search and selection machinery in detail.

docs.title: A problem with a known answer¶
docs.text: We generate data where the target is a known function of the inputs, so we can check whether beamfeat recovers it. The relationship is y = (a * b) / c, which no linear model on the raw columns can represent.

docs.title: Fitting¶
docs.text: BeamFeatRegressor follows the usual scikit-learn interface. The two parameters that matter most are max_depth, which bounds expression complexity, and beam_width, which bounds how many expressions survive each depth.

docs.title: Watching it work¶
docs.text: verbose is a level. 0 is silent, 1 prints a line per stage, and 2 adds per-depth search detail and the strongest certified candidates with their p- and q-values. It is the quickest way to see where a fit spent its effort, and to tell a search that found nothing from a screen that rejected no null.

docs.title: Reading what it found¶
docs.text: This is the part a gradient-boosted model cannot give you. The fitted model exposes both the individual feature formulas and the full equation.

docs.title: Comparing against a linear baseline¶
docs.text: The point of constructing features is to let a simple model fit a relationship it otherwise could not.

docs.title: Using it in a pipeline¶
docs.text: BeamFeatTransformer constructs features without fitting a model, so it composes with any downstream estimator. Because construction happens inside fit, cross-validating the pipeline does not leak information across folds.

docs.title: Classification¶
docs.text: BeamFeatClassifier works the same way, with predict_proba and decision_function available as usual.

docs.title: Choosing a setting¶
docs.text: The default prints the equation that predicts best. Two options change what the equation is for: parsimony_alpha=0.05 asks for a short equation, and input_test=True tests every column inside each formula. The difference shows on a noisier version of the same law, beside eight more columns that play no part in it.

docs.title: What to read next¶
docs.text:
• 02: Search and scoring — how the beam search works, and how the scoring strategies differ in what they detect and what they cost.
  • 03: Selection and units — how false discovery rate control works, why the default is not knockoffs, and how dimensional analysis constrains the search.
  • 04: Reading a fit — what to do when the equation contains columns you did not expect, how to read a fit in which no null was rejected, and how to list, typeset and export the equation.

docs.title: Search and scoring¶
docs.text:
This notebook covers how beamfeat explores the space of expressions, and how the choice of scorer changes what it finds.

The core problem is that expression space is enormous. With 5 input columns, 5 unary operators, and 4 binary operators, exhaustive expansion to depth 3 produces well over a million candidates, and each must be evaluated before it can be judged. Beam search avoids this by scoring candidates as they are generated and extending only the most promising.

docs.title: Running a search directly¶
docs.text: BeamSearch is the layer beneath the estimators. Using it directly is useful when you want to inspect the search rather than fit a model.

docs.title: The trace¶
docs.text: Every search records what happened at each depth. This is how you attribute cost, and how you notice a beam that collapsed or saturated.

docs.title: How beam width controls cost¶
docs.text: Beam width is the parameter that bounds work. Widening it explores more of the space at a cost that grows faster than the width, since each expression in the beam is combined with every expression kept so far; narrowing it risks pruning a parent whose children would have been valuable.

docs.title: How depth controls expressiveness¶
docs.text: Some relationships simply cannot be expressed below a certain depth. (a * b) / c needs depth 2: one step to build a * b, another to divide by c.

docs.title: Workers and memory¶
docs.text:
At the defaults a depth may propose up to 200,000 candidates (max_candidates_per_depth), so the search evaluates and scores a depth in chunks and keeps only the scores; the candidates the redundancy check reaches, usually a small share of the round, are evaluated again. Memory stays bounded however many candidates a depth proposes. chunk_size sets how many candidates make a chunk, by default as many as fit in 8 MiB. Mutual information is the exception: it draws its noise for the whole batch, so it still scores a depth at once.

n_jobs spreads the chunks over joblib workers: threads, since numpy releases the GIL, or processes for gradient boosting, whose model fits hold it. -1 uses every core. A depth of fewer than 4096 candidates stays in the calling thread unless the scorer fits models, since starting workers would cost more than it saves, so on the four-column problem above n_jobs changes nothing. The estimators take the same argument.

Neither setting changes the result, for the scorers that draw random numbers too: no seed depends on a worker or a chunk. On forty columns, where both depths are large enough for workers:

docs.title: Choosing a scorer¶
docs.text:
Four scoring strategies are available, and they differ in what they can detect and what they cost.

  • "correlation" — absolute Pearson correlation against the residual. One dot product per candidate. The default.
  • "spearman" — absolute rank correlation against the same residual, for a sort per column more. Sees any monotone relationship and is insensitive to outlying values.
  • "mutual_information" — nearest-neighbour mutual information. Detects dependence that correlation misses.
  • "gradient_boosting" — measured out-of-fold predictive improvement. Scores what is actually being optimised.

docs.title: Where they agree¶
docs.text: On a relationship whose nonlinearity is captured by the expression itself, the first three find the same thing, and correlation is much the cheapest. Gradient boosting is left out: it fits models for every candidate, which on a round of this size takes far longer still.

docs.title: Where they differ¶
docs.text: Correlation is blind to symmetric relationships. If the target depends on the magnitude of a feature but not its sign, correlation sees nothing while mutual information sees the dependence clearly.

docs.title: Redundancy control¶
docs.text: A beam scored purely on individual merit fills with variants of the same signal. beamfeat scores each candidate against the residual left by what the beam already holds as well as against the target, and ranks it on the larger of the two, so a refinement of a beam member survives while novelty is still rewarded. It also drops a candidate too correlated with one already admitted at the same depth; the final ranking applies the same check across depths.

docs.title: Auditing what the search ruled out¶
docs.text: Candidates excluded during evaluation are recorded rather than silently dropped. This matters when a search returns less than expected: the log tells you whether candidates were outside an operator's domain — a logarithm of a negative value, or a quotient whose denominator comes near zero — numerically invalid, degenerate, copies of a column already there — abs of a column that is never negative is the column itself — or simply never proposed.

def gaussian_design(seed, n=300, n_signal=5, n_noise=20, effect=3.0):
    trial_rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n_features = n_signal + n_noise
    features = trial_rng.standard_normal((n, n_features))
    coefficients = np.zeros(n_features)
    coefficients[:n_signal] = effect
    target = features @ coefficients + trial_rng.standard_normal(n)
    truth = np.zeros(n_features, dtype=bool)
    truth[:n_signal] = True
    return features, target, truth


def realised_fdr(selector_factory, nominal, n_trials=15):
    false_rates, recalls = [], []
    for trial in range(n_trials):
        features, target, truth = gaussian_design(3000 + trial)
        result = selector_factory(nominal, trial).select(features, target)
        if result.n_selected:
            false_rates.append(np.sum(~truth[result.selected]) / result.n_selected)
        else:
            false_rates.append(0.0)
        recalls.append(np.sum(truth[result.selected]) / truth.sum())
    return np.mean(false_rates), np.mean(recalls)


print(f"{'nominal':>8} {'realised FDR':>14} {'power':>8}")
for nominal in (0.05, 0.1, 0.2):
    fdr, power = realised_fdr(
        lambda f, s: PermutationSelector(target_fdr=f, random_state=s, n_permutations=25), nominal
    )
    print(f"{nominal:>8.2f} {fdr:>14.3f} {power:>8.2f}")

Realised FDR tracks the nominal level, and power is full. Two reading notes, both scientifically important. First, FDR is an expectation: individual trials may exceed the level, and a mean over 15 trials carries visible Monte Carlo noise, so values a little above nominal are consistent with control. Second, a well-calibrated test spends its error budget — realised FDR near nominal is the signature of a calibrated procedure, where a realised FDR pinned at zero would signal wasted power.

def engineered_design(seed, n=300):
    trial_rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    a = trial_rng.uniform(1.0, 5.0, n)
    b = trial_rng.uniform(1.0, 5.0, n)
    c = trial_rng.uniform(1.0, 5.0, n)
    columns = [
        a, b, c, np.log(a), np.log(b), np.sqrt(a), 1.0 / a,
        a * b, a / b, b / a, a * c, a - b, a + b, a**2, b**2,
    ]
    return np.column_stack(columns), a * b + trial_rng.normal(0, 0.1, n)

So the practical division of labour: the permutation selector is the default because its validity does not depend on the design at all; fixed-X knockoffs are a strong choice when there are more than twice as many rows as candidates and the noise is roughly Gaussian (the features can be anything); model-X is a last resort for n <= 2p.

One further caveat, measured rather than assumed: the offset parameter dominates knockoff power on narrow designs. offset=1 (knockoff+) requires (1 + #negatives) / #positives <= target_fdr, which cannot be satisfied when there are fewer than 1 / target_fdr features, regardless of signal strength.

docs.title: Selection and units¶
docs.text:
Feature construction proposes far more candidates than any dataset can support. Selection decides which of them are reported, and it is where most automated feature engineering tools are weakest: an importance threshold gives no guarantee about how many reported features are noise, and the expected number of false discoveries grows with the size of the candidate pool.

beamfeat tests each candidate against its own null hypothesis, that the candidate is independent of the target, and selects the candidates whose nulls it rejects. It controls the false discovery rate — the expected proportion of rejected nulls that are true, that is, of selected features that are spurious.

docs.title: The problem, demonstrated¶
docs.text: With a pure-noise target every null is true, so every rejection is a false rejection. A well-calibrated selector should reject almost nothing.

docs.title: Measured calibration¶
docs.text: More usefully: with real signal present, what fraction of the rejections are false? This is the quantity the library claims to control.

docs.title: Knockoffs: two constructions, two sets of assumptions¶
docs.text:
The knockoff filter comes in two forms, and it matters which one you mean.

Fixed-X knockoffs (Barber & Candès, 2015) treat the design as fixed and make no assumption about the distribution of the features — deterministic engineered columns are admissible. The guarantee needs n > 2p and Gaussian noise in y = Xβ + ε. Engineered designs strain it in two ways. Near-duplicate columns drive the construction's s toward zero, the knockoffs become nearly identical to the originals, and the filter loses the ability to tell them apart: a cost in power, not validity. Exact dependence is worse. When the design covariance has an eigenvalue below 1e-6 — a constant column, or one that is a linear combination of others, as a + b is of a and b — the knockoffs of the columns involved can only equal the originals, the lasso's tie-breaking then favours the originals, and that costs validity. beamfeat leaves such columns out of the construction, so they cannot be selected, and names them in its warning.

Model-X knockoffs (Candès et al., 2018) instead assume the features are jointly Gaussian — which engineered features are not: log(a) and a * b are deterministic functions of shared parents. beamfeat only uses this construction when n <= 2p, where the fixed-X construction does not exist, and warns.

beamfeat routes between the two automatically and reports which assumptions are under strain, rather than pretending otherwise.

One thing knockoffs will not do, since the conditional null invites the inference: they cannot prune a term out of an expression. Selection operates on whole candidate columns, so a candidate like noise + (a * b) / c is one column with one null, rejected or not as a whole — switching the selector does not reach inside it. Two levers do: constraining what gets built, which notebook 04 does with units, and testing each column inside a candidate, which the estimators' input_test=True does.

docs.title: End to end¶
docs.text: Putting search and selection together: construct candidates, then keep only those whose nulls the FDR-controlled test rejects.

docs.title: Dimensional analysis¶
docs.text:
If your columns carry physical units, supplying them restricts the search to dimensionally valid expressions. Adding a mass to a length is ruled out at construction time, before any numerical work happens.

This is both a correctness feature and a performance one: it prunes large parts of the search space for free.

docs.title: Units through the estimator API¶
docs.text: The same constraint is available on the estimators via the units argument. The fitted equation is compact because, after FDR screening, the estimator keeps a parsimonious forward-selected subset of the screened features by default (parsimony="forward"); the equation's suffix records how many of the certified terms it printed, and the full screened set with per-candidate p- and q-values is available in selection_report_.

from beamfeat import UnitError
from beamfeat.expression import combine, leaf, transform


# The same expression built with the units above; UnitError if they rule it out.
def with_units(node):
    if node.is_leaf:
        return leaf(node.column, units[node.column])
    children = [with_units(child) for child in node.children]
    if len(children) == 1:
        return transform(node.op, children[0], node.const)
    return combine(node.op, *children)


# Formulas of the whole certified set, not only the pruned equation, that the
# units rule out.
def ruled_out(model):
    full = BeamFeatRegressor(**{**model.get_params(), "parsimony": None, "verbose": 0}).fit(X, y)
    count = 0
    for node in full.features_:
        try:
            with_units(node)
        except UnitError:
            count += 1
    return count, full.n_features_out_


for label, m in (("no units", deep), ("units", gated)):
    count, total = ruled_out(m)
    print(f"certified formulas the units rule out, {label:8s}: {count} of {total}")
