The same over-deep search now returns the clean core. Identical R^2, no parasites — and the effect is not just in the pruned equation: rebuilt with the units, almost every formula the unlabelled search certified is ruled out, most of them for adding a noise column to a dimensioned quantity, and not one of those certified under the units is. That is the general lesson — where a statistical criterion cannot separate two candidates, a structural constraint often can, and it costs nothing because it applies before any numerical work.

Two cautions about what units check.

They enforce that an expression is internally coherent, not that it matches the target's dimension. rho * Q * H / eta is kg·m/s while power is watts, and nothing objects, because g was absorbed. Units rule out nonsense; they will not tell you a factor is missing.

And a dimensionless column is legal almost everywhere. Q / noise_7 is still m³/s, and noise_3 + noise_5 adds one dimensionless column to another, so noise can ride in even under a full labelling, and most of the certified set still mentions one. What units removed is the whole class of violations — adding a bare number to a physical quantity — not every appearance of an irrelevant column.

  (((H * Q) * (Q * rho)) + ((H * Q) * (H - noise_3)))            p=1.78e-04 q=8.33e-04
  (((H + noise_2) * (Q * rho)) + ((Q * rho) * (H - noise_6)))    p=1.78e-04 q=8.33e-04

The gap matters. Parsimony picks a subset by greedy forward selection on the same rows, and a data-dependent subset of an FDR-controlled set does not inherit the guarantee: pruning cannot add false discoveries, but it can raise the false discovery proportion, because the denominator shrinks faster than the numerator, and fdp_inflation_ reports by how much. This is why fdr_controlled_ and fdr_scope_ are two attributes rather than one: the flag is True and the scope is the screened set, not the printed equation. What that costs in fit is small and has been measured — about a thousandth of R^2 across 308 paired fits, held out in every study but one scored in-sample, in benchmarks/PARSIMONY_COST.md. Report the screened set when you need the guarantee; use the equation when you need something to read.

* the fitted model (the forward step stops before the first gain below parsimony_tol=0.001).
The FDR guarantee covers the screened set of 50 terms (line 50), not an equation chosen from this list.

Line 1, marked, is the fitted model. Lines 2 to 4 each add a term that pairs part of the core with a noise column and gains less than 1e-4 of R^2 — the noisy members of the fifty certified formulas, met one at a time, and the reason the forward step stopped after line 1. Complexity counts the nodes of each term's expression tree, plus one per term for its coefficient. The R^2 is in-sample, on the rows screening used, and the lines carry no coefficients because only the marked one has been fitted.

The last line of the output is the one to keep in mind. Every line is a subset of the screened set chosen on the rows screening used, so picking line 3 because it reads well is the same kind of choice the forward step makes, and the guarantee covers it no more than it covers line 1. It covers line 50, the screened set itself, which is the equation parsimony=None fits. The records behind the text are in equations_.

An intercept-only model and a visible warning, which is the correct answer: there was nothing to find, and the constructor declined to invent it. fdr_controlled_ reads False here rather than True — no feature was returned, so nothing carries the guarantee, and the flag describes what came back rather than how hard the procedure tried.

The other case looks identical from the outside but is not. If the candidate pool is large enough that the multiplicity threshold falls below the smallest p-value the permutation budget can produce, the correction cannot reject anything, whatever the data say. The selector detects this and says so in its warning, naming the correction and what to change. So read the warning before concluding there is no signal: an empty selection with a budget warning means that no null could have been rejected at that budget, not that the data are silent.

modules="jax" or modules="torch" (sympy 1.14 or newer) gives the same function on JAX or PyTorch arrays, with jnp.stack(..., axis=1) or torch.stack(..., dim=1) in place of np.column_stack; the coefficients and offset are plain arrays to convert once. Neither library is needed for this notebook, so only NumPy runs here. The column names are valid identifiers, so the symbols carry them unchanged; other names are sanitised, and the expressions' free_symbols show what they became.

Two differences from predict remain. sympy may rewrite an expression into an equivalent form — (H * Q) / (eta / rho) came back as H*Q*rho/eta — so a value can overflow in one and not the other. And a row outside a formula's domain gives whatever the array library gives there, where predict gives NaN and a warning.

docs.title: Reading a fit¶
docs.text:
The three notebooks before this one plant an answer and check that beamfeat finds it. Real fits do not arrive that way. They arrive as an equation you did not write, containing columns you did not expect, with fdr_controlled_ reporting True and no obvious way to tell a triumph from a coincidence.

This notebook is about that moment. We take a problem with a known physical answer, hide it among noise, and then get it wrong on purpose — because the ways it goes wrong are more instructive than the way it goes right, and every one of them has a fix.

docs.title: The problem¶
docs.text:
Hydraulic power of a centrifugal pump, P = rho * g * Q * H / eta: density, gravity, flow rate, head, efficiency. Five real variables, buried among eight columns of plausible-looking nonsense — the ambient noise any plant historian is full of.

Note that g is a constant. Keep an eye on it.

docs.title: Start at the defaults¶
docs.text: Always. The defaults are max_depth=2, beam_width=50.

docs.title: Where did gravity go?¶
docs.text:
It is in the coefficient. g never varies, so no expression containing it can be distinguished from the same expression without it: rho * g is just 9.81 * rho, perfectly collinear with rho, and the redundancy pass keeps one representative of the pair. The scaling then lands in the linear model, which is why the fitted coefficient reads 9.80 rather than 1. Under parsimony=None the same scaling is shared across fifty collinear terms and the leading coefficient reads lower, which is why a constant is easiest to read off the compact fit.

This generalises. A multiplicative constant is absorbed into the coefficient rather than recovered as a symbol, so its absence from the formula is not a miss. Check the coefficient before concluding a factor was lost.

docs.title: Searching harder makes it worse¶
docs.text: Five variables feels like it should need a deep search. Let us give it one: depth 3, and a wider beam. verbose=1 shows what each stage did.

docs.title: Why the flag is still True¶
docs.text:
This is the single most important thing to understand about the guarantee, and it is not a defect.

The null being tested is marginal: is this expression, as a whole, independent of the target? An expression that combines the true core with a noise column is emphatically not independent of the target — the core sees to that — so its null is false and rejecting it is not an error under the criterion. The guarantee bounds the expected share of selected formulas that are pure noise. It says nothing about whether every column inside a formula earns its place.

So fdr_controlled_ = True means what it says, and it is not the property you wanted here. Noise hitchhikes on a strong signal.

docs.title: Depth is not the number of variables¶
docs.text:
The instinct that sent us to max_depth=3 was wrong arithmetic. Depth counts composition levels, not variables, and a binary operator combines any two surviving expressions — not a variable onto a chain.

So rho * Q * H / eta, four variables, is depth two:

depth built 1 (Q * H) and (eta / rho) 2 (Q * H) / (eta / rho)

The default reached it on the first try. The extra level bought no accuracy and gave the search room to decorate a finished answer with noise. Raise max_depth when a target you expect is not being recovered, never speculatively: a deeper search enlarges the candidate pool, every threshold scales as 1/m, and each extra candidate costs power on the ones that matter.

docs.title: Units are the fix¶
docs.text: The screen cannot tell that noise_0 does not belong — as we just saw, the expression is genuinely associated with the target once noise_0 is attached to the core. Physics can. You cannot add a dimensionless number to a quantity in kg·m/s, and beamfeat rules out such expressions at construction, before they are ever scored. (There is a statistical route too: input_test=True tests each column inside each term, as the guide describes.)

docs.title: Cover every column¶
docs.text: Labelling the five real measurements and leaving the noise columns blank looks like the careful thing to do. It is not.

docs.title: The equation is not the certified set¶
docs.text: equation() prints the parsimony subset, and its suffix says so. The guarantee covers the larger screened set, which selection_report_ holds in full, with a permutation p-value and its q-value per candidate.

docs.title: The equation at every size¶
docs.text: The forward step adds terms one at a time and stops when the next would add less than parsimony_tol to R^2. equations() continues it through the whole screened set, one equation per number of terms, so you can see what the stopping point traded away. On the default fit from the start:

docs.title: When nothing is selected¶
docs.text: Two very different situations produce an empty selection, and they have different fixes. Here is the honest one — a target that is pure noise.

docs.title: Writing it down¶
docs.text: latex() typesets equation(), with the same terms, coefficients and note. It returns a string without math delimiters, which a notebook renders with IPython.display.Math:

docs.title: Running it elsewhere¶
docs.text: to_sympy() returns each feature as a sympy expression in real symbols named after the columns, so sympy.lambdify turns the features into a function of plain arrays. Fold the model's standardisation into its coefficients and that reproduces predict:

docs.title: A checklist¶
docs.text:
• Start at the defaults. Raise beam_width when an expected target is missed; raise max_depth only when the target genuinely needs the depth, and count composition levels, not variables.
  • An equation that grew noise terms is a sign you searched too deep, not that you need to search deeper.
  • fdr_controlled_ = True says the guarantee holds: on average at most target_fdr of the certified formulas are noise. It does not say every column in a formula belongs; input_test=True tests that.
  • On a noisy target the default equation can carry terms that each add a little by fitting noise; parsimony_alpha=0.05 stops them, when you want an equation to read rather than the best prediction.
  • Supply units when you have them, for every column.
  • A missing constant is usually in the coefficient.
  • Quote selection_report_ when you need the guarantee; quote equation() when you need a sentence.
  • An equation picked from equations() carries no more of the guarantee than equation() does, and latex(note=False) drops the note, not the caveat.
  • Read the warnings. They distinguish states that look identical from outside.
